Using a recur(cid:173) rent form of the back-propagation algorithm, control is achieved by optimizing the control gains and task-adapted switch parame(cid:173) ters. A mean quadratic cost function computed across a nominal plant trajectory is minimized along with performance constraint penalties. The approach is demonstrated for a control task con(cid:173) sisting of landing a commercial aircraft in difficult wind conditions. paragraphs: The authors propose a neural architecture for controlling nonlinear systems, demonstrated through the task of landing a commercial aircraft in difficult winds. The network is structured around several dynamic linear maps operating in parallel. Nonlinear switches gate these maps, giving the controller a combination of linear components and nonlinear selection behavior.

Training uses a recurrent form of back-propagation to optimize both control gains and switch parameters suited to the task. The objective includes a mean quadratic cost evaluated along a nominal system trajectory, together with penalties for violating performance constraints. Learning therefore considers the desired control behavior and restrictions on how that behavior is achieved.

The aircraft-landing demonstration reports excellent performance while remaining within acceptable damping-response constraints. That qualification matters because a controller’s response over time is part of its usefulness, alongside task completion. The paper’s contribution is a structured learning approach that brings control gains, switching behavior, trajectory cost, and response constraints into one optimization framework.
summary.tldr: A neural controller learns gated linear dynamics to land an aircraft in difficult winds while respecting damping constraints.

title: Neural Networks Structured for Control Application to Aircraft Landing

Using sta(cid:173) tistical physics techniques including the Gibbs distribution, binary decision fields and effective energies, we propose self-organizing PCA rules which are capable of resisting outliers while fulfilling various PCA-related tasks such as obtaining the first principal com(cid:173) ponent vector, the first k principal component vectors, and directly finding the subspace spanned by the first k vector principal com(cid:173) ponent vectors without solving for each vector individually. Using sta(cid:173) tistical physics techniques including the Gibbs distribution, binary decision fields and effective energies, we propose self-organizing PCA rules which are capable of resisting outliers while fulfilling various PCA-related tasks such as obtaining the first principal com(cid:173) ponent vector, the first k principal component vectors, and directly finding the subspace spanned by the first k vector principal com(cid:173) ponent vectors without solving for each vector individually. paragraphs: The paper addresses the sensitivity of self-organizing principal component analysis to outliers. PCA seeks important directions or subspaces in data, but unusual observations can distort the result. The authors propose learning rules intended to retain useful PCA behavior when such observations are present.

Their derivation uses tools from statistical physics, including the Gibbs distribution, binary decision fields, and effective energies. The proposed rules cover several objectives: finding the first principal component, finding the first several components, and directly learning the subspace those components span. The last objective treats the shared subspace as the desired result without requiring each component vector to be solved individually.

Comparative experiments show significant improvements over existing PCA algorithms when the data contain outliers. This supports the value of incorporating resistance to unusual observations into the learning rules themselves. The contribution also spans different forms of the PCA task, connecting robustness to both individual-direction estimation and direct estimation of a multidimensional subspace.
summary.tldr: Statistical-physics-based learning rules make self-organizing PCA more resistant to outliers across component and subspace estimation tasks.

title: Self-Organizing Rules for Robust Principal Component Analysis

paragraphs: Memory-based classifiers must search stored examples to determine which ones best match a query. That search becomes expensive when each comparison uses a complex distance calculation. This paper accelerates searches using tangent distance by arranging the computation into stages, so that the most demanding comparisons are used selectively.

The method recursively searches nested subsets of the prototype database. It increases distance complexity by adding tangent vectors, starting with none and progressing toward the full calculation. It also uses wavelets to examine multiple image resolutions. At each stage, the algorithm estimates classification confidence and can stop before computing more complex distances when confidence is sufficiently high.

Applied to character recognition, the resulting algorithm is reported to be nearly three orders of magnitude faster than calculating full tangent distance against every prototype. The comparison concerns that exhaustive computation. The broader methodological point is that a sophisticated similarity measure need not carry its full cost on every candidate when a hierarchy can resolve many decisions earlier.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical filtering makes tangent-distance character recognition nearly three orders of magnitude faster than full comparisons against every prototype.

title: Efficient Computation of Complex Distance Metrics Using Hierarchical Filtering

paragraphs: A winner-take-all circuit selects the largest input by allowing one cell to remain active while suppressing the others. This paper modifies that familiar computation so that selection also depends on how inputs change over time. The aim is to make the input derivative, or rate of change, an important influence on which cell wins.

The authors add floating-gate transistors to a classic winner-take-all circuit. These components gradually cancel their inputs, introducing adaptation into a circuit otherwise concerned with comparing current input levels. As a result, the history of an input affects its influence on competition: a sustained signal is progressively treated differently from a changing one.

The circuit was designed, fabricated in a standard CMOS process, and tested, with a simplified analysis and experimental data presented. Saliency maps motivate the adaptation, connecting winner selection with the question of which signals attract attention. The contribution is a physical modification of competitive circuitry that adds temporal sensitivity while retaining the basic function of selecting among competing inputs.
summary.tldr: Floating-gate transistors add adaptation to a winner-take-all circuit, making input changes influence winner selection.

title: An Adaptive WTA using Floating Gate Technology

abstract: A one-dimensional visual tracking chip has been implemented us(cid:173) ing neuromorphic, analog VLSI techniques to model selective visual attention in the control of saccadic and smooth pursuit eye move(cid:173) ments. The chip incorporates focal-plane processing to compute image saliency and a winner-take-all circuit to select a feature for tracking. The target position and direction of motion are reported as the target moves across the array. We demonstrate its function(cid:173) ality in a closed-loop system which performs saccadic and smooth pursuit tracking movements using a one-dimensional mechanical eye.

The chip incorporates focal-plane processing to compute image saliency and a winner-take-all circuit to select a feature for tracking. The target position and direction of motion are reported as the target moves across the array. paragraphs: This paper implements a one-dimensional visual tracking chip using neuromorphic analog circuitry. The system models selective visual attention as part of controlling two kinds of eye movement: rapid shifts toward a target and smooth movements that follow it. Attention supplies the choice of which visual feature the system should track.

The chip processes the image at the focal plane to calculate saliency, a signal indicating which features should attract selection. A winner-take-all circuit then chooses a feature for tracking. As that target moves across the sensor array, the chip reports both its position and its direction of motion, linking feature selection to information needed for movement control.

The authors demonstrate the chip in a closed-loop system with a one-dimensional mechanical eye. The system performs both saccadic and smooth pursuit tracking movements. This demonstration matters because the selected visual information is used to drive an actual moving device, completing the connection between sensing, attention, and action. The reported implementation and demonstration operate along one dimension.
summary.tldr: An analog visual chip selects salient features and guides a one-dimensional mechanical eye through rapid and smooth tracking movements.

title: Analog VLSI Circuits for Attention-Based, Visual Tracking

For the special case q = 1, the VC-dimension is 8(ws log d).

paragraphs: The paper analyzes the capacity of neural networks whose activation functions consist of polynomial pieces. It uses VC dimension, a measure of the variety of classification patterns a model family can realize. The goal is to characterize this capacity through architectural quantities rather than through experiments on a particular learning task.

The bounds depend on the number of adjustable parameters, network depth, number of hidden units, maximum number of polynomial segments, and maximum polynomial degree. The authors provide two upper bounds and a lower bound. Taken together, these results describe both limits on representational capacity and capacity that networks in the studied family can attain.

The bounds are tight in the stated cases of constant depth and depth proportional to the number of hidden units. For activations with a single polynomial segment, the abstract gives a tight order involving parameter count, depth, and the logarithm of polynomial degree. The contribution is therefore a quantitative connection between network structure and capacity, with matching characterizations in specified architectural regimes.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the VC dimension of piecewise-polynomial neural networks, obtaining tight characterizations in specified depth regimes.

title: Tight Bounds for the VC-Dimension of Piecewise Polynomial Networks

Inference is based on Bayesian methodology, using a combination of analytical and a variety of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling techniques. The ad(cid:173) vantage of this method is that detection of short time learning effects be(cid:173) tween repeated trials is possible since inference is based only on single trial experiments.
authors: Pedro A. d. F. R. Højen-Sørensen

Inference is based on Bayesian methodology, using a combination of analytical and a variety of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling techniques. The ad(cid:173) vantage of this method is that detection of short time learning effects be(cid:173) tween repeated trials is possible since inference is based only on single trial experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to infer an unobserved psychological state, or underlying neural activity, from an individual fMRI activation trial. The setting is a blocked task paradigm. The central challenge is that the state of interest is hidden, so the model must infer it from the observed time series.

The authors use a hidden Markov model to represent that hidden state over time. Inference follows a Bayesian approach, combining analytical calculations with several Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling techniques. These methods support inference about hidden quantities from the measurements, with the analysis organized around individual trials.

The stated advantage is the possibility of detecting learning effects that occur over short timescales between repeated trials. Because each trial can be analyzed separately, inference can retain distinctions between trials that matter for studying such changes. This makes the method relevant to questions about how responses evolve during repeated task performance. The abstract presents this detection capability as possible, rather than reporting a particular measured learning effect.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian hidden Markov model analyzes individual fMRI trials, making short-term learning effects between trials potentially detectable.

title: Bayesian Modelling of fMRI lime Series

abstract: The bootstrap has become a popular method for exploring model (structure) uncertainty. Our experiments with artiﬁcial and real- world data demonstrate that the graphs learned from bootstrap samples can be severely biased towards too complex graphical mod- els. Accounting for this bias is hence essential, e.g., when explor- ing model uncertainty. We ﬁnd that this bias is intimately tied to (well-known) spurious dependences induced by the bootstrap. The leading-order bias-correction equals one half of Akaike’s penalty for model complexity. We demonstrate the eﬀect of this simple bias-correction in our experiments. We also relate this bias to the bias of the plug-in estimator for entropy, as well as to the diﬀer- ence between the expected test and training errors of a graphical model, which asymptotically equals Akaike’s penalty (rather than one half).

Our experiments with artiﬁcial and real- world data demonstrate that the graphs learned from bootstrap samples can be severely biased towards too complex graphical mod- els. Accounting for this bias is hence essential, e.g., when explor- ing model uncertainty. We ﬁnd that this bias is intimately tied to (well-known) spurious dependences induced by the bootstrap. The leading-order bias-correction equals one half of Akaike’s penalty for model complexity. We demonstrate the eﬀect of this simple bias-correction in our experiments. We also relate this bias to the bias of the plug-in estimator for entropy, as well as to the diﬀer- ence between the expected test and training errors of a graphical model, which asymptotically equals Akaike’s penalty (rather than one half).

paragraphs: Bootstrap sampling is often used to explore uncertainty about a model’s structure. This paper shows through experiments on artificial and real-world data that graphical models learned from bootstrap samples can be strongly biased toward excessive complexity. Consequently, variation among the learned graphs can reflect a systematic distortion introduced by resampling.

The authors connect this distortion to spurious dependencies induced by the bootstrap. Such dependencies can make additional structure appear warranted. They derive a leading-order correction equal to half of Akaike’s model-complexity penalty and demonstrate its effect experimentally. The correction targets the tendency to favor overly elaborate graphs when using bootstrap results to assess structural uncertainty.

The analysis also relates the effect to bias in the plug-in entropy estimator and to the difference between expected training and test errors. These connections distinguish two penalty sizes: the bootstrap correction is half of Akaike’s penalty, while the expected test–training error difference approaches the full penalty asymptotically. Keeping these quantities separate matters when interpreting or correcting the respective biases.
summary.tldr: Bootstrap samples can favor overly complex graphical models, and the paper derives a leading-order correction equal to half of Akaike’s complexity penalty.

title: Bias-Corrected Bootstrap and Model Uncertainty

abstract: A novel approach to combining clustering and feature selection is pre- sented. It implements a wrapper strategy for feature selection, in the sense that the features are directly selected by optimizing the discrimina- tive power of the used partitioning algorithm. On the technical side, we present an efﬁcient optimization algorithm with guaranteed local con- vergence property. The only free parameter of this method is selected by a resampling-based stability analysis. Experiments with real-world datasets demonstrate that our method is able to infer both meaningful partitions and meaningful subsets of features.
originalAbstract: A novel approach to combining clustering and feature selection is pre- sented. It implements a wrapper strategy for feature selection, in the sense that the features are directly selected by optimizing the discrimina- tive power of the used partitioning algorithm. On the technical side, we present an efﬁcient optimization algorithm with guaranteed local con- vergence property. The only free parameter of this method is selected by a resampling-based stability analysis. Experiments with real-world datasets demonstrate that our method is able to infer both meaningful partitions and meaningful subsets of features.

paragraphs: This paper combines finding groups in data with selecting the features used to define those groups. Its approach is a wrapper strategy: features are evaluated through the partitioning algorithm itself. The selection objective directly reflects that algorithm's ability to distinguish the resulting groups, tying the chosen representation to the clustering procedure.

The authors provide an efficient optimization algorithm with a guarantee of local convergence. This gives the procedure a stated convergence property without asserting that it always reaches the globally best solution. The method has one free parameter, which is selected using a resampling-based stability analysis. Repeatedly reconsidering the data through resampling supplies the basis for this parameter choice.

Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that the method can recover both meaningful partitions and meaningful feature subsets. Those are complementary outputs: one describes how observations group together, and the other identifies which variables support the grouping. The contribution is an integrated way to obtain both, with feature selection guided by the clustering algorithm and parameter selection guided by stability.
summary.tldr: A clustering wrapper selects useful features directly, with locally convergent optimization and stability-based tuning.

title: Feature Selection in Clustering Problems

abstract: We provide a worst-case analysis of selective sampling algorithms for learning linear threshold functions. The algorithms considered in this paper are Perceptron-like algorithms, i.e., algorithms which can be efﬁ- ciently run in any reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Our algorithms ex- ploit a simple margin-based randomized rule to decide whether to query the current label. We obtain selective sampling algorithms achieving on average the same bounds as those proven for their deterministic coun- terparts, but using much fewer labels. We complement our theoretical ﬁndings with an empirical comparison on two text categorization tasks. The outcome of these experiments is largely predicted by our theoreti- cal results: Our selective sampling algorithms tend to perform as good as the algorithms receiving the true label after each classiﬁcation, while observing in practice substantially fewer labels.

paragraphs: The paper studies selective sampling: a learner decides whether to request the correct label for each example it encounters. The target models are linear threshold functions, and the algorithms resemble the Perceptron. They can also run efficiently in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, extending the setting in which the analysis applies.

The decision to request a label follows a simple randomized rule based on the margin. The authors provide a worst-case analysis showing that the selective algorithms achieve, on average, the same bounds as their deterministic counterparts while using many fewer labels. The averaging qualification belongs to the theoretical guarantee; it does not promise identical behavior for every individual run.

Experiments on two text categorization tasks broadly match the theoretical picture. The selective methods tend to perform as well as algorithms that receive the true label after every classification, while observing substantially fewer labels in practice. The contribution combines a label-request strategy with theoretical and empirical evidence that much of the full-feedback performance can be retained with reduced labeling.
summary.tldr: Margin-based randomized label requests let Perceptron-like learners match deterministic bounds on average while using substantially fewer labels.

title: Worst-Case Analysis of Selective Sampling for Linear-Threshold Algorithms

abstract: It is becoming increasingly important to learn from a partially-observed random matrix and predict its missing elements. We assume that the entire matrix is a single sample drawn from a matrix-variate t distribution and suggest a matrix-variate t model (MVTM) to predict those missing elements. We show that MVTM generalizes a range of known probabilistic models, and automatically performs model selection to encourage sparse predictive models. Due to the non-conjugacy of its prior, it is difficult to make predictions by computing the mode or mean of the posterior distribution. We suggest an optimization method that sequentially minimizes a convex upper-bound of the log-likelihood, which is very efficient and scalable. The experiments on a toy data and EachMovie dataset show a good predictive accuracy of the model.

paragraphs: Predicting missing entries in a partially observed matrix requires a model of the matrix’s observed and unobserved values. This paper assumes that the entire matrix is one sample from a matrix-variate t distribution. It introduces a predictive model built around that joint assumption, called a matrix-variate t model.

The authors show that the model generalizes a range of existing probabilistic models and automatically performs model selection that encourages sparse predictive models. Computation presents a challenge because the prior is non-conjugate, making prediction through the posterior mean or mode difficult. The proposed solution is an optimization procedure that successively minimizes a convex upper bound of the log-likelihood.

The authors describe this procedure as efficient and scalable, and report good predictive accuracy on toy data and the EachMovie dataset. The contribution joins a matrix-level probabilistic assumption with a practical optimization method. Its findings support the proposed model for missing-entry prediction in those experiments, while the whole-matrix distributional assumption defines how the prediction problem is represented.
summary.tldr: A matrix-variate t model predicts missing entries, encourages sparse predictive models, and uses efficient sequential bound optimization.

title: Predictive Matrix-Variate t Models

abstract: In a multiple instance (MI) learning problem, instances are naturally organized into bags and it is the bags, instead of individual instances, that are labeled for training. MI learners assume that every instance in a bag labeled negative is actually negative, whereas at least one instance in a bag labeled positive is actually positive. We present a framework for active learning in the multiple-instance setting. In particular, we consider the case in which an MI learner is allowed to selectively query unlabeled instances in positive bags. This approach is well motivated in domains in which it is inexpensive to acquire bag labels and possible, but expensive, to acquire instance labels. We describe a method for learning from labels at mixed levels of granularity, and introduce two active query selection strategies motivated by the MI setting. Our experiments show that learning from instance labels can significantly improve performance of a basic MI learning algorithm in two multiple-instance domains: content-based image recognition and text classification.
originalAbstract: In a multiple instance (MI) learning problem, instances are naturally organized into bags and it is the bags, instead of individual instances, that are labeled for training. MI learners assume that every instance in a bag labeled negative is actually negative, whereas at least one instance in a bag labeled positive is actually positive. We present a framework for active learning in the multiple-instance setting. In particular, we consider the case in which an MI learner is allowed to selectively query unlabeled instances in positive bags. This approach is well motivated in domains in which it is inexpensive to acquire bag labels and possible, but expensive, to acquire instance labels. We describe a method for learning from labels at mixed levels of granularity, and introduce two active query selection strategies motivated by the MI setting. Our experiments show that learning from instance labels can significantly improve performance of a basic MI learning algorithm in two multiple-instance domains: content-based image recognition and text classification.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning uses labels attached to groups of examples, called bags. A negative bag is assumed to contain only negative instances, while a positive bag must contain at least one positive instance. This creates an information gap: a positive group label does not reveal which of its members is responsible for that label.

The paper introduces an active learning framework that lets a learner request labels for selected instances inside positive bags. This fits situations where group labels are cheap to obtain but individual labels are possible and costly. The authors develop a method that learns from both levels of labeling and propose two query-selection strategies motivated by the multiple-instance setting.

Experiments in content-based image recognition and text classification show that instance labels can significantly improve a basic multiple-instance learner’s performance. The result supports selectively adding finer-grained supervision to an existing collection of bag labels. The approach matters because it makes the location of labeling effort part of the learning procedure, focusing attention on instances whose status remains unresolved by their group labels.
summary.tldr: Selectively labeling instances within positive bags can improve multiple-instance learning while combining coarse and fine supervision.

title: Multiple-Instance Active Learning

abstract: Randomly connected recurrent neural circuits have proven t o be very powerful models for online computations when a trained memoryless re adout function is appended. Such Reservoir Computing (RC) systems are commonly used in two flavors: with analog or binary (spiking) neurons in the recur rent circuits. Previous work showed a fundamental difference between these two incarnations of the RC idea. The performance of a RC system built from binary neuron s seems to depend strongly on the network connectivity structure. In network s of analog neurons such dependency has not been observed. In this article we investigate this apparent dichotomy in terms of the in-degree of the circuit nodes. Our analyses based amongst others on the Lyapunov exponent reveal that the phase transition between ordered and chaotic network behavior of binary circuits qua litatively differs from the one in analog circuits. This explains the observed decre ased computational performance of binary circuits of high node in-degree. Furt hermore, a novel mean-field predictor for computational performance is intr oduced and shown to accurately predict the numerically obtained results.

paragraphs: Reservoir computing uses a recurrent neural circuit together with a trained, memoryless readout to perform online computations. Such circuits can use analog or binary neurons. Earlier observations suggested that binary circuits depend strongly on their connectivity structure, whereas a comparable dependence had not been observed for analog circuits.

This paper investigates that apparent difference through node in-degree, the number of incoming connections at each node. The analyses include the Lyapunov exponent and examine the transition between ordered and chaotic dynamics. The authors find that this transition differs qualitatively between binary and analog circuits, connecting network dynamics to the observed difference in computational behavior.

The analysis explains the reported reduction in computational performance of binary circuits with high in-degree. The authors also introduce a mean-field predictor of computational performance and show that it accurately predicts their numerical results. Together, these contributions offer an explanation for the observed connectivity effect and a way to predict performance in the studied systems, tying structural differences to the dynamics of the recurrent circuit.
summary.tldr: Different order-to-chaos transitions help explain why high connectivity reduces performance in the studied binary reservoir circuits.

title: On Computational Power and the Order-Chaos Phase Transition in Reservoir Computing

abstract: Imaging techniques such as optical imaging of intrinsic signals, 2-photon calcium imaging and voltage sensitive dye imaging can be used to measure the functional organization of visual cortex across different spatial scales. Here, we present Bayesian methods based on Gaussian processes for extracting topographic maps from functional imaging data. In particular, we focus on the estimation of orientation preference maps (OPMs) from intrinsic signal imaging data. We model the underlying map as a bivariate Gaussian process, with a prior covariance function that reflects known properties of OPMs, and a noise covariance adjusted to the data. The posterior mean can be interpreted as an optimally smoothed estimate of the map, and can be used for model based interpolations of the map from sparse measurements. By sampling from the posterior distribution, we can get error bars on statistical properties such as preferred orientations, pinwheel locations or -counts. Finally, the use of an explicit probabilistic model facilitates interpretation of parameters and provides the basis for decoding studies. We demonstrate our model both on simulated data and on intrinsic signaling data from ferret visual cortex.

summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process model estimates visual-cortex orientation maps and quantifies uncertainty in their spatial features.

title: Bayesian estimation of orientation preference maps

abstract: Efficient coding provides a powerful principle for explaining early sensory coding. Most attempts to test this principle have been limited to linear, noiseless models, and when applied to natural images, have yielded oriented filters consistent with responses in primary visual cortex. Here we show that an efficient coding model that incorporates biologically realistic ingredients input and output noise, nonlinear response functions, and a metabolic cost on the firing rate predicts receptive fields and response nonlinearities similar to those observed in the retina. Specifically, we develop numerical methods for simultaneously learning the linear filters and response nonlinearities of a population of model neurons, so as to maximize information transmission subject to metabolic costs. When applied to an ensemble of natural images, the method yields filters that are center-surround and nonlinearities that are rectifying. The filters are organized into two populations, with On- and Off-centers, which independently tile the visual space. As observed in the primate retina, the Off-center neurons are more numerous and have filters with smaller spatial extent. In the absence of noise, our method reduces to a generalized version of independent components analysis, with an adapted nonlinear "contrast" function; in this case, the optimal filters are localized and oriented.

paragraphs: Efficient coding asks how a sensory system can transmit information under constraints. Earlier tests using noiseless linear models of natural images produced oriented filters resembling responses in primary visual cortex. This paper investigates how the predicted representation changes when the model includes input and output noise, nonlinear responses, and a metabolic cost for firing.

The authors develop numerical methods that jointly learn each model neuron's linear filter and response nonlinearity. The objective balances information transmission against metabolic expense. On natural images, the learned filters have center-surround organization, while the response functions are rectifying. Separate On-center and Off-center populations each cover the visual space.

The Off-center neurons are more numerous and have smaller filters, matching a stated feature of primate retina. These results show that a richer efficient-coding model predicts retinal characteristics. Without noise, the method becomes a generalized form of independent components analysis and instead produces localized, oriented filters, demonstrating that noise changes the model's preferred representation.
summary.tldr: Adding noise, nonlinear responses, and firing costs to efficient coding produces natural-image representations resembling retinal receptive fields.

title: Efficient coding of natural images with a population of noisy Linear-Nonlinear neurons

abstract: This paper studies the problem of accurately recovering a sparse vector $\beta^{\star}$ from highly corrupted linear measurements $y = X \beta^{\star} + e^{\star} + w$ where $e^{\star}$ is a sparse error vector whose nonzero entries may be unbounded and $w$ is a bounded noise. We propose a so-called extended Lasso optimization which takes into consideration sparse prior information of both $\beta^{\star}$ and $e^{\star}$. Our first result shows that the extended Lasso can faithfully recover both the regression and the corruption vectors. Our analysis is relied on a notion of extended restricted eigenvalue for the design matrix $X$. Our second set of results applies to a general class of Gaussian design matrix $X$ with i.i.d rows $\oper N(0, \Sigma)$, for which we provide a surprising phenomenon: the extended Lasso can recover exact signed supports of both $\beta^{\star}$ and $e^{\star}$ from only $\Omega(k \log p \log n)$ observations, even the fraction of corruption is arbitrarily close to one. Our analysis also shows that this amount of observations required to achieve exact signed support is optimal.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse linear regression when measurements include both bounded noise and a sparse corruption vector whose nonzero values may be arbitrarily large. Its extended Lasso uses sparsity information about the regression coefficients and the corruptions simultaneously. The aim is to recover the underlying signal while also identifying the errors affecting individual measurements.

A first result establishes faithful recovery of both vectors through an extended restricted-eigenvalue property of the design matrix. A second analysis considers Gaussian design matrices with independent, identically distributed rows and covariance Sigma. In that setting, the authors establish recovery of the exact signed supports: which entries are nonzero and whether they are positive or negative.

The stated observation requirement is of order k log(p) log(n), even when the corrupted fraction is arbitrarily close to one under the analyzed conditions. The authors also show that the required amount of data for exact signed-support recovery is optimal. This is a particularly strong robustness result, tied to the specified design setting and recovery analysis.
summary.tldr: Extended Lasso jointly recovers sparse regression coefficients and large corruptions, with strong signed-support guarantees under the analyzed design conditions.

title: Robust Lasso with missing and grossly corrupted observations

abstract: Modern applications in sensitive domains such as biometrics and medicine frequently require the use of non-decomposable loss functions such as precision@k, F-measure etc. Compared to point loss functions such as hinge-loss, these offer much more fine grained control over prediction, but at the same time present novel challenges in terms of algorithm design and analysis. In this work we initiate a study of online learning techniques for such non-decomposable loss functions with an aim to enable incremental learning as well as design scalable solvers for batch problems. To this end, we propose an online learning framework for such loss functions. Our model enjoys several nice properties, chief amongst them being the existence of efficient online learning algorithms with sublinear regret and online to batch conversion bounds. Our model is a provable extension of existing online learning models for point loss functions. We instantiate two popular losses, Prec @k and pAUC, in our model and prove sublinear regret bounds for both of them. Our proofs require a novel structural lemma over ranked lists which may be of independent interest. We then develop scalable stochastic gradient descent solvers for non-decomposable loss functions. We show that for a large family of loss functions satisfying a certain uniform convergence property (that includes Prec @k, pAUC, and F-measure), our methods provably converge to the empirical risk minimizer. Such uniform convergence results were not known for these losses and we establish these using novel proof techniques. We then use extensive experimentation on real life and benchmark datasets to establish that our method can be orders of magnitude faster than a recently proposed cutting plane method.

This paper develops an online learning framework for these non-decomposable losses and uses it to build scalable batch solvers.

summary.tldr: An online learning framework enables regret guarantees and scalable stochastic solvers for non-decomposable losses, with convergence under a uniform convergence condition.

title: Online and Stochastic Gradient Methods for Non-decomposable Loss Functions

abstract: We present a new probabilistic model for transcribing piano music from audio to a symbolic form. Our model reflects the process by which discrete musical events give rise to acoustic signals that are then superimposed to produce the observed data. As a result, the inference procedure for our model naturally resolves the source separation problem introduced by the the piano's polyphony. In order to adapt to the properties of a new instrument or acoustic environment being transcribed, we learn recording specific spectral profiles and temporal envelopes in an unsupervised fashion. Our system outperforms the best published approaches on a standard piano transcription task, achieving a 10.6% relative gain in note onset F1 on real piano audio.

paragraphs: This paper converts piano recordings into symbolic musical events using a probabilistic model of how notes produce sound. The model starts with discrete events, represents the acoustic signals they generate, and combines those signals to explain the recording. This follows the structure of piano audio, where multiple notes can sound simultaneously.

Because overlapping sounds are built into the model, inference naturally addresses the source-separation problem caused by polyphony. The system also learns spectral profiles and temporal envelopes specific to the recording without supervision. These describe the frequency content of sounds and how they develop over time, allowing adaptation to the particular instrument or acoustic environment.

On a standard piano-transcription task, the system outperforms the best published approaches cited by the authors. It achieves a 10.6% relative improvement in note-onset F1 on real piano audio, measuring the quality of detecting when notes begin. The result supports combining an explicit sound-generation model with recording-specific adaptation to improve transcription of overlapping piano notes.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic piano model learns recording-specific sounds without supervision and reports a 10.6% relative gain in note-onset F1.

title: Unsupervised Transcription of Piano Music

abstract: Selecting a good column (or row) subset of massive data matrices has found many applications in data analysis and machine learning. We propose a new adaptive sampling algorithm that can be used to improve any relative-error column selection algorithm. Our algorithm delivers a tighter theoretical bound on the approximation error which we also demonstrate empirically using two well known relative-error column subset selection algorithms. Our experimental results on synthetic and real-world data show that our algorithm outperforms non-adaptive sampling as well as prior adaptive sampling approaches.
originalAbstract: Selecting a good column (or row) subset of massive data matrices has found many applications in data analysis and machine learning. Our experimental results on synthetic and real-world data show that our algorithm outperforms non-adaptive sampling as well as prior adaptive sampling approaches.

paragraphs: Large data matrices can be represented using a selected subset of their columns or rows. The central challenge is choosing a subset that preserves the matrix well enough for subsequent analysis. This paper addresses that selection problem through an adaptive sampling algorithm designed to improve existing methods.

The proposed algorithm applies to any column-selection algorithm with a relative-error guarantee. Rather than introducing only a separate selection procedure, it provides a way to strengthen that class of methods. Its theoretical contribution is a tighter bound on approximation error, making the quality of the selected representation more tightly controlled.

The authors also demonstrate the improvement using two established relative-error column-selection algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show better results than non-adaptive sampling and earlier adaptive approaches. Together, the bound and experiments support the value of adaptation in column selection: the method improves a mathematical guarantee and produces corresponding empirical benefits when attached to existing selection algorithms.
summary.tldr: An adaptive sampling algorithm strengthens relative-error column selection, with tighter approximation bounds and improvements on synthetic and real data.

title: Column Selection via Adaptive Sampling

abstract: We propose a new deep architecture for topic modeling, based on Poisson Factor Analysis (PFA) modules. The model is composed of a Poisson distribution to model observed vectors of counts, as well as a deep hierarchy of hidden binary units. Rather than using logistic functions to characterize the probability that a latent binary unit is on, we employ a Bernoulli-Poisson link, which allows PFA modules to be used repeatedly in the deep architecture. We also describe an approach to build discriminative topic models, by adapting PFA modules. We derive efficient inference via MCMC and stochastic variational methods, that scale with the number of non-zeros in the data and binary units, yielding significant efficiency, relative to models based on logistic links. Experiments on several corpora demonstrate the advantages of our model when compared to related deep models.

paragraphs: This paper builds a deep topic model for observations represented as counts. A Poisson distribution describes the observed count vectors, while a hierarchy of hidden binary units supplies multiple layers of latent structure. The architecture is assembled from Poisson Factor Analysis modules.

The key modeling choice is how to specify whether a hidden binary unit is active. Instead of a logistic function, the authors use a Bernoulli-Poisson link. That link enables repeated use of the same factor-analysis building blocks throughout the hierarchy. They also adapt the modules to construct discriminative topic models.

The paper derives both MCMC and stochastic variational inference methods. Their computation scales with nonzero entries in the data and binary units, giving efficiency advantages over models with logistic links. Experiments on several text corpora demonstrate advantages over related deep models. The approach ties its representational design to its computational design: the chosen link supports depth while making inference responsive to sparsity in the modeled quantities.
summary.tldr: A Bernoulli-Poisson link enables deep topic models built from reusable Poisson factor modules with efficient inference that scales with nonzero entries.

title: Deep Poisson Factor Modeling

abstract: Variational approaches are often used to approximate intractable posteriors or normalization constants in hierarchical latent variable models. While often effective in practice, it is known that the approximation error can be arbitrarily large. We propose a new class of bounds on the marginal log-likelihood of directed latent variable models. Our approach relies on random projections to simplify the posterior. In contrast to standard variational methods, our bounds are guaranteed to be tight with high probability. We provide a new approach for learning latent variable models based on optimizing our new bounds on the log-likelihood. We demonstrate empirical improvements on benchmark datasets in vision and language for sigmoid belief networks, where a neural network is used to approximate the posterior.

paragraphs: Variational methods approximate difficult posterior distributions or normalization constants in latent-variable models. Although often useful, their approximation error can be arbitrarily large. This paper addresses that concern by constructing a new class of bounds on the marginal log-likelihood of directed latent-variable models.

The method uses random projections to simplify the posterior. Its distinguishing theoretical claim is that the resulting bounds are tight with high probability. That qualification matters: the guarantee is probabilistic, reflecting the randomized construction. The authors then turn the bounds into a learning approach by optimizing them as objectives for fitting latent-variable models.

The empirical evaluation considers sigmoid belief networks on vision and language benchmarks, with a neural network approximating the posterior. The authors report improvements on these datasets. The contribution therefore joins two aspects of approximate inference: controlling the quality of a likelihood bound and using that bound to learn model parameters. The experiments provide evidence for the approach in the specified model family and application domains.
summary.tldr: Random projections produce marginal log-likelihood bounds that are tight with high probability and improve learning in evaluated sigmoid belief networks.

title: Variational Bayes on Monte Carlo Steroids

abstract: We consider a variant of the multiarmed bandit problem where jobs queue for service, and service rates of different servers may be unknown. We study algorithms that minimize queue-regret: the (expected) difference between the queue-lengths obtained by the algorithm, and those obtained by a genie-aided matching algorithm that knows exact service rates. A naive view of this problem would suggest that queue-regret should grow logarithmically: since queue-regret cannot be larger than classical regret, results for the standard MAB problem give algorithms that ensure queue-regret increases no more than logarithmically in time. Our paper shows surprisingly more complex behavior. In particular, the naive intuition is correct as long as the bandit algorithm's queues have relatively long regenerative cycles: in this case queue-regret is similar to cumulative regret, and scales (essentially) logarithmically. However, we show that this "early stage" of the queueing bandit eventually gives way to a "late stage", where the optimal queue-regret scaling is O(1/t). We demonstrate an algorithm that (order-wise) achieves this asymptotic queue-regret, and also exhibits close to optimal switching time from the early stage to the late stage.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning which servers to use when jobs wait in queues and service rates may be unknown. Its performance measure is queue-regret: the expected difference between the learner’s queue lengths and those of a matching algorithm that knows the true service rates. The focus is therefore the queueing consequence of learning, rather than only accumulated decision losses.

Classical bandit reasoning suggests logarithmic growth, since standard regret bounds also bound queue-regret. The paper shows that this picture describes an early stage when the learner’s queues have relatively long regenerative cycles. In that regime, queue-regret behaves similarly to cumulative regret and grows essentially logarithmically.

Eventually, the system enters a different regime in which optimal queue-regret scales as O(1/t). The expected queue-length gap then decreases with time instead of continuing to accumulate like classical regret. The authors provide an algorithm that achieves this asymptotic order and switches between the early and late stages at a nearly optimal time. The result highlights why queue dynamics change the interpretation and trajectory of learning costs.
summary.tldr: Queue-regret can shift from essentially logarithmic early growth to optimal O(1/t) late decay, and the proposed algorithm attains that asymptotic order.

title: Regret of Queueing Bandits

abstract: Person Re-Identification is the task of matching images of a person across multiple camera views. Almost all prior approaches address this challenge by attempting to learn the possible transformations that relate the different views of a person from a training corpora. Then, they utilize these transformation patterns for matching a query image to those in a gallery image bank at test time. This necessitates learning good feature representations of the images and having a robust feature matching technique. Deep learning approaches, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), simultaneously do both and have shown great promise recently. In this work, we propose two CNN-based architectures for Person Re-Identification. In the first, given a pair of images, we extract feature maps from these images via multiple stages of convolution and pooling. A novel inexact matching technique then matches pixels in the first representation with those of the second. Furthermore, we search across a wider region in the second representation for matching. Our novel matching technique allows us to tackle the challenges posed by large viewpoint variations, illumination changes or partial occlusions. Our approach shows a promising performance and requires only about half the parameters as a current state-of-the-art technique. Nonetheless, it also suffers from false matches at times. In order to mitigate this issue, we propose a fused architecture that combines our inexact matching pipeline with a state-of-the-art exact matching technique. We observe substantial gains with the fused model over the current state-of-the-art on multiple challenging datasets of varying sizes, with gains of up to about 21%.

paragraphs: Person re-identification matches pictures of the same person across cameras. Changes in viewpoint, lighting, and visibility make direct correspondence difficult. The paper proposes two convolutional neural network architectures that combine learned image representations with matching mechanisms designed to handle these differences.

The first architecture extracts feature maps through convolution and pooling, then uses inexact matching between their locations. Searching a wider region in the second representation allows a feature to match even when its location has shifted between views. The authors report promising performance with about half the parameters of a contemporary state-of-the-art technique. However, this flexibility sometimes produces false matches.

The second architecture addresses that stated weakness by fusing the inexact pipeline with an existing exact-matching technique. The two matching approaches provide complementary evidence about whether images show the same person. Across several challenging datasets of different sizes, the fused model delivers substantial gains over the contemporary state of the art, reaching about 21% in the reported comparisons. That figure describes the largest reported gain, not a uniform improvement across datasets.
summary.tldr: Combining flexible spatial matching with exact matching improves person re-identification, with reported gains of up to about 21%.

title: Deep Neural Networks with Inexact Matching for Person Re-Identification

abstract: We consider the Hypothesis Transfer Learning (HTL) problem where one incorporates a hypothesis trained on the source domain into the learning procedure of the target domain. Existing theoretical analysis either only studies specific algorithms or only presents upper bounds on the generalization error but not on the excess risk. In this paper, we propose a unified algorithm-dependent framework for HTL through a novel notion of transformation functions, which characterizes the relation between the source and the target domains. We conduct a general risk analysis of this framework and in particular, we show for the first time, if two domains are related, HTL enjoys faster convergence rates of excess risks for Kernel Smoothing and Kernel Ridge Regression than those of the classical non-transfer learning settings. We accompany this framework with an analysis of cross-validation for HTL to search for the best transfer technique and gracefully reduce to non-transfer learning when HTL is not helpful. Experiments on robotics and neural imaging data demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

Existing theoretical analysis either only studies specific algorithms or only presents upper bounds on the generalization error but not on the excess risk. In this paper, we propose a unified algorithm-dependent framework for HTL through a novel notion of transformation functions, which characterizes the relation between the source and the target domains. We conduct a general risk analysis of this framework and in particular, we show for the first time, if two domains are related, HTL enjoys faster convergence rates of excess risks for Kernel Smoothing and Kernel Ridge Regression than those of the classical non-transfer learning settings. paragraphs: Hypothesis transfer learning incorporates a model trained on a source domain into learning on a target domain. The paper develops a unified framework for analyzing this process while retaining dependence on the learning algorithm. Its central device is a transformation function that describes the relationship between the source and target domains.

The analysis focuses on excess risk, the gap between a learned predictor's risk and the relevant optimum. For kernel smoothing and kernel ridge regression, the authors show faster convergence of excess risk than in classical learning without transfer when the two domains are related. The relationship between domains is therefore a condition supporting the benefit, rather than transfer being universally advantageous.

The framework also includes an analysis of cross-validation for choosing a transfer technique. This selection procedure can return to ordinary learning when transfer is unhelpful. Experiments with robotics and neural imaging data demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. Together, the results connect potential gains from an existing model with a principled mechanism for deciding whether that model actually helps the target task.
summary.tldr: Transformation functions provide a framework for analyzing when a source model accelerates target learning and selecting when to use transfer.

title: Hypothesis Transfer Learning via Transformation Functions

abstract: Word embeddings are an effective tool to analyze language. They have been recently extended to model other types of data beyond text, such as items in recommendation systems. Embedding models consider the probability of a target observation (a word or an item) conditioned on the elements in the context (other words or items). In this paper, we show that conditioning on all the elements in the context is not optimal. Instead, we model the probability of the target conditioned on a learned subset of the elements in the context. We use amortized variational inference to automatically choose this subset. Compared to standard embedding models, this method improves predictions and the quality of the embeddings.

paragraphs: Embedding models learn representations by predicting an observation from its context. In language, the observation can be a word and the context other words; in recommendation, both can be items. This paper examines a modeling choice within that setup: whether every available context element should participate in predicting the target.

The authors show that using the entire context is not optimal and instead learn a subset on which to condition the target probability. They use amortized variational inference to choose that subset automatically. Context selection therefore becomes part of the learned probabilistic model, connecting the representation task with the decision about which surrounding observations to use.

Compared with standard embedding models, the proposed method improves both predictions and embedding quality. These findings indicate that selecting context can benefit the representations themselves, as well as the immediate prediction task. The contribution is a way to learn what information to condition on within the embedding framework, rather than treating the supplied context as uniformly useful.
summary.tldr: Learning which context elements to use improves predictions and representation quality over standard embedding models.

title: Context Selection for Embedding Models

abstract: Gradient matching is a promising tool for learning parameters and state dynamics of ordinary differential equations. It is a grid free inference approach, which, for fully observable systems is at times competitive with numerical integration. However, for many real-world applications, only sparse observations are available or even unobserved variables are included in the model description. In these cases most gradient matching methods are difficult to apply or simply do not provide satisfactory results. That is why, despite the high computational cost, numerical integration is still the gold standard in many applications. Using an existing gradient matching approach, we propose a scalable variational inference framework which can infer states and parameters simultaneously, offers computational speedups, improved accuracy and works well even under model misspecifications in a partially observable system.

paragraphs: Ordinary differential equations describe systems whose states evolve over time, but learning their parameters and hidden states can be computationally demanding. Gradient matching offers a grid-free inference approach that can sometimes compete with numerical integration when the system is fully observed. Sparse observations and entirely unobserved variables make that approach much harder to use effectively.

This paper builds on an existing gradient matching method to develop a scalable variational inference framework. The framework infers system states and parameters simultaneously, addressing the coupled problem of determining how a system behaves and what values its unobserved states take. This focus targets situations where many existing gradient matching methods are difficult to apply or give unsatisfactory results.

The authors report computational speedups and improved accuracy, along with good performance under model misspecification in a partially observable system. Those findings support extending gradient matching to more demanding observation settings. They also offer an alternative inference route in applications where numerical integration remains common despite its substantial computational cost.
summary.tldr: A variational gradient matching framework jointly infers dynamical states and parameters, with reported speed and accuracy benefits under partial observability.

title: Scalable Variational Inference for Dynamical Systems

abstract: Despite their impressive performance on diverse tasks, neural networks fail catastrophically in the presence of adversarial inputs—imperceptibly but adversarially perturbed versions of natural inputs. We have witnessed an arms race between defenders who attempt to train robust networks and attackers who try to construct adversarial examples. One promise of ending the arms race is developing certified defenses, ones which are provably robust against all attackers in some family. These certified defenses are based on convex relaxations which construct an upper bound on the worst case loss over all attackers in the family. Previous relaxations are loose on networks that are not trained against the respective relaxation. In this paper, we propose a new semidefinite relaxation for certifying robustness that applies to arbitrary ReLU networks. We show that our proposed relaxation is tighter than previous relaxations and produces meaningful robustness guarantees on three different foreign networks whose training objectives are agnostic to our proposed relaxation.

paragraphs: Adversarial perturbations can cause neural networks to fail even when the modified input appears nearly unchanged. Certified defenses seek mathematical guarantees covering every attacker within a specified family. One route is to upper-bound the worst possible loss, so the guarantee depends on how accurately that bound captures the network's behavior.

This paper introduces a semidefinite relaxation for certifying robustness of arbitrary ReLU networks. A relaxation makes the certification problem more tractable while bounding the original worst case. The authors show that their relaxation is tighter than previous alternatives, addressing loose bounds that can make otherwise relevant certificates uninformative.

A central result is that the method produces meaningful guarantees on three networks whose training objectives were not designed around this relaxation. This matters because earlier relaxations can be loose when applied to networks trained without them. The guarantees still concern the specified attacker family; applicability to arbitrary ReLU networks does not mean that every such network is robust or will receive a strong certificate.
summary.tldr: A tighter semidefinite relaxation provides meaningful robustness certificates for three ReLU networks trained without using that relaxation.

title: Semidefinite relaxations for certifying robustness to adversarial examples

abstract: A fundamental challenge in imperfect-information games is that states do not have well-defined values. As a result, depth-limited search algorithms used in single-agent settings and perfect-information games do not apply. This paper introduces a principled way to conduct depth-limited solving in imperfect-information games by allowing the opponent to choose among a number of strategies for the remainder of the game at the depth limit. Each one of these strategies results in a different set of values for leaf nodes. This forces an agent to be robust to the different strategies an opponent may employ. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by building a master-level heads-up no-limit Texas hold'em poker AI that defeats two prior top agents using only a 4-core CPU and 16 GB of memory. Developing such a powerful agent would have previously required a supercomputer.

paragraphs: Searching only partway through a game requires evaluating positions at the search boundary. In games with hidden information, those positions do not have a single well-defined value independent of strategic choices. This prevents the direct application of depth-limited methods used in single-agent problems and games where all information is visible.

The paper handles the boundary by allowing the opponent to choose among several strategies for the rest of the game. Each continuation strategy produces a different collection of values for the leaf positions. Solving against these alternatives forces the agent to account for multiple possible opponent behaviors when deciding how to act before the boundary.

The authors demonstrate the method in a heads-up no-limit Texas hold’em agent that reaches master-level play and defeats two previous top agents. It runs using a four-core CPU and 16 GB of memory. The result illustrates how a principled treatment of uncertain continuation values can support strong play with modest computing resources; the abstract states that comparable agent development previously required a supercomputer.
summary.tldr: Considering multiple opponent continuations enables depth-limited solving in hidden-information games and supports a strong poker agent on modest hardware.

title: Depth-Limited Solving for Imperfect-Information Games

abstract: Human scene understanding uses a variety of visual and non-visual cues to perform inference on object types, poses, and relations. Physics is a rich and universal cue which we exploit to enhance scene understanding. We integrate the physical cue of stability into the learning process using a REINFORCE approach coupled to a physics engine, and apply this to the problem of producing the 3D bounding boxes and poses of objects in a scene. We first show that applying physics supervision to an existing scene understanding model increases performance, produces more stable predictions, and allows training to an equivalent performance level with fewer annotated training examples. We then present a novel architecture for 3D scene parsing named Prim R-CNN, learning to predict bounding boxes as well as their 3D size, translation, and rotation. With physics supervision, Prim R-CNN outperforms existing scene understanding approaches on this problem. Finally, we show that applying physics supervision on unlabeled real images improves real domain transfer of models training on synthetic data.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene involves more than recognizing visual patterns: predicted objects should also form a physically plausible arrangement. This paper uses physical stability as a learning signal for estimating three-dimensional object boxes and poses. It couples a physics engine with a REINFORCE approach so that stability can influence the scene-understanding model during training.

They report better performance, more stable predictions, and the ability to reach equivalent performance using fewer annotated examples. They then introduce Prim R-CNN, an architecture that predicts bounding boxes together with three-dimensional size, translation, and rotation. Across these results, physics supplies information beyond explicit object annotations, helping connect geometric predictions to a property of the scene that can be evaluated through physical behavior.
summary.tldr: Physics-based stability supervision improves 3D scene parsing, annotation efficiency, and synthetic-to-real transfer in the reported experiments.

title: Learning to Exploit Stability for 3D Scene Parsing

abstract: We introduce a new convex optimization problem, termed quadratic decomposable submodular function minimization. The problem is closely related to decomposable submodular function minimization and arises in many learning on graphs and hypergraphs settings, such as graph-based semi-supervised learning and PageRank. We approach the problem via a new dual strategy and describe an objective that may be optimized via random coordinate descent (RCD) methods and projections onto cones. We also establish the linear convergence rate of the RCD algorithm and develop efficient projection algorithms with provable performance guarantees. Numerical experiments in semi-supervised learning on hypergraphs confirm the efficiency of the proposed algorithm and demonstrate the significant improvements in prediction accuracy with respect to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces quadratic decomposable submodular function minimization, a convex optimization problem connected to learning on graphs and hypergraphs. Relevant settings include graph-based semi-supervised learning and PageRank. Its contribution is to identify this optimization formulation and develop an efficient method for solving it, with both convergence analysis and learning experiments.

The authors approach the problem through a new dual formulation. This produces an objective that can be optimized using random coordinate descent together with projections onto cones. They establish a linear convergence rate for the coordinate descent algorithm and develop efficient projection procedures with provable performance guarantees, addressing both the outer optimization and its necessary subproblems.

Numerical experiments focus on semi-supervised learning with hypergraphs. They confirm the algorithm's efficiency and show significant prediction-accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art methods in those experiments. These results connect the mathematical formulation to a practical learning outcome: the proposed optimization machinery supports effective prediction, as well as providing guarantees about how the solver progresses.
summary.tldr: A new convex formulation for graph and hypergraph learning comes with efficient projection algorithms and a linearly convergent coordinate descent solver.

title: Quadratic Decomposable Submodular Function Minimization

abstract: Online portfolio selection is a sequential decision-making problem in which a learner repetitively selects a portfolio over a set of assets, aiming to maximize long-term return. In this paper, we study the problem with the cardinality constraint that the number of assets in a portfolio is restricted to be at most k, and consider two scenarios: (i) in the full-feedback setting, the learner can observe price relatives (rates of return to cost) for all assets, and (ii) in the bandit-feedback setting, the learner can observe price relatives only for invested assets. We propose efficient algorithms for these scenarios that achieve sublinear regrets. We also provide regret (statistical) lower bounds for both scenarios which nearly match the upper bounds when k is a constant. In addition, we give a computational lower bound which implies that no algorithm maintains both computational efficiency, as well as a small regret upper bound.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential portfolio selection when each portfolio may contain at most k assets. The learner repeatedly allocates investments while aiming for strong long-term returns. The cardinality restriction makes the choice of which assets to include an explicit part of the learning problem.

The authors consider two information settings. Under full feedback, the learner observes return-to-cost ratios for every asset. Under bandit feedback, it observes those ratios only for assets it invested in. They give efficient algorithms with sublinear regret in both cases, meaning the regret bounds grow more slowly than the number of rounds.

Statistical lower bounds nearly match the upper bounds when k is constant, showing that the guarantees approach the limits identified by the analysis in that setting. A separate computational lower bound establishes a tension between efficiency and obtaining a small regret upper bound. Together, the results distinguish what limited observations make statistically difficult from what the portfolio-selection problem makes computationally difficult.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sublinear-regret algorithms for portfolios with limited asset counts and establishes statistical and computational limits in two feedback settings.

title: Regret Bounds for Online Portfolio Selection with a Cardinality Constraint

abstract: We propose a sparse and low-rank tensor regression model to relate a univariate outcome to a feature tensor, in which each unit-rank tensor from the CP decomposition of the coefficient tensor is assumed to be sparse. This structure is both parsimonious and highly interpretable, as it implies that the outcome is related to the features through a few distinct pathways, each of which may only involve subsets of feature dimensions. We take a divide-and-conquer strategy to simplify the task into a set of sparse unit-rank tensor regression problems. To make the computation efficient and scalable, for the unit-rank tensor regression, we propose a stagewise estimation procedure to efficiently trace out its entire solution path. We show that as the step size goes to zero, the stagewise solution paths converge exactly to those of the corresponding regularized regression. The superior performance of our approach is demonstrated on various real-world and synthetic examples.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction of a single outcome from features arranged as a multidimensional tensor. Its regression model gives the coefficient tensor both low rank and sparsity. Specifically, it assumes that each unit-rank component in a CP decomposition is sparse. This describes the relationship through a small collection of components, each involving only selected feature dimensions.

That structure offers an interpretation of prediction through a few distinct pathways. It also creates a computational strategy: divide the overall estimation problem into sparse unit-rank tensor regression problems. For these smaller problems, the authors introduce a stagewise procedure that traces a solution path, covering the progression of fitted models associated with regularized regression.

The theoretical result connects this incremental procedure to the regularized formulation: as the step size approaches zero, their solution paths converge exactly. That is a limiting statement about the paths, rather than an assertion that every finite step size gives identical results. Experiments on synthetic and real-world examples report superior performance, supporting the combination of compact structure, interpretability, and efficient estimation.
summary.tldr: Sparse, low-rank tensor regression expresses predictions through a few interpretable pathways and uses stagewise estimation to compute regularization paths efficiently.

title: Boosted Sparse and Low-Rank Tensor Regression

abstract: Neural models operating over structured spaces such as knowledge graphs require a continuous embedding of the discrete elements of this space (such as entities) as well as the relationships between them. Relational embeddings with high expressivity, however, have high model complexity, making them computationally difficult to train. We propose a new family of embeddings for knowledge graphs that interpolate between a method with high model complexity and one, namely Holographic embeddings (HolE), with low dimensionality and high training efficiency. This interpolation, termed HolEx, is achieved by concatenating several linearly perturbed copies of original HolE. We formally characterize the number of perturbed copies needed to provably recover the full entity-entity or entity-relation interaction matrix, leveraging ideas from Haar wavelets and compressed sensing. In practice, using just a handful of Haar-based or random perturbation vectors results in a much stronger knowledge completion system. On the Freebase FB15K dataset, HolEx outperforms originally reported HolE by 14.7\% on the HITS@10 metric, and the current path-based state-of-the-art method, PTransE, by 4\% (absolute).

paragraphs: Knowledge graph models represent discrete entities and relationships with continuous embeddings. Richer representations can capture more interactions, but their complexity can make training difficult. This paper introduces HolEx, a family of embeddings that connects efficient, low-dimensional Holographic embeddings with a more complex representation, providing a way to expand expressive capacity.

These results support expanding a compact embedding through multiple perturbations as an effective approach on the evaluated dataset.
summary.tldr: HolEx expands efficient holographic embeddings with perturbed copies, strengthening knowledge completion and enabling theoretical guarantees about representable interactions.

title: Expanding Holographic Embeddings for Knowledge Completion

abstract: We introduce the Kronecker factored online Laplace approximation for overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks. The method is grounded in a Bayesian online learning framework, where we recursively approximate the posterior after every task with a Gaussian, leading to a quadratic penalty on changes to the weights. The Laplace approximation requires calculating the Hessian around a mode, which is typically intractable for modern architectures. In order to make our method scalable, we leverage recent block-diagonal Kronecker factored approximations to the curvature. Our algorithm achieves over 90% test accuracy across a sequence of 50 instantiations of the permuted MNIST dataset, substantially outperforming related methods for overcoming catastrophic forgetting.

The method is grounded in a Bayesian online learning framework, where we recursively approximate the posterior after every task with a Gaussian, leading to a quadratic penalty on changes to the weights. The Laplace approximation requires calculating the Hessian around a mode, which is typically intractable for modern architectures. In order to make our method scalable, we leverage recent block-diagonal Kronecker factored approximations to the curvature.
