paragraphs: Neural networks can lose previously learned capabilities when trained on successive tasks, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. This paper approaches the problem through Bayesian online learning. After each task, it approximates the posterior distribution over network weights with a Gaussian and carries that approximation forward into learning the next task.

The resulting procedure introduces a quadratic penalty on weight changes. Constructing the Laplace approximation requires curvature information around a mode, normally involving a Hessian that is impractical to compute for modern networks. The authors make the method scalable through block-diagonal, Kronecker-factored approximations to this curvature.

This design connects information retained from earlier tasks with a structured, computationally manageable constraint on later weight updates. In experiments, the algorithm achieves more than 90% test accuracy across a sequence of 50 versions of permuted MNIST and substantially outperforms related methods for catastrophic forgetting. The result supports the approach on that sequential benchmark, while the methodological contribution is the scalable online approximation used to retain previous learning.
summary.tldr: A scalable structured Gaussian approximation carries information between tasks to reduce catastrophic forgetting in neural networks.

title: Online Structured Laplace Approximations for Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting

abstract: We consider the black-box adversarial setting, where the adversary has to generate adversarial perturbations without access to the target models to compute gradients. Previous methods tried to approximate the gradient either by using a transfer gradient of a surrogate white-box model, or based on the query feedback. However, these methods often suffer from low attack success rates or poor query efficiency since it is non-trivial to estimate the gradient in a high-dimensional space with limited information. To address these problems, we propose a prior-guided random gradient-free (P-RGF) method to improve black-box adversarial attacks, which takes the advantage of a transfer-based prior and the query information simultaneously. The transfer-based prior given by the gradient of a surrogate model is appropriately integrated into our algorithm by an optimal coefficient derived by a theoretical analysis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method requires much fewer queries to attack black-box models with higher success rates compared with the alternative state-of-the-art methods.

To address these problems, we propose a prior-guided random gradient-free (P-RGF) method to improve black-box adversarial attacks, which takes the advantage of a transfer-based prior and the query information simultaneously. paragraphs: A black-box adversarial attack must find input changes that fool a model without directly computing that model’s gradients. Two available clues are gradients from an accessible surrogate model and feedback obtained by querying the target. Either clue alone can be inadequate: estimating a useful direction in a high-dimensional input space is difficult when information is limited.

The proposed prior-guided random gradient-free method, P-RGF, combines these two information sources. A surrogate gradient supplies a transfer-based prior about promising directions, while target queries contribute information about the actual model being attacked. The authors derive an optimal coefficient through theoretical analysis to integrate the prior into the algorithm. This makes the combination an analyzed part of the method rather than an arbitrary weighting.

Experiments report substantially fewer target queries and higher attack success rates than alternative leading methods. The findings support using transferable information to guide query-based gradient estimation. They also show that surrogate knowledge and target feedback can be complementary: the method exploits both within the same attack procedure.
summary.tldr: P-RGF combines surrogate gradients with target-query feedback to improve black-box attack success while using substantially fewer queries in experiments.

title: Improving Black-box Adversarial Attacks with a Transfer-based Prior

abstract: Super resolution (SR) methods typically assume that the low-resolution (LR) image was downscaled from the unknown high-resolution (HR) image by a fixed `ideal’ downscaling kernel (e.g. Bicubic downscaling). However, this is rarely the case in real LR images, in contrast to synthetically generated SR datasets. When the assumed downscaling kernel deviates from the true one, the performance of SR methods significantly deteriorates. This gave rise to Blind-SR - namely, SR when the downscaling kernel ( SR-kernel’’) is unknown. It was further shown that the true SR-kernel is the one that maximizes the recurrence of patches across scales of the LR image. In this paper we show how this powerful cross-scale recurrence property can be realized using Deep Internal Learning. We introduce KernelGAN’’, an image-specific Internal-GAN, which trains solely on the LR test image at test time, and learns its internal distribution of patches. Its Generator is trained to produce a downscaled version of the LR test image, such that its Discriminator cannot distinguish between the patch distribution of the downscaled image, and the patch distribution of the original LR image. The Generator, once trained, constitutes the downscaling operation with the correct image-specific SR-kernel. KernelGAN is fully unsupervised, requires no training data other than the input image itself, and leads to state-of-the-art results in Blind-SR when plugged into existing SR algorithms.

paragraphs: Super-resolution methods often assume a particular process converted a high-resolution image into its low-resolution input. Real images frequently depart from that assumed process, and the mismatch can substantially damage reconstruction quality. This paper tackles blind super-resolution by estimating the image’s unknown downscaling kernel from the low-resolution image itself.

KernelGAN uses the recurrence of small image patches across scales as its learning signal. It trains a separate adversarial model on the input image at test time. The generator produces a further-downscaled image, while the discriminator tries to distinguish its patches from patches in the original input. Training encourages the two patch distributions to become indistinguishable.

The trained generator supplies the image-specific downscaling operation that an existing super-resolution algorithm can then use. The method is unsupervised and needs no training images beyond the input being processed. The authors report state-of-the-art blind super-resolution results when combining this kernel estimator with existing reconstruction algorithms, demonstrating the practical value of learning how an image was downscaled.
summary.tldr: KernelGAN estimates an image’s downscaling kernel by learning recurring patch patterns within that image, improving blind super-resolution.

title: Blind Super-Resolution Kernel Estimation using an Internal-GAN

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown remarkable results in modeling complex distributions, but their evaluation remains an unsettled issue. Evaluations are essential for: (i) relative assessment of different models and (ii) monitoring the progress of a single model throughout training. The latter cannot be determined by simply inspecting the generator and discriminator loss curves as they behave non-intuitively. We leverage the notion of duality gap from game theory to propose a measure that addresses both (i) and (ii) at a low computational cost. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of this measure to rank different GAN models and capture the typical GAN failure scenarios, including mode collapse and non-convergent behaviours. This evaluation metric also provides meaningful monitoring on the progression of the loss during training. It highly correlates with FID on natural image datasets, and with domain specific scores for text, sound and cosmology data where FID is not directly suitable. In particular, our proposed metric requires no labels or a pretrained classifier, making it domain agnostic.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative adversarial network involves two different questions: which model performs better, and whether one model is improving during training. The generator and discriminator losses do not answer these questions reliably because their behavior can be difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a shared measure for both purposes, based on the game-theoretic notion of a duality gap.

The approach treats evaluation as a property of the interaction between the generator and discriminator. Its practical attraction is that it requires neither labeled examples nor a pretrained classifier. That removes dependencies that can make an evaluation method suitable for images but difficult to apply to other kinds of generated data.

Experiments show that the measure can rank GANs and detect familiar failures, including missing modes and training that does not converge. It correlates strongly with FID on natural images and with specialized scores for text, sound, and cosmology data. These findings support its use as a low-cost monitoring tool across the tested domains.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic evaluation measure monitors GAN training and compares models without labels or a pretrained classifier.

title: A Domain Agnostic Measure for Monitoring and Evaluating GANs

abstract: Can a stable matching that achieves high equity among the two sides of a market be reached in quadratic time? The Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm finds a stable matching that is biased in favor of one side; optimizing apt equity measures is strongly NP-hard. A proposed approximation algorithm offers a guarantee only with respect to the DA solutions. Recent work introduced Deferred Acceptance with Compensation Chains (DACC), a class of algorithms that can reach any stable matching in O(n^4) time, but did not propose a way to achieve good equity. In this paper, we propose an alternative that is computationally simpler and achieves high equity too. We introduce Monotonic Deferred Acceptance (MDA), a class of algorithms that progresses monotonically towards a stable matching; we couple MDA with a mechanism we call Strongly Deferred Acceptance (SDA), to build an algorithm that reaches an equitable stable matching in quadratic time; we amend this algorithm with a few low-cost local search steps to what we call Deferred Local Search (DLS), and demonstrate experimentally that it outperforms previous solutions in terms of equity measures and matches the most efficient ones in runtime.

paragraphs: Stable matching methods must balance computational efficiency with how fairly outcomes treat the two sides of a market. Deferred Acceptance produces a stable outcome but favors one side. Optimizing suitable equity measures is strongly NP-hard, so the paper seeks a practical way to obtain high equity without the cost of exact equity optimization.

The authors introduce Monotonic Deferred Acceptance, a family of algorithms that moves monotonically toward a stable matching. They combine it with a mechanism called Strongly Deferred Acceptance to obtain an equitable stable matching in quadratic time. This gives a computationally simpler route than a previously described class capable of reaching any stable matching in fourth-order polynomial time.

A further variant, Deferred Local Search, adds a small number of inexpensive local search steps. Experiments show that this variant improves equity measures over previous solutions while matching the runtime of the most efficient methods. The result is an efficient approach to better-balanced stable outcomes; the reported equity improvements do not amount to solving the NP-hard equity optimization problem exactly.
summary.tldr: A quadratic-time stable matching method, enhanced with inexpensive local search, achieves strong empirical equity without sacrificing runtime.

title: Equitable Stable Matchings in Quadratic Time

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs), which learn the representation of a node by aggregating its neighbors, have become an effective computational tool in downstream applications. Over-smoothing is one of the key issues which limit the performance of GNNs as the number of layers increases. It is because the stacked aggregators would make node representations converge to indistinguishable vectors. Several attempts have been made to tackle the issue by bringing linked node pairs close and unlinked pairs distinct. However, they often ignore the intrinsic community structures and would result in sub-optimal performance. The representations of nodes within the same community/class need be similar to facilitate the classification, while different classes are expected to be separated in embedding space. To bridge the gap, we introduce two over-smoothing metrics and a novel technique, i.e., differentiable group normalization (DGN). It normalizes nodes within the same group independently to increase their smoothness, and separates node distributions among different groups to significantly alleviate the over-smoothing issue. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that DGN makes GNN models more robust to over-smoothing and achieves better performance with deeper GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks repeatedly combine information from neighboring nodes. As layers accumulate, these representations can become too similar to distinguish, a problem known as over-smoothing. The paper argues that addressing this solely through linked and unlinked node pairs can overlook community structure, where some similarity is useful and some separation is necessary.

The authors introduce two measures of over-smoothing and differentiable group normalization. The normalization treats each group independently, encouraging smooth representations within a group while separating distributions across groups. This reflects the classification goal: nodes sharing a community or class should have related representations, while different classes should remain distinguishable.

Experiments on real-world datasets show improved resistance to over-smoothing and better performance with deeper graph networks. The contribution is therefore more selective than simply discouraging all similarity between nodes. It organizes similarity around groups, preserving the distinction between useful agreement within a group and the loss of information caused by different groups becoming indistinguishable.
summary.tldr: Differentiable group normalization reduces over-smoothing by encouraging similarity within node groups while keeping different groups separated.

title: Towards Deeper Graph Neural Networks with Differentiable Group Normalization

abstract: Normalizing flows are a class of probabilistic generative models which allow for both fast density computation and efficient sampling and are effective at modelling complex distributions like images. A drawback among current methods is their significant training cost, sometimes requiring months of GPU training time to achieve state-of-the-art results. This paper introduces Wavelet Flow, a multi-scale, normalizing flow architecture based on wavelets. A Wavelet Flow has an explicit representation of signal scale that inherently includes models of lower resolution signals and conditional generation of higher resolution signals, i.e., super resolution. A major advantage of Wavelet Flow is the ability to construct generative models for high resolution data (e.g., 1024 × 1024 images) that are impractical with previous models. Furthermore, Wavelet Flow is competitive with previous normalizing flows in terms of bits per dimension on standard (low resolution) benchmarks while being up to 15× faster to train.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows are generative models that support efficient sampling and fast density computation, but training them on complex images can be expensive. This paper introduces Wavelet Flow to reduce that cost and make higher-resolution modeling practical. Its architecture uses wavelets to organize the generative model around explicit signal scales.

The multiscale representation naturally includes models for lower-resolution signals and conditional generation of higher-resolution signals. This gives the architecture a built-in connection to super resolution: higher-resolution content is modeled in relation to lower-resolution content. Scale is therefore an explicit part of the model’s organization, tying together coarse signals and their finer detail.

The authors demonstrate generative modeling of high-resolution data, including 1024-by-1024 images, described as impractical for previous models. On standard low-resolution benchmarks, Wavelet Flow remains competitive with earlier normalizing flows in bits per dimension while training up to 15 times faster. The results support its combination of reduced training cost and competitive density modeling in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Wavelet Flow explicitly models image scales to enable high-resolution generation and up to 15-fold faster training.

title: Wavelet Flow: Fast Training of High Resolution Normalizing Flows

abstract: Stochastic Approximation (SA) is a popular approach for solving fixed-point equations where the information is corrupted by noise. In this paper, we consider an SA involving a contraction mapping with respect to an arbitrary norm, and show its finite-sample error bounds while using different stepsizes. The idea is to construct a smooth Lyapunov function using the generalized Moreau envelope, and show that the iterates of SA have negative drift with respect to that Lyapunov function. Our result is applicable in Reinforcement Learning (RL). In particular, we use it to establish the first-known convergence rate of the V-trace algorithm for off-policy TD-learning [18]. Importantly, our construction results in only a logarithmic dependence of the convergence bound on the size of the state-space.

paragraphs: Stochastic approximation solves fixed-point problems when the information used in each update is noisy. This paper considers mappings that are contractions with respect to an arbitrary norm. That contraction assumption supplies a way to control progress toward a fixed point, while the noise makes it necessary to analyze how much error remains after finitely many updates.

The authors construct a smooth Lyapunov function using a generalized Moreau envelope. A Lyapunov function serves as a measure of progress, and they show that the stochastic iterates have negative drift according to this measure. This construction yields finite-sample error bounds for different choices of step size, turning the progress argument into quantitative convergence guarantees.

The analysis also applies to reinforcement learning. In particular, the paper establishes what it identifies as the first known convergence rate for V-trace, an off-policy temporal-difference learning algorithm. Its construction produces a convergence bound with only logarithmic dependence on the number of states. This gives a favorable state-space dependence within the stated bound and shows how the general proof technique resolves a specific reinforcement learning question.
summary.tldr: A smooth Lyapunov construction gives finite-sample bounds for contractive stochastic approximation and a V-trace convergence rate with logarithmic state-space dependence.

title: Finite-Sample Analysis of Contractive Stochastic Approximation Using Smooth Convex Envelopes

abstract: The ability to compose learned skills to solve new tasks is an important property for lifelong-learning agents. In this work we formalise the logical composition of tasks as a Boolean algebra. This allows us to formulate new tasks in terms of the negation, disjunction and conjunction of a set of base tasks. We then show that by learning goal-oriented value functions and restricting the transition dynamics of the tasks, an agent can solve these new tasks with no further learning. We prove that by composing these value functions in specific ways, we immediately recover the optimal policies for all tasks expressible under the Boolean algebra. We verify our approach in two domains---including a high-dimensional video game environment requiring function approximation---where an agent first learns a set of base skills, and then composes them to solve a super-exponential number of new tasks.

We then show that by learning goal-oriented value functions and restricting the transition dynamics of the tasks, an agent can solve these new tasks with no further learning. We prove that by composing these value functions in specific ways, we immediately recover the optimal policies for all tasks expressible under the Boolean algebra. paragraphs: An agent that has learned several skills should ideally be able to combine them when a new task arrives. This paper gives that idea a precise logical structure: tasks form a Boolean algebra, so new objectives can be expressed using AND, OR, and NOT applied to previously learned base tasks.

The method learns goal-oriented value functions and then combines those functions according to specific rules. These functions provide the information needed to choose actions for the composed objectives. Under restrictions on the tasks' transition dynamics, the authors prove that these combinations recover optimal policies for every task expressible in the algebra, without additional learning.

The approach is tested in two domains, including a high-dimensional video game that requires function approximation. After learning base skills, the agent composes them to address a super-exponential number of new tasks. The significance is that logical task descriptions become a mechanism for reusing learned behavior. The optimality result depends on the stated transition restrictions; it is not a claim about unrestricted combinations of arbitrary skills.
summary.tldr: Under restrictions on task dynamics, Boolean combinations of learned value functions yield optimal policies for new tasks without further learning.

title: A Boolean Task Algebra for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose CaSPR, a method to learn object-centric Canonical Spatiotemporal Point Cloud Representations of dynamically moving or evolving objects. Our goal is to enable information aggregation over time and the interrogation of object state at any spatiotemporal neighborhood in the past, observed or not. Different from previous work, CaSPR learns representations that support spacetime continuity, are robust to variable and irregularly spacetime-sampled point clouds, and generalize to unseen object instances. Our approach divides the problem into two subtasks. First, we explicitly encode time by mapping an input point cloud sequence to a spatiotemporally-canonicalized object space. We then leverage this canonicalization to learn a spatiotemporal latent representation using neural ordinary differential equations and a generative model of dynamically evolving shapes using continuous normalizing flows. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several applications including shape reconstruction, camera pose estimation, continuous spatiotemporal sequence reconstruction, and correspondence estimation from irregularly or intermittently sampled observations.

paragraphs: CaSPR represents objects that move or change shape using sequences of point clouds. Its goal is to combine observations over time and support queries about an object's past state, including locations and times that were not directly observed. This requires a representation that remains meaningful when measurements arrive irregularly or contain different numbers of points.

The method first maps a point-cloud sequence into a canonical object space that explicitly includes time. This creates a common representation for observations across the sequence. It then uses neural ordinary differential equations to learn a continuous spatiotemporal latent representation, together with continuous normalizing flows to model evolving shapes generatively.

The authors report representations that support continuity across space and time, tolerate irregular sampling, and generalize to unseen object instances. They demonstrate the approach through shape reconstruction, camera pose estimation, continuous sequence reconstruction, and correspondence estimation. These applications show why bringing observations into a shared object-centered representation matters: the model can aggregate incomplete measurements and use their temporal relationships to infer object structure across a sequence.
summary.tldr: CaSPR learns continuous object-centered representations of changing point clouds to combine irregular observations and reconstruct object states across space and time.

title: CaSPR: Learning Canonical Spatiotemporal Point Cloud Representations

abstract: Adversarial robustness is a critical property in a variety of modern machine learning applications. While it has been the subject of several recent theoretical studies, many important questions related to adversarial robustness are still open. In this work, we study a fundamental question regarding Bayes optimality for adversarial robustness. We provide general sufficient conditions under which the existence of a Bayes optimal classifier can be guaranteed for adversarial robustness. Our results can provide a useful tool for a subsequent study of surrogate losses in adversarial robustness and their consistency properties.
originalAbstract: Adversarial robustness is a critical property in a variety of modern machine learning applications. While it has been the subject of several recent theoretical studies, many important questions related to adversarial robustness are still open. In this work, we study a fundamental question regarding Bayes optimality for adversarial robustness. We provide general sufficient conditions under which the existence of a Bayes optimal classifier can be guaranteed for adversarial robustness. Our results can provide a useful tool for a subsequent study of surrogate losses in adversarial robustness and their consistency properties.

paragraphs: This paper studies a foundational question in adversarial robustness: under what conditions does an optimal classifier actually exist? Bayes optimality identifies the best achievable classification rule for the relevant statistical objective. In the adversarial setting, that objective must account for the adversarial changes against which the classifier is meant to be robust.

The authors provide general sufficient conditions guaranteeing the existence of an adversarial Bayes-optimal classifier. The qualification matters: satisfying those conditions ensures existence, but the abstract does not assert that they are necessary. The result establishes that an optimal rule is attained under the stated conditions, giving later theoretical work a well-defined object to study.

The authors identify surrogate losses and their consistency as a possible use of this existence result. Such work concerns how an alternative training objective relates to the desired robust classification objective. Establishing that an adversarial optimum exists can support that analysis. The contribution is therefore a mathematical foundation for studying robust learning objectives, with its proposed value for subsequent consistency research expressed as a possibility.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for an adversarial Bayes-optimal classifier to exist, supporting possible future analysis of surrogate-loss consistency.

title: On the Existence of The Adversarial Bayes Classifier

abstract: This paper presents two Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithms with theoretical performance guarantee to maximize the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of a black-box function: CV-UCB and CV-TS which are based on the well-established principle of optimism in the face of uncertainty and Thompson sampling, respectively. To achieve this, we develop an upper confidence bound of CVaR and prove the no-regret guarantee of CV-UCB by utilizing an interesting connection between CVaR and value-at-risk (VaR). For CV-TS, though it is straightforwardly performed with Thompson sampling, bounding its Bayesian regret is non-trivial because it requires a tail expectation bound for the distribution of CVaR of a black-box function, which has not been shown in the literature. The performances of both CV-UCB and CV-TS are empirically evaluated in optimizing CVaR of synthetic benchmark functions and simulated real-world optimization problems.

To achieve this, we develop an upper confidence bound of CVaR and prove the no-regret guarantee of CV-UCB by utilizing an interesting connection between CVaR and value-at-risk (VaR). paragraphs: Optimizing a black-box function can involve caring about the unfavorable tail of outcomes rather than only typical performance. This paper targets conditional value-at-risk, or CVaR, with two Bayesian optimization algorithms. Both have theoretical performance guarantees, but they choose evaluations through different principles for handling uncertainty.

CV-UCB follows optimism in the face of uncertainty. The authors construct an upper confidence bound for CVaR and use its connection to value-at-risk to prove a no-regret guarantee. CV-TS instead uses Thompson sampling. Although applying that sampling principle is straightforward, its Bayesian regret analysis requires controlling a tail expectation for the distribution of the function's CVaR.

The theoretical work therefore addresses both how to choose promising evaluations and how to justify those choices for a tail-focused objective. The paper evaluates both algorithms on synthetic benchmark functions and simulated real-world optimization problems. Those experiments examine their practical performance, while the guarantees establish analytical support for optimizing CVaR through Bayesian optimization. The two contributions bring uncertainty-guided search to an explicitly risk-sensitive target.
summary.tldr: CV-UCB and CV-TS extend Bayesian optimization to conditional value-at-risk, with theoretical guarantees and evaluations on synthetic and simulated problems.

title: Optimizing Conditional Value-At-Risk of Black-Box Functions

abstract: Pruning the weights of randomly initialized neural networks plays an important role in the context of lottery ticket hypothesis. Ramanujan et al. (2020) empirically showed that only pruning the weights can achieve remarkable performance instead of optimizing the weight values. However, to achieve the same level of performance as the weight optimization, the pruning approach requires more parameters in the networks before pruning and thus more memory space. To overcome this parameter inefficiency, we introduce a novel framework to prune randomly initialized neural networks with iteratively randomizing weight values (IteRand). Theoretically, we prove an approximation theorem in our framework, which indicates that the randomizing operations are provably effective to reduce the required number of the parameters. We also empirically demonstrate the parameter efficiency in multiple experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

However, to achieve the same level of performance as the weight optimization, the pruning approach requires more parameters in the networks before pruning and thus more memory space. To overcome this parameter inefficiency, we introduce a novel framework to prune randomly initialized neural networks with iteratively randomizing weight values (IteRand). Theoretically, we prove an approximation theorem in our framework, which indicates that the randomizing operations are provably effective to reduce the required number of the parameters. We also empirically demonstrate the parameter efficiency in multiple experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

paragraphs: A randomly initialized neural network can contain a useful subnetwork that is found by pruning weights rather than optimizing their numerical values. Earlier empirical work showed promising performance from this approach. However, matching the performance of weight optimization required a larger initial network, creating a parameter and memory cost before pruning even began.

IteRand addresses this inefficiency by combining pruning with repeated randomization of weight values. It changes the framework from selecting exclusively among the weights available in one initial draw to allowing further randomization during the process. The authors prove an approximation theorem showing that these randomizing operations can reduce the number of parameters required within their framework.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet also demonstrate parameter efficiency. The theoretical and empirical results therefore point to repeated randomization as a useful ingredient for finding effective pruned networks with smaller starting parameter requirements. The contribution concerns the efficiency of this pruning framework, rather than claiming that randomization universally replaces ordinary weight training.
summary.tldr: IteRand combines pruning with repeated weight randomization to reduce the initial parameter requirements of randomly initialized networks.

title: Pruning Randomly Initialized Neural Networks with Iterative Randomization

abstract: Kernel $k$-means is one of the most popular approaches to clustering and its theoretical properties have been investigated for decades. However, the existing state-of-the-art risk bounds are of order $\mathcal{O}(k/\sqrt{n})$, which do not match with the stated lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{k/n})$ in terms of $k$, where $k$ is the number of clusters and $n$ is the size of the training set. In this paper, we study the statistical properties of kernel $k$-means and Nystr\"{o}m-based kernel $k$-means, and obtain optimal clustering risk bounds, which improve the existing risk bounds. Particularly, based on a refined upper bound of Rademacher complexity [21], we first derive an optimal risk bound of rate $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{k/n})$ for empirical risk minimizer (ERM), and further extend it to general cases beyond ERM. Then, we analyze the statistical effect of computational approximations of Nystr\"{o}m kernel $k$-means, and prove that it achieves the same statistical accuracy as the original kernel $k$-means considering only $\Omega(\sqrt{nk})$ Nystr\"{o}m landmark points. We further relax the restriction of landmark points from $\Omega(\sqrt{nk})$ to $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ under a mild condition. Finally, we validate the theoretical findings via numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper sharpens the statistical guarantees for kernel k-means clustering. Earlier upper bounds scaled as k divided by the square root of n, where k is the number of clusters and n the training-set size. That dependence on cluster count did not match the stated lower bound, leaving a gap in the theoretical account of clustering accuracy.

Using a refined Rademacher-complexity bound, the authors derive an optimal risk bound of O(sqrt(k/n)) for an empirical risk minimizer. They also extend the analysis beyond exact empirical minimization. The improvement reduces the cluster-count dependence in the guarantee, giving a tighter characterization of how statistical error scales as the number of clusters grows.

The paper then studies Nyström approximation, which uses landmark points to reduce computation. It proves that the approximation can preserve the original method's statistical accuracy with a landmark count on the order specified by Ω(sqrt(nk)). Under an additional mild condition, the requirement relaxes to Ω(sqrt(n)). Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings, linking computational approximation to retained statistical accuracy.
summary.tldr: Sharper kernel k-means risk bounds match the stated lower-bound rate and show when Nyström approximations preserve statistical accuracy.

title: Refined Learning Bounds for Kernel and Approximate $k$-Means

abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms are widely used in domains where it is desirable to provide a personalized service. In these domains it is common that user data contains sensitive information that needs to be protected from third parties. Motivated by this, we study privacy in the context of finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by requiring information to be obfuscated on the user side. We formulate this notion of privacy for RL by leveraging the local differential privacy (LDP) framework. We establish a lower bound for regret minimization in finite-horizon MDPs with LDP guarantees which shows that guaranteeing privacy has a multiplicative effect on the regret. This result shows that while LDP is an appealing notion of privacy, it makes the learning problem significantly more complex. Finally, we present an optimistic algorithm that simultaneously satisfies $\varepsilon$-LDP requirements, and achieves $\sqrt{K}/\varepsilon$ regret in any finite-horizon MDP after $K$ episodes, matching the lower bound dependency on the number of episodes $K$.

Motivated by this, we study privacy in the context of finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by requiring information to be obfuscated on the user side. We formulate this notion of privacy for RL by leveraging the local differential privacy (LDP) framework. We establish a lower bound for regret minimization in finite-horizon MDPs with LDP guarantees which shows that guaranteeing privacy has a multiplicative effect on the regret. This result shows that while LDP is an appealing notion of privacy, it makes the learning problem significantly more complex. Finally, we present an optimistic algorithm that simultaneously satisfies $\varepsilon$-LDP requirements, and achieves $\sqrt{K}/\varepsilon$ regret in any finite-horizon MDP after $K$ episodes, matching the lower bound dependency on the number of episodes $K$.

paragraphs: Personalized reinforcement learning can depend on sensitive user information. This paper studies privacy when information must be obscured on the user's side before it reaches a third party. It formulates that requirement using local differential privacy for finite-horizon Markov decision processes, where learning unfolds over episodes with bounded duration.

The theoretical lower bound shows that this privacy requirement imposes a multiplicative cost on regret, the loss accumulated relative to optimal decisions. Privacy therefore changes the difficulty of learning itself, rather than merely adding a separate processing step. The result identifies an unavoidable performance burden within the studied private learning setting.

The authors also construct an optimistic algorithm satisfying ε-local differential privacy. After K episodes, its stated regret scales as √K/ε, matching the lower bound's dependence on the number of episodes. That match establishes the episode-count dependence, without claiming that every aspect of the bound is optimal. Together, the algorithm and lower bound characterize both a feasible learning strategy and the additional challenge created by protecting information locally.
summary.tldr: Local differential privacy increases reinforcement learning regret multiplicatively, and the proposed algorithm matches the lower bound's episode-count dependence.

title: Local Differential Privacy for Regret Minimization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Transformers have achieved success in both language and vision domains. However, it is prohibitively expensive to scale them to long sequences such as long documents or high-resolution images, because self-attention mechanism has quadratic time and memory complexities with respect to the input sequence length. In this paper, we propose Long-Short Transformer (Transformer-LS), an efficient self-attention mechanism for modeling long sequences with linear complexity for both language and vision tasks. It aggregates a novel long-range attention with dynamic projection to model distant correlations and a short-term attention to capture fine-grained local correlations. We propose a dual normalization strategy to account for the scale mismatch between the two attention mechanisms. Transformer-LS can be applied to both autoregressive and bidirectional models without additional complexity. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art models on multiple tasks in language and vision domains, including the Long Range Arena benchmark, autoregressive language modeling, and ImageNet classification. For instance, Transformer-LS achieves 0.97 test BPC on enwik8 using half the number of parameters than previous method, while being faster and is able to handle 3x as long sequences compared to its full-attention version on the same hardware. On ImageNet, it can obtain the state-of-the-art results (e.g., a moderate size of 55.8M model solely trained on 224x224 ImageNet-1K can obtain Top-1 accuracy 84.1%), while being more scalable on high-resolution images. The source code and models are released at https://github.com/NVIDIA/transformer-ls.

paragraphs: Standard self-attention becomes expensive as sequences grow because its time and memory requirements increase quadratically with sequence length. Transformer-LS addresses this obstacle for language and vision by combining two attention mechanisms with linear complexity: one for distant relationships and another for fine-grained local relationships.

The long-range component uses dynamic projection, while short-term attention preserves local correlations. A dual normalization strategy handles differences in scale between the two components. The architecture applies to both autoregressive and bidirectional models without additional complexity, allowing the same overall approach to support different kinds of sequence processing.

Reported results outperform leading models on multiple language and vision tasks. On enwik8, Transformer-LS reaches 0.97 test bits per character with half the parameters of the previous method. It is also faster and handles sequences three times as long as its full-attention version on the same hardware. ImageNet results include 84.1% top-1 accuracy for a 55.8-million-parameter model trained solely on ImageNet-1K at 224-by-224 resolution.
summary.tldr: Transformer-LS combines dynamic long-range attention with local attention to process long language and vision sequences with linear complexity.

title: Long-Short Transformer: Efficient Transformers for Language and Vision

abstract: Although deep learning models have driven state-of-the-art performance on a wide array of tasks, they are prone to spurious correlations that should not be learned as predictive clues. To mitigate this problem, we propose a causality-based training framework to reduce the spurious correlations caused by observed confounders. We give theoretical analysis on the underlying general Structural Causal Model (SCM) and propose to perform Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) on the interventional distribution instead of the observational distribution, namely Counterfactual Maximum Likelihood Estimation (CMLE). As the interventional distribution, in general, is hidden from the observational data, we then derive two different upper bounds of the expected negative log-likelihood and propose two general algorithms, Implicit CMLE and Explicit CMLE, for causal predictions of deep learning models using observational data. We conduct experiments on both simulated data and two real-world tasks: Natural Language Inference (NLI) and Image Captioning. The results show that CMLE methods outperform the regular MLE method in terms of out-of-domain generalization performance and reducing spurious correlations, while maintaining comparable performance on the regular evaluations.

paragraphs: Deep networks can learn predictive associations that reflect confounding rather than the relationship of interest. This paper addresses spurious correlations caused by observed confounders through a causal training framework. Its focus is on changing the distribution that training seeks to fit, so that the learning objective reflects interventions rather than only observed associations.

Counterfactual Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or CMLE, applies maximum likelihood to an interventional distribution. The authors analyze this idea using a structural causal model. Because observational data generally do not directly reveal that distribution, they derive two upper bounds on the expected negative log-likelihood. These bounds lead to two algorithms, Implicit CMLE and Explicit CMLE, that can train deep models using observational data.

Experiments cover simulated data, natural language inference, and image captioning. Compared with regular maximum likelihood training, the CMLE methods improve out-of-domain generalization and reduce spurious correlations while retaining comparable performance on regular evaluations. The findings support using a causally motivated objective to address observed confounding without giving up ordinary predictive performance in the reported tests.
summary.tldr: CMLE uses tractable bounds on a causal likelihood objective to reduce spurious correlations from observed confounders and improve out-of-domain generalization.

title: Counterfactual Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Training Deep Networks

abstract: Current transfer learning algorithm designs mainly focus on the similarities between source and target tasks, while the impacts of the sample sizes of these tasks are often not sufficiently addressed. This paper proposes a mathematical framework for quantifying the transferability in multi-source transfer learning problems, with both the task similarities and the sample complexity of learning models taken into account. In particular, we consider the setup where the models learned from different tasks are linearly combined for learning the target task, and use the optimal combining coefficients to measure the transferability. Then, we demonstrate the analytical expression of this transferability measure, characterized by the sample sizes, model complexity, and the similarities between source and target tasks, which provides fundamental insights of the knowledge transferring mechanism and the guidance for algorithm designs. Furthermore, we apply our analyses for practical learning tasks, and establish a quantifiable transferability measure by exploiting a parameterized model. In addition, we develop an alternating iterative algorithm to implement our theoretical results for training deep neural networks in multi-source transfer learning tasks. Finally, experiments on image classification tasks show that our approach outperforms existing transfer learning algorithms in multi-source and few-shot scenarios.

paragraphs: When several source tasks are available, deciding how much each should contribute to a target task involves more than measuring similarity. The amount of data available for each task also affects what can be learned reliably. This paper develops a mathematical framework that incorporates both considerations when quantifying transferability.

The analysis considers a specific setup: models learned on different tasks are combined linearly to learn the target task. The optimal weights in that combination become the transferability measure. Their analytical form depends on sample sizes, model complexity, and source–target similarity. This connects the usefulness of a source model to both its relationship with the target and the statistical resources behind it.

The authors then use a parameterized model to make the measure applicable to practical learning tasks. They develop an alternating iterative training algorithm for deep networks that implements the theoretical ideas. Image classification experiments show improvements over existing transfer learning algorithms in multi-source and few-shot settings, supporting the value of jointly considering similarity and sample availability.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies source-task usefulness through combination weights that account for task similarity, sample sizes, and model complexity.

title: A Mathematical Framework for Quantifying Transferability in Multi-source Transfer Learning

abstract: Machine learning datasets have elicited concerns about privacy, bias, and unethical applications, leading to the retraction of prominent datasets such as DukeMTMC, MS-Celeb-1M, and Tiny Images. In response, the machine learning community has called for higher ethical standards in dataset creation. To help inform these efforts, we studied three influential but ethically problematic face and person recognition datasets---Labeled Faces in the Wild (LFW), MS-Celeb-1M, and DukeMTMC---by analyzing nearly 1000 papers that cite them. We found that the creation of derivative datasets and models, broader technological and social change, the lack of clarity of licenses, anddataset management practices can introduce a wide range of ethical concerns. We conclude by suggesting a distributed approach to harm mitigation that considers the entire life cycle of a dataset.

paragraphs: Concerns about privacy, bias, and unethical applications have led to prominent machine-learning datasets being withdrawn. This paper asks what the subsequent use of datasets can teach researchers about reducing harm. It studies three influential face and person recognition datasets: Labeled Faces in the Wild, MS-Celeb-1M, and DukeMTMC.

The authors analyze nearly 1,000 papers citing those datasets. Their findings identify several ways ethical concerns can arise over time, including derivative datasets and models, changes in technology and society, unclear licenses, and dataset-management practices. This places dataset use and continued management alongside initial collection as relevant parts of understanding potential harm.

The paper concludes by proposing a distributed approach to mitigation that covers the entire dataset life cycle. The idea follows from the range of activities and changes identified in the study: ethical concerns can develop as data are reused and their surroundings change. The contribution is evidence from citation-based analysis that informs a broader conception of dataset stewardship and responsibility.
summary.tldr: An analysis of nearly 1,000 papers motivates distributed dataset stewardship that addresses harms throughout reuse, management, and broader social change.

title: Mitigating dataset harms requires stewardship: Lessons from 1000 papers

abstract: The goal of understanding decision-making behaviours in clinical environments is of paramount importance if we are to bring the strengths of machine learning to ultimately improve patient outcomes. Mainstream development of algorithms is often geared towards optimal performance in tasks that do not necessarily translate well into the medical regime---due to several factors including the lack of public availability of realistic data, the intrinsically offline nature of the problem, as well as the complexity and variety of human behaviours. We therefore present a new benchmarking suite designed specifically for medical sequential decision modelling: the Medkit-Learn(ing) Environment, a publicly available Python package providing simple and easy access to high-fidelity synthetic medical data. While providing a standardised way to compare algorithms in a realistic medical setting, we employ a generating process that disentangles the policy and environment dynamics to allow for a range of customisations, thus enabling systematic evaluation of algorithms’ robustness against specific challenges prevalent in healthcare.

paragraphs: Modeling sequences of medical decisions poses challenges that standard machine-learning tasks may not capture well. The authors point to limited public access to realistic data, the offline nature of the problem, and the variety and complexity of human behavior. Medkit-Learn provides a benchmark suite designed specifically around these medical decision-modeling needs.

The suite is a public Python package offering access to high-fidelity synthetic medical data. Its generating process separates the policy governing decisions from the dynamics of the environment. This separation allows customization of these components, creating a way to examine algorithm behavior under controlled changes in the simulated medical setting.

The main contribution is a standardized but configurable environment for comparing algorithms and investigating robustness to healthcare-specific challenges. The synthetic data and adjustable generating process support systematic evaluation where suitable public data are scarce. The paper positions this capability as a foundation for understanding clinical decision-making behavior, with improved patient outcomes serving as the broader motivation for the research.
summary.tldr: Medkit-Learn offers configurable synthetic medical data for benchmarking sequential decision models and their robustness.

title: The Medkit-Learn(ing) Environment: Medical Decision Modelling through Simulation

abstract: Numerical simulations of Earth's weather and climate require substantial amounts of computation. This has led to a growing interest in replacing subroutines that explicitly compute physical processes with approximate machine learning (ML) methods that are fast at inference time. Within weather and climate models, atmospheric radiative transfer (RT) calculations are especially expensive. This has made them a popular target for neural network-based emulators. However, prior work is hard to compare due to the lack of a comprehensive dataset and standardized best practices for ML benchmarking. To fill this gap, we build a large dataset, ClimART, with more than 10 million samples from present, pre-industrial, and future climate conditions, based on the Canadian Earth System Model. ClimART poses several methodological challenges for the ML community, such as multiple out-of-distribution test sets, underlying domain physics, and a trade-off between accuracy and inference speed. We also present several novel baselines that indicate shortcomings of datasets and network architectures used in prior work.

paragraphs: Weather and climate simulations spend substantial computation on physical processes, including atmospheric radiative transfer. Neural networks offer a way to approximate these expensive calculations with faster predictions. However, comparing such replacements has been difficult because prior studies lacked a comprehensive shared dataset and standardized benchmarking practices.

ClimART addresses that evaluation gap with more than 10 million samples derived from the Canadian Earth System Model. The data span present, pre-industrial, and future climate conditions. This scope makes the benchmark relevant to evaluating approximations across different climate conditions, alongside the more basic question of how accurately a network reproduces the target calculations.

The benchmark includes multiple tests outside the training distribution and highlights the need to account for domain physics and the trade-off between accuracy and prediction speed. The authors also introduce baselines whose results expose shortcomings in datasets and architectures used previously. The contribution is a resource for assessing radiative-transfer emulators, with computational efficiency and generalization treated as central parts of the problem.
summary.tldr: ClimART provides over 10 million climate-model samples for comparing the accuracy, speed, and generalization of atmospheric radiative-transfer emulators.

title: ClimART: A Benchmark Dataset for Emulating Atmospheric Radiative Transfer in Weather and Climate Models

abstract: We consider local kernel metric learning for off-policy evaluation (OPE) of deterministic policies in contextual bandits with continuous action spaces. Our work is motivated by practical scenarios where the target policy needs to be deterministic due to domain requirements, such as prescription of treatment dosage and duration in medicine. Although importance sampling (IS) provides a basic principle for OPE, it is ill-posed for the deterministic target policy with continuous actions. Our main idea is to relax the target policy and pose the problem as kernel-based estimation, where we learn the kernel metric in order to minimize the overall mean squared error (MSE). We present an analytic solution for the optimal metric, based on the analysis of bias and variance. Whereas prior work has been limited to scalar action spaces or kernel bandwidth selection, our work takes a step further being capable of vector action spaces and metric optimization. We show that our estimator is consistent, and significantly reduces the MSE compared to baseline OPE methods through experiments on various domains.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a proposed decision policy would perform using data collected under another policy. This paper considers contextual bandits with continuous actions and deterministic target policies. Such policies matter when an application requires a specific decision, such as a treatment dosage and duration, but ordinary importance sampling is ill-posed in this setting.

The authors relax the target policy and reformulate evaluation as kernel-based estimation. A key choice is the metric determining how the kernel measures proximity between actions. They learn that metric to minimize overall mean squared error, deriving an analytic solution through an analysis of the estimator's bias and variance.

The method handles vector-valued actions and optimizes the metric, extending beyond prior approaches limited to scalar actions or kernel bandwidth selection. The authors establish consistency of their estimator and report substantially lower mean squared error than baseline evaluation methods across experiments in several domains. The contribution makes the geometry of nearby actions an explicit part of accurate policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: Learning a local kernel metric improves evaluation of deterministic policies with continuous, potentially multidimensional actions.

title: Local Metric Learning for Off-Policy Evaluation in Contextual Bandits with Continuous Actions

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the regret of undiscounted reinforcement learning in MDPs with a birth and death structure. Specifically, we consider a controlled queue with impatient jobs and the main objective is to optimize a trade-off between energy consumption and user-perceived performance. Within this setting, the diameter $D$ of the MDP is $\Omega(S^S)$, where $S$ is the number of states. Therefore, the existing lower and upper bounds on the regret at time $T$, of order $O (\sqrt{DSAT})$ for MDPs with $S$ states and $A$ actions, may suggest that reinforcement learning is inefficient here. In our main result however, we exploit the structure of our MDPs to show that the regret of a slightly-tweaked version of the classical learning algorithm UCRL2 is in fact upper bounded by $\tilde{\mathcal{O}} (\sqrt{E_2AT})$ where $E_2$ is a weighted second moment of the stationary measure of a reference policy. Importantly, $E_2$ is bounded independently of $S$. Thus, our bound is asymptotically independent of the number of states and of the diameter. This result is based on a careful study of the number of visits performed by the learning algorithm to the states of the MDP, which is highly non-uniform.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning for a controlled queue whose jobs may leave when kept waiting. The objective balances energy consumption with user-perceived performance. Although the system has a birth-and-death structure, its Markov decision process can have an enormous diameter, making general regret bounds suggest that learning could be inefficient.

The authors analyze a slightly modified UCRL2 algorithm using the queue’s particular structure. Their regret bound scales, up to logarithmic factors, as the square root of E2 times the number of actions and elapsed time. E2 is a weighted second moment of the stationary distribution under a reference policy, and it is bounded independently of the number of states.

The resulting bound is asymptotically independent of both state count and diameter. A central part of the proof tracks how unevenly the learner visits different states. This shows why treating every state through general size and diameter measures can be overly pessimistic for this structured queueing problem.
summary.tldr: Exploiting a queue’s birth-and-death structure yields a regret bound asymptotically independent of its state count and enormous diameter.

title: Reinforcement Learning in a Birth and Death Process: Breaking the Dependence on the State Space

abstract: Controlled feature selection aims to discover the features a response depends on while limiting the false discovery rate (FDR) to a predefined level. Recently, multiple deep-learning-based methods have been proposed to perform controlled feature selection through the Model-X knockoff framework. We demonstrate, however, that these methods often fail to control the FDR for two reasons. First, these methods often learn inaccurate models of features. Second, the "swap" property, which is required for knockoffs to be valid, is often not well enforced. We propose a new procedure called FlowSelect to perform controlled feature selection that does not suffer from either of these two problems. To more accurately model the features, FlowSelect uses normalizing flows, the state-of-the-art method for density estimation. Instead of enforcing the "swap" property, FlowSelect uses a novel MCMC-based procedure to calculate p-values for each feature directly. Asymptotically, FlowSelect computes valid p-values. Empirically, FlowSelect consistently controls the FDR on both synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, whereas competing knockoff-based approaches do not. FlowSelect also demonstrates greater power on these benchmarks. Additionally, FlowSelect correctly infers the genetic variants associated with specific soybean traits from GWAS data.

paragraphs: Controlled feature selection seeks relevant variables while keeping the false discovery rate below a chosen level. The paper identifies two reasons existing deep-learning approaches based on Model-X knockoffs can fail: inaccurate models of the feature distribution and insufficient enforcement of the swap property required for valid knockoffs. FlowSelect takes a different route to statistical testing.

FlowSelect models the feature distribution with normalizing flows and uses an MCMC procedure to calculate a p-value for each feature directly. This avoids having to enforce the knockoff swap property. The theoretical validity statement is asymptotic: the procedure computes valid p-values in the limit, rather than establishing an unconditional finite-sample guarantee in the abstract.

On synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, FlowSelect consistently controls the false discovery rate and has greater power, while the compared knockoff approaches fail to maintain control. An application to soybean association data also identifies genetic variants linked to specific traits. The results support combining density estimation with direct testing as an effective alternative to learned knockoff construction.
summary.tldr: FlowSelect combines normalizing flows and MCMC-based p-values to select features with asymptotic validity and empirical false-discovery control.

title: Normalizing Flows for Knockoff-free Controlled Feature Selection

abstract: While behavior learning has made impressive progress in recent times, it lags behind computer vision and natural language processing due to its inability to leverage large, human-generated datasets. Human behavior has a wide variance, multiple modes, and human demonstrations naturally do not come with reward labels. These properties limit the applicability of current methods in Offline RL and Behavioral Cloning to learn from large, pre-collected datasets. In this work, we present Behavior Transformer (BeT), a new technique to model unlabeled demonstration data with multiple modes. BeT retrofits standard transformer architectures with action discretization coupled with a multi-task action correction inspired by offset prediction in object detection. This allows us to leverage the multi-modal modeling ability of modern transformers to predict multi-modal continuous actions. We experimentally evaluate BeT on a variety of robotic manipulation and self-driving behavior datasets. We show that BeT significantly improves over prior state-of-the-art work on solving demonstrated tasks while capturing the major modes present in the pre-collected datasets. Finally, through an extensive ablation study, we further analyze the importance of every crucial component in BeT. Videos of behavior generated by BeT are available here: https://mahis.life/bet

paragraphs: Human demonstrations contain multiple ways of behaving, and they usually lack reward labels. Learning from a large collection therefore requires representing several distinct behavior patterns without relying on rewards to identify desirable actions. Behavior Transformer, or BeT, addresses this problem by learning from demonstrations with multiple modes.

BeT adapts a standard transformer using action discretization and an action correction task. Discretization gives the model a way to represent distinct action alternatives, while correction supports predictions in a continuous action space. The correction mechanism draws inspiration from offset prediction in object detection. Together, these components let a transformer model varied behavior while still producing continuous actions.

The authors evaluate BeT on robotic manipulation and self-driving behavior datasets. It improves substantially over the prior methods considered at completing demonstrated tasks, while capturing the major behavior modes in the data. An ablation study examines the contribution of its key components. The findings indicate that task success and preservation of behavioral variety can be pursued together within this architecture.
summary.tldr: Behavior Transformer combines discrete action modeling with continuous corrections to learn multiple behavior patterns from demonstrations without reward labels.

title: Behavior Transformers: Cloning $k$ modes with one stone

abstract: Adversarial training (AT) with imperfect supervision is significant but receives limited attention. To push AT towards more practical scenarios, we explore a brand new yet challenging setting, i.e., AT with complementary labels (CLs), which specify a class that a data sample does not belong to. However, the direct combination of AT with existing methods for CLs results in consistent failure, but not on a simple baseline of two-stage training. In this paper, we further explore the phenomenon and identify the underlying challenges of AT with CLs as intractable adversarial optimization and low-quality adversarial examples. To address the above problems, we propose a new learning strategy using gradually informative attacks, which consists of two critical components: 1) Warm-up Attack (Warm-up) gently raises the adversarial perturbation budgets to ease the adversarial optimization with CLs; 2) Pseudo-Label Attack (PLA) incorporates the progressively informative model predictions into a corrected complementary loss. Extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a range of benchmarked datasets. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RoyalSkye/ATCL.

title: Adversarial Training with Complementary Labels: On the Benefit of Gradually Informative Attacks

abstract: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are formal models commonly used in sequential decision-making. MDPs capture the stochasticity that may arise, for instance, from imprecise actuators via probabilities in the transition function. However, in data-driven applications, deriving precise probabilities from (limited) data introduces statistical errors that may lead to unexpected or undesirable outcomes.Uncertain MDPs (uMDPs) do not require precise probabilities but instead use so-called uncertainty sets in the transitions, accounting for such limited data.Tools from the formal verification community efficiently compute robust policies that provably adhere to formal specifications, like safety constraints, under the worst-case instance in the uncertainty set. We continuously learn the transition probabilities of an MDP in a robust anytime-learning approach that combines a dedicated Bayesian inference scheme with the computation of robust policies. In particular, our method (1) approximates probabilities as intervals, (2) adapts to new data that may be inconsistent with an intermediate model, and (3) may be stopped at any time to compute a robust policy on the uMDP that faithfully captures the data so far. Furthermore, our method is capable of adapting to changes in the environment. We show the effectiveness of our approach and compare it to robust policies computed on uMDPs learned by the UCRL2 reinforcement learning algorithm in an experimental evaluation on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: A Markov decision process describes how actions lead probabilistically to future states. Estimating those probabilities from limited data introduces uncertainty that can undermine planning. This paper learns uncertain MDPs, which represent possible transition probabilities through uncertainty sets and support policies evaluated against the worst-case model within those sets.

The approach combines a dedicated Bayesian inference scheme with robust policy computation. It represents transition probabilities as intervals and updates them as observations arrive, including when new data conflict with the current intermediate model. Learning can be stopped at any point to compute a robust policy from an uncertain MDP that reflects the data collected so far.

This anytime capability allows policy computation without waiting for a fixed learning process to finish, and the method can adapt to environmental changes. Robust specifications, such as safety constraints, are assessed relative to the modeled uncertainty set. Benchmark experiments demonstrate effectiveness and compare the approach with robust policies based on uncertain MDPs learned using the UCRL2 reinforcement-learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: An anytime Bayesian method learns uncertain transition models that support robust policy computation and adapt to conflicting data or environmental changes.

title: Robust Anytime Learning of Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Despite surprising performance on zero-shot transfer, pre-training a large-scale multimodal model is often prohibitive as it requires a huge amount of data and computing resources. In this paper, we propose a method (BeamCLIP) that can effectively transfer the representations of a large pre-trained multimodal model (CLIP-ViT) into a small target model (e.g., ResNet-18). For unsupervised transfer, we introduce cross-modal similarity matching (CSM) that enables a student model to learn the representations of a teacher model by matching the relative similarity distribution across text prompt embeddings. To better encode the text prompts, we design context-based prompt augmentation (CPA) that can alleviate the lexical ambiguity of input text prompts. Our experiments show that unsupervised representation transfer of a pre-trained vision-language model enables a small ResNet-18 to achieve a better ImageNet-1K top-1 linear probe accuracy (66.2%) than vision-only self-supervised learning (SSL) methods (e.g., SimCLR: 51.8%, SwAV: 63.7%), while closing the gap with supervised learning (69.8%).

paragraphs: Large vision-language models can transfer well to new tasks, but pretraining them requires substantial data and computation. BeamCLIP addresses a different part of that process: transferring representations from an already trained CLIP-ViT teacher into a smaller model such as ResNet-18. The aim is to make the teacher's learned representation useful within a compact model.

For unsupervised transfer, cross-modal similarity matching teaches the student to match the teacher's relative similarity distribution across text-prompt embeddings. This uses relationships to language representations as the training signal. Context-based prompt augmentation improves the encoding of those prompts by reducing ambiguity in their wording.

In the reported ImageNet-1K linear-probe evaluation, the transferred ResNet-18 reaches 66.2% top-1 accuracy, compared with 51.8% for SimCLR and 63.7% for SwAV. It also approaches the stated supervised result of 69.8%. These findings show that unsupervised transfer from a pretrained vision-language teacher can produce stronger small-model representations than the compared vision-only self-supervised methods.
summary.tldr: BeamCLIP transfers a large vision-language teacher's representations into a smaller model by matching similarities to text prompts.

title: Transferring Pre-trained Multimodal Representations with Cross-modal Similarity Matching

abstract: Current work in object-centric learning has been motivated by developing learning algorithms that infer independent and symmetric entities from the perceptual input. This often requires the use iterative refinement procedures that break symmetries among equally plausible explanations for the data, but most prior works differentiate through the unrolled refinement process, which can make optimization exceptionally challenging. In this work, we observe that such iterative refinement methods can be made differentiable by means of the implicit function theorem, and develop an implicit differentiation approach that improves the stability and tractability of training such models by decoupling the forward and backward passes. This connection enables us to apply recent advances in optimizing implicit layers to not only improve the stability and optimization of the slot attention module in SLATE, a state-of-the-art method for learning entity representations, but do so with constant space and time complexity in backpropagation and only one additional line of code.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning seeks separate entity representations from perceptual inputs. Several possible explanations can initially be equally plausible, so models often refine their representations repeatedly to distinguish among them. Training through all of those refinement steps can make optimization difficult, because the backward computation becomes tied to the entire sequence of updates.

This paper treats the refined representations as fixed points and uses the implicit function theorem to differentiate them. The resulting approach separates the forward refinement process from the backward gradient calculation. That separation allows techniques developed for implicit layers to improve the stability and tractability of learning object representations.

The authors apply the approach to the slot attention module in SLATE, a leading entity-representation method. They report improved training stability and optimization, with backpropagation taking constant space and time relative to the refinement process, and requiring only one additional line of code. The complexity claim concerns backpropagation; the central contribution is changing how refinement-based models receive their training gradients.
summary.tldr: Implicit differentiation improves training of iterative object representations by separating refinement from backpropagation through every refinement step.

title: Object Representations as Fixed Points: Training Iterative Refinement Algorithms with Implicit Differentiation

abstract: This paper presents a language-powered paradigm for ordinal regression. Existing methods usually treat each rank as a category and employ a set of weights to learn these concepts. These methods are easy to overfit and usually attain unsatisfactory performance as the learned concepts are mainly derived from the training set. Recent large pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP have shown impressive performance on various visual tasks. In this paper, we propose to learn the rank concepts from the rich semantic CLIP latent space. Specifically, we reformulate this task as an image-language matching problem with a contrastive objective, which regards labels as text and obtains a language prototype from a text encoder for each rank. While prompt engineering for CLIP is extremely time-consuming, we propose OrdinalCLIP, a differentiable prompting method for adapting CLIP for ordinal regression. OrdinalCLIP consists of learnable context tokens and learnable rank embeddings. The learnable rank embeddings are constructed by explicitly modeling numerical continuity, resulting in well-ordered, compact language prototypes in the CLIP space. Once learned, we can only save the language prototypes and discard the huge language model, resulting in zero additional computational overhead compared with the linear head counterpart. Experimental results show that our paradigm achieves competitive performance in general ordinal regression tasks, and gains improvements in few-shot and distribution shift settings for age estimation. The code is available at https://github.com/xk-huang/OrdinalCLIP.
