paragraphs: Ordinal regression predicts labels with an inherent ordering. The paper argues that treating each rank as an independently learned category can overfit the training data. OrdinalCLIP instead draws rank concepts from CLIP's pretrained vision-language representation, casting prediction as image-language matching with a contrastive objective.

For each rank, a text encoder produces a language prototype. The method learns context tokens and rank embeddings through differentiable prompting, avoiding reliance on time-consuming manual prompt engineering. Its rank embeddings explicitly model numerical continuity, producing compact prototypes whose arrangement respects the order of the labels.

Once training is complete, the language prototypes can be saved and the large language model discarded. The authors report no additional computational overhead compared with a linear prediction head at this stage. Experiments show competitive performance on general ordinal regression tasks and improvements for age estimation with few examples or distribution shift. The findings support using pretrained language semantics and explicit rank continuity together, while preserving a lightweight prediction component after learning.
summary.tldr: OrdinalCLIP learns ordered language prototypes for ordinal prediction, reporting gains in challenging age-estimation settings without extra inference overhead over a linear head.

title: OrdinalCLIP: Learning Rank Prompts for Language-Guided Ordinal Regression

abstract: Facial expression data is characterized by a significant imbalance, with most collected data showing happy or neutral expressions and fewer instances of fear or disgust. This imbalance poses challenges to facial expression recognition (FER) models, hindering their ability to fully understand various human emotional states. Existing FER methods typically report overall accuracy on highly imbalanced test sets but exhibit low performance in terms of the mean accuracy across all expression classes. In this paper, our aim is to address the imbalanced FER problem. Existing methods primarily focus on learning knowledge of minor classes solely from minor-class samples. However, we propose a novel approach to extract extra knowledge related to the minor classes from both major and minor class samples. Our motivation stems from the belief that FER resembles a distribution learning task, wherein a sample may contain information about multiple classes. For instance, a sample from the major class surprise might also contain useful features of the minor class fear. Inspired by that, we propose a novel method that leverages re-balanced attention maps to regularize the model, enabling it to extract transformation invariant information about the minor classes from all training samples. Additionally, we introduce re-balanced smooth labels to regulate the cross-entropy loss, guiding the model to pay more attention to the minor classes by utilizing the extra information regarding the label distribution of the imbalanced training data. Extensive experiments on different datasets and backbones show that the two proposed modules work together to regularize the model and achieve state-of-the-art performance under the imbalanced FER task. Code is available at https://github.com/zyh-uaiaaaa.

paragraphs: Facial-expression datasets contain many examples of some expressions and few of others. Overall accuracy on similarly imbalanced test data can conceal weak performance across expression classes. This paper aims to improve recognition of less common classes by looking for information about them throughout the training set, including examples labeled as common expressions.

The motivating idea is that an image can contain features relevant to multiple expressions. A surprise example, for instance, may also carry useful information about fear. The method uses rebalanced attention maps to encourage extraction of transformation-invariant information about minority expressions from all samples. It also introduces rebalanced smooth labels that adjust cross-entropy training using information about the imbalanced label distribution.

These two modules guide both which visual information the model extracts and how its training loss emphasizes minority classes. Experiments with different datasets and backbone networks show that the modules work together and achieve state-of-the-art performance on imbalanced facial-expression recognition. The contribution is a way to use potentially shared expression information, extending minority-class learning beyond the relatively few samples assigned those labels.
summary.tldr: Rebalanced attention and smooth labels help facial-expression models learn about rare expressions from both common-class and rare-class examples.

title: Leave No Stone Unturned: Mine Extra Knowledge for Imbalanced Facial Expression Recognition

abstract: We study the problem of designing adaptive multi-armed bandit algorithms that perform optimally in both the stochastic setting and the adversarial setting simultaneously (often known as a best-of-both-world guarantee). A line of recent works shows that when configured and analyzed properly, the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) algorithm, originally designed for the adversarial setting, can in fact optimally adapt to the stochastic setting as well. Such results, however, critically rely on an assumption that there exists one unique optimal arm. Recently, Ito [2021] took the first step to remove such an undesirable uniqueness assumption for one particular FTRL algorithm withthe 1/2-Tsallis entropy regularizer. In this work, we significantly improve and generalize this result, showing that uniqueness is unnecessary for FTRL with a broad family of regularizers and a new learning rate schedule. For some regularizers, our regret bounds also improve upon prior results even when uniqueness holds. We further provide an application of our results to the decoupled exploration and exploitation problem, demonstrating that our techniques are broadly applicable.

paragraphs: A best-of-both-worlds bandit algorithm aims to perform optimally in both stochastic and adversarial environments. Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, or FTRL, was developed for the adversarial setting, but suitable configurations can also adapt to stochastic problems. Many earlier guarantees depended on there being exactly one optimal arm, restricting their treatment of problems with tied best choices.

This paper removes that uniqueness requirement for a broad family of FTRL regularizers using a new learning-rate schedule. It extends an earlier result that handled multiple optimal arms for one particular regularizer, the one-half Tsallis entropy. The contribution therefore broadens the range of algorithmic choices for which adaptation can be justified without requiring a unique best action.

For some regularizers, the new regret bounds improve on previous results even when the best arm is unique. The authors also apply their analysis to a setting with decoupled exploration and exploitation. Together, the results strengthen theoretical guarantees while demonstrating that the techniques apply beyond the original bandit formulation.
summary.tldr: New FTRL guarantees accommodate multiple optimal arms across a broad family of regularizers and improve some existing regret bounds.

title: Improved Best-of-Both-Worlds Guarantees for Multi-Armed Bandits: FTRL with General Regularizers and Multiple Optimal Arms

abstract: Pre-trained text-to-image generative models can produce diverse, semantically rich, and realistic images from natural language descriptions. Compared with language, images usually convey information with more details and less ambiguity. In this study, we propose Learning from the Void (LfVoid), a method that leverages the power of pre-trained text-to-image models and advanced image editing techniques to guide robot learning. Given natural language instructions, LfVoid can edit the original observations to obtain goal images, such as "wiping" a stain off a table. Subsequently, LfVoid trains an ensembled goal discriminator on the generated image to provide reward signals for a reinforcement learning agent, guiding it to achieve the goal. The ability of LfVoid to learn with zero in-domain training on expert demonstrations or true goal observations (the void) is attributed to the utilization of knowledge from web-scale generative models. We evaluate LfVoid across three simulated tasks and validate its feasibility in the corresponding real-world scenarios. In addition, we offer insights into the key considerations for the effective integration of visual generative models into robot learning workflows. We posit that our work represents an initial step towards the broader application of pre-trained visual generative models in the robotics field. Our project page: https://lfvoid-rl.github.io/.

paragraphs: A robot given a language instruction still needs a learning signal that indicates whether its actions are accomplishing the task. Learning from the Void, or LfVoid, uses a pretrained text-to-image model to turn that instruction into a visual goal. It edits the robot's original observation to depict the desired outcome, such as a table after a stain has been wiped away.

The generated goal image then supports training an ensemble of goal discriminators. These discriminators provide reward signals for a reinforcement learning agent, guiding its behavior toward the pictured result. This connects the generative model's knowledge about visual outcomes to the agent's need for feedback during learning.

The method requires no in-domain expert demonstrations or true goal observations for training, drawing instead on knowledge in web-scale generative models. The authors evaluate three simulated tasks and demonstrate feasibility in corresponding real-world scenarios. They position the work as an initial step toward using pretrained visual generators in robotics, with generated goals serving as a practical connection between language instructions and reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: LfVoid edits observations into visual goals and uses them to reward robot learning without in-domain demonstrations or true goal images.

title: Can Pre-Trained Text-to-Image Models Generate Visual Goals for Reinforcement Learning?

abstract: We present improved algorithms with worst-case regret guarantees for the stochastic linear bandit problem. The widely used "optimism in the face of uncertainty" principle reduces a stochastic bandit problem to the construction of a confidence sequence for the unknown reward function. The performance of the resulting bandit algorithm depends on the size of the confidence sequence, with smaller confidence sets yielding better empirical performance and stronger regret guarantees. In this work, we use a novel tail bound for adaptive martingale mixtures to construct confidence sequences which are suitable for stochastic bandits. These confidence sequences allow for efficient action selection via convex programming. We prove that a linear bandit algorithm based on our confidence sequences is guaranteed to achieve competitive worst-case regret. We show that our confidence sequences are tighter than competitors, both empirically and theoretically. Finally, we demonstrate that our tighter confidence sequences give improved performance in several hyperparameter tuning tasks.

paragraphs: In a stochastic linear bandit problem, an algorithm repeatedly chooses actions while learning an unknown reward function. Optimistic algorithms use uncertainty about that function to guide their choices. Their behavior depends on confidence sequences: evolving sets of reward functions that remain plausible as more observations arrive.

This paper constructs tighter confidence sequences using a new tail bound for adaptive martingale mixtures. The statistical result is designed to handle information collected through adaptive decisions. The resulting confidence sets also allow efficient action selection through convex programming, connecting the uncertainty calculation to a tractable decision procedure.

The authors prove that a linear bandit algorithm using these sets achieves competitive worst-case regret guarantees. They show theoretically and empirically that their confidence sequences are tighter than competing ones, and demonstrate improved performance on several hyperparameter-tuning tasks. The contribution is therefore both statistical and algorithmic: more precise uncertainty estimates can improve decisions while retaining a guarantee on accumulated regret in the worst case.
summary.tldr: New martingale tail bounds yield tighter confidence sequences and improved linear bandit algorithms with competitive worst-case regret guarantees.

title: Improved Algorithms for Stochastic Linear Bandits Using Tail Bounds for Martingale Mixtures

abstract: Embedding-based retrieval methods construct vector indices to search for document representations that are most similar to the query representations. They are widely used in document retrieval due to low latency and decent recall performance. Recent research indicates that deep retrieval solutions offer better model quality, but are hindered by unacceptable serving latency and the inability to support document updates. In this paper, we aim to enhance the vector index with end-to-end deep generative models, leveraging the differentiable advantages of deep retrieval models while maintaining desirable serving efficiency. We propose Model-enhanced Vector Index (MEVI), a differentiable model-enhanced index empowered by a twin-tower representation model. MEVI leverages a Residual Quantization (RQ) codebook to bridge the sequence-to-sequence deep retrieval and embedding-based models. To substantially reduce the inference time, instead of decoding the unique document ids in long sequential steps, we first generate some semantic virtual cluster ids of candidate documents in a small number of steps, and then leverage the well-adapted embedding vectors to further perform a fine-grained search for the relevant documents in the candidate virtual clusters. We empirically show that our model achieves better performance on the commonly used academic benchmarks MSMARCO Passage and Natural Questions, with comparable serving latency to dense retrieval solutions.

paragraphs: Document retrieval often uses vector representations to find documents similar to a query quickly. Deep retrieval models offer stronger model quality, but their serving latency and difficulties supporting document updates can hinder deployment. Model-enhanced Vector Index, or MEVI, aims to combine the learning advantages of deep generative retrieval with efficient vector search.

MEVI connects a sequence-to-sequence retrieval model and an embedding-based model through a residual quantization codebook. A twin-tower representation model supplies the embeddings. During retrieval, the generative component first predicts semantic identifiers for candidate virtual clusters in a small number of steps. Vector search then finds relevant documents within those candidate clusters.

This two-stage process avoids spending many sequential decoding steps on complete, unique document identifiers. Generation narrows the search, and adapted embeddings perform the detailed comparison. Experiments on MSMARCO Passage and Natural Questions show improved retrieval performance with serving latency comparable to dense retrieval systems. The reported result supports integrating learned cluster selection into a vector index while retaining practical search speed.
summary.tldr: MEVI generates candidate document clusters and searches them with embeddings, improving retrieval performance at latency comparable to dense retrieval.

title: Model-enhanced Vector Index

abstract: The McKean-Vlasov equation (MVE) describes the collective behavior of particles subject to drift, diffusion, and mean-field interaction. In physical systems, the interaction term can be singular, i.e. it diverges when two particles collide. Notable examples of such interactions include the Coulomb interaction, fundamental in plasma physics, and the Biot-Savart interaction, present in the vorticity formulation of the 2D Navier-Stokes equation (NSE) in fluid dynamics. Solving MVEs that involve singular interaction kernels presents a significant challenge, especially when aiming to provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. In this work, we propose a novel approach based on the concept of entropy dissipation in the underlying system. We derive a potential function that effectively controls the KL divergence between a hypothesis solution and the ground truth. Building upon this theoretical foundation, we introduce the Entropy-dissipation Informed Neural Network (EINN) framework for solving MVEs. In EINN, we utilize neural networks (NN) to approximate the underlying velocity field and minimize the proposed potential function. By leveraging the expressive power of NNs, our approach offers a promising avenue for tackling the complexities associated with singular interactions. To assess the empirical performance of our method, we compare EINN with SOTA NN-based MVE solvers. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in solving MVEs across various example problems.

abstract: We introduce a general method for achieving robust group-invariance in group-equivariant convolutional neural networks ($G$-CNNs), which we call the $G$-triple-correlation ($G$-TC) layer. The approach leverages the theory of the triple-correlation on groups, which is the unique, lowest-degree polynomial invariant map that is also \textit{complete}. Many commonly used invariant maps\textemdash such as the \texttt{max}\textemdash are incomplete: they remove both group and signal structure. A complete invariant, by contrast, removes only the variation due to the actions of the group, while preserving all information about the structure of the signal. The completeness of the triple correlation endows the $G$-TC layer with strong robustness, which can be observed in its resistance to invariance-based adversarial attacks. In addition, we observe that it yields measurable improvements in classification accuracy over standard Max $G$-Pooling in $G$-CNN architectures. We provide a general and efficient implementation of the method for any discretized group, which requires only a table defining the group's product structure. We demonstrate the benefits of this method for $G$-CNNs defined on both commutative and non-commutative groups\textemdash $SO(2)$, $O(2)$, $SO(3)$, and $O(3)$ (discretized as the cyclic $C8$, dihedral $D16$, chiral octahedral $O$ and full octahedral $O_h$ groups)\textemdash acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ on both $G$-MNIST and $G$-ModelNet10 datasets.

paragraphs: A network that recognizes objects across transformations needs a way to discard those transformations without discarding what makes the objects different. This paper addresses that problem in group-equivariant convolutional networks. It introduces a triple-correlation layer that converts transformation-sensitive representations into invariant ones while preserving the signal structure that distinguishes different inputs.

The central mathematical property is completeness: the representation removes variation attributable to the chosen transformation group while retaining the remaining information. Common alternatives such as maximum pooling are incomplete because they can also erase meaningful signal differences. The authors connect their layer to the theory of triple correlation, described as the unique complete polynomial invariant of lowest degree.

Experiments show resistance to attacks that exploit invariance and improved classification accuracy relative to standard Max G-Pooling. The implementation needs only a table specifying the discretized group's multiplication rules. Demonstrations cover commutative and noncommutative transformation groups in two and three dimensions, showing that the approach applies across several symmetry settings.
summary.tldr: A triple-correlation layer preserves signal information while removing group transformations, improving tested robustness and classification accuracy.

title: A General Framework for Robust G-Invariance in G-Equivariant Networks

abstract: Common statistical measures of uncertainty such as $p$-values and confidence intervals quantify the uncertainty due to sampling, that is, the uncertainty due to not observing the full population. However, sampling is not the only source of uncertainty. In practice, distributions change between locations and across time. This makes it difficult to gather knowledge that transfers across data sets. We propose a measure of instability that quantifies the distributional instability of a statistical parameter with respect to Kullback-Leibler divergence, that is, the sensitivity of the parameter under general distributional perturbations within a Kullback-Leibler divergence ball. In addition, we quantify the instability of parameters with respect to directional or variable-specific shifts. Measuring instability with respect to directional shifts can be used to detect under which kind of distribution shifts a statistical conclusion might be reversed. We discuss how such knowledge can inform data collection for transfer learning of statistical parameters under shifted distributions. We evaluate the performance of the proposed measure on real data and show that it can elucidate the distributional instability of a parameter with respect to certain shifts and can be used to improve estimation accuracy under shifted distributions.

paragraphs: Confidence intervals and p-values describe uncertainty arising from observing a sample instead of a whole population. A separate problem arises when the population itself changes across places or times. This paper introduces the s-value to assess how sensitive a statistical parameter is to such distributional changes.

The proposed measure evaluates instability within a neighborhood defined by Kullback-Leibler divergence, which specifies the allowed size of a distributional perturbation. The authors also consider shifts restricted to particular directions or variables. These more targeted assessments help identify which kinds of changes could reverse a statistical conclusion, making the source of instability more interpretable.

The paper discusses how this information can guide data collection when transferring estimates between distributions. Evaluations on real data show that the measure can reveal sensitivity to particular shifts and can help improve estimation accuracy under changed distributions. Its contribution is to make distributional stability an explicit object of analysis alongside sampling uncertainty, connecting that diagnosis to decisions about obtaining more informative data.
summary.tldr: The s-value measures a statistical parameter's sensitivity to distribution shifts and can guide data collection and estimation under changed conditions.

title: The s-value: evaluating stability with respect to distributional shifts

abstract: Point clouds are versatile representations of 3D objects and have found widespread application in science and engineering. Many successful deep-learning models have been proposed that use them as input. The domain of chemical and materials modeling is especially challenging because exact compliance with physical constraints is highly desirable for a model to be usable in practice. These constraints include smoothness and invariance with respect to translations, rotations, and permutations of identical atoms. If these requirements are not rigorously fulfilled, atomistic simulations might lead to absurd outcomes even if the model has excellent accuracy. Consequently, dedicated architectures, which achieve invariance by restricting their design space, have been developed. General-purpose point-cloud models are more varied but often disregard rotational symmetry. We propose a general symmetrization method that adds rotational equivariance to any given model while preserving all the other requirements.Our approach simplifies the development of better atomic-scale machine-learning schemes by relaxing the constraints on the design space and making it possible to incorporate ideas that proved effective in other domains.We demonstrate this idea by introducing the Point Edge Transformer (PET) architecture, which is not intrinsically equivariant but achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets of molecules and solids. A-posteriori application of our general protocol makes PET exactly equivariant, with minimal changes to its accuracy.

paragraphs: For models of molecules and materials, predictive accuracy alone may not ensure physically sensible behavior. Smoothness and the correct response to translations, rotations, and permutations of identical atoms also matter. Architectures designed to enforce these requirements can restrict the range of model designs available to researchers.

The paper proposes a general symmetrization method that adds exact rotational equivariance to a given model while preserving the other requirements. Equivariance means that rotating the input produces the corresponding transformation of the output. This allows researchers to draw on more varied point-cloud architectures while supplying rotational behavior through a separate protocol.

The authors demonstrate the idea with the Point Edge Transformer, or PET. Although PET is not intrinsically equivariant, it achieves state-of-the-art results on several molecular and solid-state benchmarks. Applying the symmetrization protocol afterward makes it exactly equivariant with minimal changes to accuracy. The contribution therefore connects architectural flexibility with rigorous symmetry requirements that are important for usable atomic-scale models.
summary.tldr: A general symmetrization protocol adds exact rotational equivariance while preserving other physical requirements, demonstrated on the accurate Point Edge Transformer.

title: Smooth, exact rotational symmetrization for deep learning on point clouds

abstract: Watermarking is a technical means to dissuade malfeasant usage of Large Language Models.This paper proposes a novel watermarking scheme, so-called WaterMax, that enjoys high detectability while sustaining the quality of the generated text of the original LLM.Its new design leaves the LLM untouched (no modification of the weights, logits or temperature).WaterMax balances robustness and computational complexity contrary to the watermarking techniques of the literature inherently provoking a trade-off between quality and robustness.Its performance is both theoretically proven and experimentally validated.It outperforms all the SotA techniques under the most complete benchmark suite.

paragraphs: WaterMax is a watermarking scheme for text generated by large language models. The paper focuses on obtaining a watermark that is easy to detect while preserving the original model’s text quality. This matters because the authors describe existing watermarking approaches as facing a trade-off in which greater robustness comes at the expense of generated-text quality.

The design leaves the language model itself untouched: it changes neither model weights, output logits, nor temperature. The authors instead frame WaterMax’s central balance as one between robustness and computational complexity. This shifts the design consideration toward the computation needed to obtain robust watermarking while sustaining the quality of the underlying generator.

The paper reports both theoretical support and experimental validation for its performance. It also reports outperforming the compared state-of-the-art techniques across its benchmark suite. Taken together, the stated findings support the possibility of combining high detectability with preserved generation quality through this design. The remaining balance highlighted in the abstract concerns computational complexity and robustness, making computational cost an explicit part of the method’s approach.
summary.tldr: WaterMax reports highly detectable text watermarks while preserving language-model output quality, balancing robustness against computational complexity.

title: WaterMax: breaking the LLM watermark detectability-robustness-quality trade-off

abstract: Diffusion models excel in solving imaging inverse problems due to their ability to model complex image priors. However, their reliance on large, clean datasets for training limits their practical use where clean data is scarce. In this paper, we propose EMDiffusion, an expectation-maximization (EM) approach to train diffusion models from corrupted observations. Our method alternates between reconstructing clean images from corrupted data using a known diffusion model (E-step) and refining diffusion model weights based on these reconstructions (M-step). This iterative process leads the learned diffusion model to gradually converge to a local optimum, that is, to approximate the true clean data distribution. We validate our method through extensive experiments on diverse computational imaging tasks, including random inpainting, denoising, and deblurring, achieving new state-of-the-art performance.

This iterative process leads the learned diffusion model to gradually converge to a local optimum, that is, to approximate the true clean data distribution. paragraphs: EMDiffusion addresses a practical obstacle in using diffusion models for image reconstruction: learning useful image structure usually requires many clean training images. In settings where observations are already corrupted, that requirement limits the models’ usefulness. The paper proposes learning a clean-image distribution through an iterative process that works from the corrupted observations.

The method alternates two connected operations using expectation-maximization. In the expectation step, an available diffusion model helps reconstruct clean images from the observations. In the maximization step, those reconstructions become the basis for updating the diffusion model’s weights. The updated model can then support the next reconstruction step, linking improvements in reconstruction and model learning.

The abstract describes this process as gradually converging to a local optimum that approximates the clean-data distribution. That qualification matters: the stated result is local convergence, rather than guaranteed recovery of the exact distribution. Experiments cover random inpainting, denoising, and deblurring, with reported state-of-the-art performance. These results support the approach’s usefulness across several forms of computational imaging corruption.
summary.tldr: EMDiffusion alternates image reconstruction and diffusion-model updates to learn an approximation of clean image data from corrupted observations.

title: An Expectation-Maximization Algorithm for Training Clean Diffusion Models from Corrupted Observations

abstract: The deep operator networks (DeepONet), a class of neural operators that learn mappings between function spaces, have recently been developed as surrogate models for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs). In this work we propose a derivative-enhanced deep operator network (DE-DeepONet), which leverages derivative information to enhance the solution prediction accuracy and provides a more accurate approximation of solution-to-parameter derivatives, especially when training data are limited. DE-DeepONet explicitly incorporates linear dimension reduction of high dimensional parameter input into DeepONet to reduce training cost and adds derivative loss in the loss function to reduce the number of required parameter-solution pairs. We further demonstrate that the use of derivative loss can be extended to enhance other neural operators, such as the Fourier neural operator (FNO). Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Deep operator networks learn mappings between functions and can serve as substitutes for solving parameter-dependent partial differential equations. Predicting a solution is one goal; accurately predicting how that solution changes when parameters change is another. This paper introduces DE-DeepONet to improve both, particularly when relatively few training examples are available.

The method makes two changes to DeepONet. First, it explicitly applies linear dimension reduction to high-dimensional parameter inputs, reducing training cost. Second, it adds a derivative loss to the training objective. This supplies information about how solutions respond to parameter changes, alongside information about the solutions themselves, and reduces the number of parameter-solution pairs required.

Numerical experiments support the approach's effectiveness for solution prediction and approximation of solution-to-parameter derivatives. The authors also demonstrate that derivative loss can improve other neural operators, including the Fourier neural operator. The broader contribution is a way to make training use both values and sensitivities, with the reported benefits especially relevant when ordinary parameter-solution training data are limited.
summary.tldr: DE-DeepONet uses derivative information and reduced-dimensional inputs to improve PDE surrogate learning when training data are limited.

title: Derivative-enhanced Deep Operator Network

abstract: We study a multi-agent imitation learning (MAIL) problem where we take the perspective of a learner attempting to *coordinate* a group of agents based on demonstrations of an expert doing so. Most prior work in MAIL essentially reduces the problem to matching the behavior of the expert *within* the support of the demonstrations. While doing so is sufficient to drive the *value gap* between the learner and the expert to zero under the assumption that agents are non-strategic, it does not guarantee robustness to deviations by strategic agents. Intuitively, this is because strategic deviations can depend on a counterfactual quantity: the coordinator's recommendations outside of the state distribution their recommendations induce. In response, we initiate the study of an alternative objective for MAIL in Markov Games we term the *regret gap* that explicitly accounts for potential deviations by agents in the group. We first perform an in-depth exploration of the relationship between the value and regret gaps. First, we show that while the value gap can be efficiently minimized via a direct extension of single-agent IL algorithms, even *value equivalence* can lead to an arbitrarily large regret gap. This implies that achieving regret equivalence is harder than achieving value equivalence in MAIL. We then provide a pair of efficient reductions to no-regret online convex optimization that are capable of minimizing the regret gap *(a)* under a coverage assumption on the expert (MALICE) or *(b)* with access to a queryable expert (BLADES).

paragraphs: A coordinator learned from demonstrations may reproduce an expert's outcomes when agents follow its recommendations. That does not establish robustness when agents can strategically deviate. This paper separates the value gap, which compares achieved outcomes, from a regret gap that explicitly accounts for opportunities to benefit from deviations.

The difficulty is that strategic behavior can depend on recommendations in situations outside the distribution generated by ordinary coordinated play. Matching demonstrated behavior may therefore leave consequential counterfactual decisions unconstrained. The authors show that value equivalence can coexist with an arbitrarily large regret gap, even though the value gap can be minimized efficiently using extensions of single-agent imitation methods.

To address the harder objective, the paper gives two efficient reductions to no-regret online convex optimization. MALICE requires a coverage assumption on the expert, while BLADES requires access to an expert that can answer queries. These conditions explain what additional support the proposed methods use to learn coordination that accounts for strategic deviations.
summary.tldr: Matching an expert coordinator's outcomes can leave large strategic vulnerabilities; minimizing a regret gap requires additional expert coverage or query access.

title: Multi-Agent Imitation Learning: Value is Easy, Regret is Hard

abstract: In the context of modern machine learning, models deployed in real-world scenarios often encounter diverse data shifts like covariate and semantic shifts, leading to challenges in both out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization and detection. Despite considerable attention to these issues separately, a unified framework for theoretical understanding and practical usage is lacking. To bridge the gap, we introduce a graph-theoretic framework to jointly tackle both OOD generalization and detection problems. By leveraging the graph formulation, data representations are obtained through the factorization of the graph's adjacency matrix, enabling us to derive provable error quantifying OOD generalization and detection performance. Empirical results showcase competitive performance in comparison to existing methods, thereby validating our theoretical underpinnings.

paragraphs: When deployment data differ from training data, a model faces two related questions: whether it can still make useful predictions, and whether it should recognize an input as outside its familiar distribution. Research often studies these questions separately. This paper introduces a graph-based framework that treats out-of-distribution generalization and detection together.

The approach obtains data representations by factorizing a graph's adjacency matrix, the mathematical object that records its connections. That shared representation provides the basis for analyzing both tasks. Within this formulation, the authors derive provable error characterizations that quantify generalization and detection performance. The significance is that both behaviors can be examined through one mathematical construction rather than disconnected analyses.

The motivation covers shifts in observed input characteristics as well as semantic changes. Empirical comparisons show competitive performance against existing methods, supporting the practical relevance of the theoretical framework. The stated result is a connection between theory and usable representations for both tasks; competitive results do not imply that the method dominates every specialized detection or generalization approach.
summary.tldr: A graph-based representation framework connects theoretical analysis and practical methods for both out-of-distribution detection and generalization.

title: Bridging OOD Detection and Generalization: A Graph-Theoretic View

abstract: We present a new class of fast polylog-linear algorithms based on the theory of structured matrices (in particular *low displacement rank*) for integrating tensor fields defined on weighted trees. Several applications of the resulting *fast tree-field integrators* (FTFIs) are presented, including: (a) approximation of graph metrics with tree metrics, (b) graph classification, (c) modeling on meshes, and finally (d) *Topological Transformers* (TTs) (Choromanski et al., 2022) for images. For Topological Transformers, we propose new relative position encoding (RPE) masking mechanisms with as few as **three** extra learnable parameters per Transformer layer, leading to **1.0-1.5\%+** accuracy gains. Importantly, most of FTFIs are **exact** methods, thus numerically equivalent to their brute-force counterparts. When applied to graphs with thousands of nodes, those exact algorithms provide **5.7-13x** speedups. We also provide an extensive theoretical analysis of our methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces fast algorithms for integrating tensor fields on weighted trees. These operations combine information distributed across a tree, and straightforward computation can be expensive. The authors exploit structured-matrix theory, particularly low displacement rank, to obtain algorithms whose cost grows linearly with problem size apart from polylogarithmic factors.

They demonstrate applications in approximating graph metrics with tree metrics, classifying graphs, modeling meshes, and processing images with Topological Transformers. For the Transformer application, they introduce relative-position encoding masks that can require as few as three additional learned parameters per layer. These masks incorporate structural relationships into the model with a small parameter increase.

Alongside extensive theoretical analysis, these findings show how tree-based structure can support both faster numerical computation and useful model components.
summary.tldr: Structured-matrix methods accelerate tree-field integration, with mostly exact algorithms and applications extending to Topological Transformers.

title: Fast Tree-Field Integrators: From Low Displacement Rank to Topological Transformers

abstract: Group equivariance has emerged as a valuable inductive bias in deep learning, enhancing generalization, data efficiency, and robustness. Classically, group equivariant methods require the groups of interest to be known beforehand, which may not be realistic for real-world data. Additionally, baking in fixed group equivariance may impose overly restrictive constraints on model architecture. This highlights the need for methods that can dynamically discover and apply symmetries as soft constraints. For neural network architectures, equivariance is commonly achieved through group transformations of a canonical weight tensor, resulting in weight sharing over a given group $G$. In this work, we propose to *learn* such a weight-sharing scheme by defining a collection of learnable doubly stochastic matrices that act as soft permutation matrices on canonical weight tensors, which can take regular group representations as a special case. This yields learnable kernel transformations that are jointly optimized with downstream tasks. We show that when the dataset exhibits strong symmetries, the permutation matrices will converge to regular group representations and our weight-sharing networks effectively become regular group convolutions. Additionally, the flexibility of the method enables it to effectively pick up on partial symmetries.

This can improve generalization and data efficiency, but conventional methods require the relevant symmetry group to be specified beforehand. Fixed symmetry constraints can also restrict architecture choices when the data only partly follows the assumed structure.

This paper learns the weight-sharing scheme itself. It introduces learnable doubly stochastic matrices that act as soft permutations of a canonical weight tensor. These matrices define kernel transformations and are optimized jointly with the downstream task. Regular group representations fit within this construction as a special case, while softer transformations give the model additional flexibility.

The authors show that when a dataset has strong symmetries, the learned permutation matrices converge to regular group representations and the resulting networks effectively become regular group convolutions. They also report that the flexibility allows the method to capture partial symmetries. The contribution is a way to discover useful transformation structure while learning the task, with exact group-like behavior arising under the stated strong-symmetry setting.
summary.tldr: Learnable soft permutations let networks discover weight-sharing symmetries, including partial symmetries, during task training.

title: Learning symmetries via weight-sharing with doubly stochastic tensors

abstract: The Mixture of Experts (MoE) paradigm provides a powerful way to decompose dense layers into smaller, modular computations often more amenable to human interpretation, debugging, and editability. However, a major challenge lies in the computational cost of scaling the number of experts high enough to achieve fine-grained specialization. In this paper, we propose the Multilinear Mixture of Experts (μMoE) layer to address this, focusing on vision models. μMoE layers enable scalable expert specialization by performing an implicit computation on prohibitively large weight tensors entirely in factorized form. Consequently, μMoEs (1) avoid the restrictively high inference-time costs of dense MoEs, yet (2) do not inherit the training issues of the popular sparse MoEs' discrete (non-differentiable) expert routing. We present both qualitative and quantitative evidence that scaling μMoE layers when fine-tuning foundation models for vision tasks leads to more specialized experts at the class-level, further enabling manual bias correction in CelebA attribute classification. Finally, we show qualitative results demonstrating the expert specialism achieved when pre-training large GPT2 and MLP-Mixer models with parameter-matched μMoE blocks at every layer, maintaining comparable accuracy. Our code is available at: https://github.com/james-oldfield/muMoE.

These findings connect scalable expert structure with opportunities to inspect and edit model behavior.
summary.tldr: Multilinear expert layers use factorized computation to scale specialization efficiently, with evidence of class-specific experts and manual bias correction.

title: Multilinear Mixture of Experts: Scalable Expert Specialization through Factorization

abstract: In this work, we study the generalizability of diffusion models by looking into the hidden properties of the learned score functions, which are essentially a series of deep denoisers trained on various noise levels. We observe that as diffusion models transition from memorization to generalization, their corresponding nonlinear diffusion denoisers exhibit increasing linearity. This discovery leads us to investigate the linear counterparts of the nonlinear diffusion models, which are a series of linear models trained to match the function mappings of the nonlinear diffusion denoisers. Surprisingly, these linear denoisers are approximately the optimal denoisers for a multivariate Gaussian distribution characterized by the empirical mean and covariance of the training dataset. This finding implies that diffusion models have the inductive bias towards capturing and utilizing the Gaussian structure (covariance information) of the training dataset for data generation. We empirically demonstrate that this inductive bias is a unique property of diffusion models in the generalization regime, which becomes increasingly evident when the model's capacity is relatively small compared to the training dataset size. In the case that the model is highly overparameterized, this inductive bias emerges during the initial training phases before the model fully memorizes its training data. Our study provides crucial insights into understanding the notable strong generalization phenomenon recently observed in real-world diffusion models.

The authors observe that these nonlinear denoisers become increasingly linear as models move from memorization toward generalization. They then train linear models to reproduce the denoisers’ mappings, using these simpler counterparts to probe what statistical structure the original models capture.

In highly overparameterized models, it appears early in training before full memorization. These observations connect generalization behavior with model capacity and training progress, offering an explanation for a component of diffusion models’ observed ability to generalize.
summary.tldr: Diffusion denoisers show a stronger tendency to capture training-data covariance structure when operating in a generalization regime.

title: Understanding Generalizability of Diffusion Models Requires Rethinking the Hidden Gaussian Structure

abstract: In the past decade, deep conditional generative models have revolutionized the generation of realistic images, extending their application from entertainment to scientific domains. Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is crucial in resolving near-atomic resolution 3D structures of proteins, such as the SARS-COV-2 spike protein. To achieve high-resolution reconstruction, a comprehensive data processing pipeline has been adopted. However, its performance is still limited as it lacks high-quality annotated datasets for training. To address this, we introduce physics-informed generative cryo-electron microscopy (CryoGEM), which for the first time integrates physics-based cryo-EM simulation with a generative unpaired noise translation to generate physically correct synthetic cryo-EM datasets with realistic noises. Initially, CryoGEM simulates the cryo-EM imaging process based on a virtual specimen. To generate realistic noises, we leverage an unpaired noise translation via contrastive learning with a novel mask-guided sampling scheme. Extensive experiments show that CryoGEM is capable of generating authentic cryo-EM images. The generated dataset can be used as training data for particle picking and pose estimation models, eventually improving the reconstruction resolution.

paragraphs: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy supports reconstruction of protein structures at near-atomic resolution. Its processing pipeline depends on tasks such as finding particles and estimating their poses, but training these components is constrained by a shortage of high-quality annotated datasets. CryoGEM addresses this bottleneck by generating synthetic microscopy data.

The method combines a physical simulation of imaging with a learned process for adding realistic noise. It first simulates images from a virtual specimen. It then uses unpaired noise translation, trained through contrastive learning and a mask-guided sampling scheme, to make the simulated data resemble noisy experimental images. The combination aims to preserve physical correctness while improving visual authenticity.

Extensive experiments show that CryoGEM can produce authentic cryo-EM images. The generated datasets can train particle-picking and pose-estimation models, ultimately improving reconstruction resolution. The significance is a connection between realistic synthetic training data and the quality of the reconstructed scientific structure, through the intermediate models that process the images.
summary.tldr: CryoGEM combines physical imaging simulation with learned realistic noise to generate training data that improves cryo-EM reconstruction.

title: CryoGEM: Physics-Informed Generative Cryo-Electron Microscopy

abstract: Neural network architecture design requires making many crucial decisions. The common desiderata is that similar decisions, with little modifications, can be reused in a variety of tasks and applications. To satisfy that, architectures must provide promising latency and performance trade-offs, support a variety of tasks, scale efficiently with respect to the amounts of data and compute, leverage available data from other tasks, and efficiently support various hardware. To this end, we introduce AsCAN---a hybrid architecture, combining both convolutional and transformer blocks. We revisit the key design principles of hybrid architectures and propose a simple and effective \emph{asymmetric} architecture, where the distribution of convolutional and transformer blocks is \emph{asymmetric}, containing more convolutional blocks in the earlier stages, followed by more transformer blocks in later stages. AsCAN supports a variety of tasks: recognition, segmentation, class-conditional image generation, and features a superior trade-off between performance and latency. We then scale the same architecture to solve a large-scale text-to-image task and show state-of-the-art performance compared to the most recent public and commercial models. Notably, without performing any optimization of inference time our model shows faster execution, even when compared to works that do such optimization, highlighting the advantages and the value of our approach.

paragraphs: AsCAN addresses the challenge of designing a neural network architecture that works across different visual tasks while balancing performance and execution time. The paper combines convolutional blocks and transformer blocks in a hybrid architecture, with the aim of making the same basic design useful for both recognition and generation.

The central design choice is an asymmetric distribution of the two block types. Earlier stages contain more convolutional blocks, while later stages contain more transformer blocks. The contribution therefore concerns where these components appear within the network, as well as their combination. The authors apply this arrangement to recognition, segmentation, and image generation conditioned on a class.

The reported results show a favorable performance–latency trade-off across these tasks. The authors also scale the architecture to large-scale text-to-image generation, reporting state-of-the-art performance against the public and commercial models they compare. Their model executes faster in those comparisons without additional inference-time optimization, including comparisons with optimized systems. These findings support architectural allocation as a useful route to efficient, broadly reusable visual models.
summary.tldr: AsCAN places more convolutional blocks early and more transformer blocks later to improve performance and latency across visual tasks.

title: AsCAN: Asymmetric Convolution-Attention Networks for Efficient Recognition and Generation

abstract: We present a novel methodology for convex optimization algorithm design using ideas from electric RLC circuits. Given an optimization problem, the first stage of the methodology is to design an appropriate electric circuit whose continuous-time dynamics converge to the solution of the optimization problem at hand. Then, the second stage is an automated, computer-assisted discretization of the continuous-time dynamics, yielding a provably convergent discrete-time algorithm. Our methodology recovers many classical (distributed) optimization algorithms and enables users to quickly design and explore a wide range of new algorithms with convergence guarantees.

Then, the second stage is an automated, computer-assisted discretization of the continuous-time dynamics, yielding a provably convergent discrete-time algorithm. Our methodology recovers many classical (distributed) optimization algorithms and enables users to quickly design and explore a wide range of new algorithms with convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper treats electric circuits as a design language for convex optimization algorithms. The approach begins with an optimization problem and constructs a suitable circuit using ideas from resistor-inductor-capacitor systems. Its continuous-time behavior is designed to converge to a solution of that problem, connecting the circuit's dynamics with the mathematical objective.

The next step converts those continuous dynamics into updates that a computer can execute one step at a time. This discretization is automated and computer assisted, and the resulting discrete-time algorithm is provably convergent. The two stages therefore link a circuit-based description of a solution process to an implementable optimization method with a convergence guarantee.

The methodology recovers many classical optimization algorithms, including distributed ones, and supports exploring new algorithms. Recovering known methods shows that the circuit perspective can express established designs; the automated discretization then provides a route to extending that design space. The contribution is a reusable construction process for algorithms with convergence guarantees, rather than a single optimization update rule.
summary.tldr: The paper designs convex optimization algorithms by constructing convergent circuit dynamics and automatically converting them into provably convergent discrete updates.

title: Optimization Algorithm Design via Electric Circuits

abstract: Generative retrieval represents a novel approach to information retrieval, utilizing an encoder-decoder architecture to directly produce relevant document identifiers (docids) for queries. While this method offers benefits, current implementations are limited to scenarios with binary relevance data, overlooking the potential for documents to have multi-graded relevance. Extending generative retrieval to accommodate multi-graded relevance poses challenges, including the need to reconcile likelihood probabilities for docid pairs and the possibility of multiple relevant documents sharing the same identifier. To address these challenges, we introduce a new framework called GRaded Generative Retrieval (GR$^2$). Our approach focuses on two key components: ensuring relevant and distinct identifiers, and implementing multi-graded constrained contrastive training. Firstly, we aim to create identifiers that are both semantically relevant and sufficiently distinct to represent individual documents effectively. This is achieved by jointly optimizing the relevance and distinctness of docids through a combination of docid generation and autoencoder models. Secondly, we incorporate information about the relationship between relevance grades to guide the training process. Specifically, we leverage a constrained contrastive training strategy to bring the representations of queries and the identifiers of their relevant documents closer together, based on their respective relevance grades.Extensive experiments on datasets with both multi-graded and binary relevance demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Generative retrieval answers a search query by producing document identifiers directly. This paper extends that approach to relevance judgments with multiple grades, where documents can be more or less useful rather than simply relevant or irrelevant. Supporting those grades requires both meaningful identifiers and training that respects differences in relevance.

The proposed GR² framework addresses two connected problems. First, it jointly optimizes identifier relevance and distinctness using document-identifier generation and autoencoder models. Distinctness matters because different relevant documents might otherwise share an identifier. Second, it introduces constrained contrastive training that uses relationships between relevance grades to bring queries and relevant document identifiers closer in representation space.

This design gives relevance information a role in both how documents are represented and how query-document relationships are learned. Experiments on datasets with graded relevance and datasets with binary relevance demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The findings support adapting generative retrieval to richer judgments of usefulness while retaining applicability to the simpler binary setting.
summary.tldr: GR² adapts generative retrieval to graded relevance through distinct, meaningful document identifiers and relevance-aware contrastive training.

title: Generative Retrieval Meets Multi-Graded Relevance

abstract: We provide a new understanding of the stochastic gradient bandit algorithm by showing that it converges to a globally optimal policy almost surely using \emph{any} constant learning rate. This result demonstrates that the stochastic gradient algorithm continues to balance exploration and exploitation appropriately even in scenarios where standard smoothness and noise control assumptions break down. The proofs are based on novel findings about action sampling rates and the relationship between cumulative progress and noise, and extend the current understanding of how simple stochastic gradient methods behave in bandit settings.
originalAbstract: We provide a new understanding of the stochastic gradient bandit algorithm by showing that it converges to a globally optimal policy almost surely using \emph{any} constant learning rate. This result demonstrates that the stochastic gradient algorithm continues to balance exploration and exploitation appropriately even in scenarios where standard smoothness and noise control assumptions break down. The proofs are based on novel findings about action sampling rates and the relationship between cumulative progress and noise, and extend the current understanding of how simple stochastic gradient methods behave in bandit settings.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a convergence result for the stochastic gradient bandit algorithm. In a bandit problem, learning must balance trying actions to gather information with selecting actions that currently appear rewarding. The authors prove that the algorithm converges to a globally optimal policy almost surely with any constant learning rate.

The strength of the result is the absence of a small-step requirement within the studied setting. A fixed learning rate need not be reduced over time to obtain the stated convergence guarantee. Almost sure convergence means convergence with probability one over the algorithm’s randomness. The claim concerns eventual convergence to an optimal policy, so the learning-rate conclusion should be read in that precise sense.

The proof develops new results about how frequently actions are sampled and how accumulated progress relates to accumulated noise. Those relationships explain how exploration and exploitation remain appropriately balanced even where standard smoothness and noise-control assumptions break down. The contribution expands the theoretical understanding of simple stochastic gradient learning in bandit settings.
summary.tldr: The stochastic gradient bandit algorithm converges almost surely to a globally optimal policy for any constant learning rate.

title: Small steps no more: Global convergence of stochastic gradient bandits for arbitrary learning rates

abstract: Graph coarsening aims to reduce the size of a large graph while preserving some of its key properties, which has been used in many applications to reduce computational load and memory footprint. For instance, in graph machine learning, training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on coarsened graphs leads to drastic savings in time and memory. However, GNNs rely on the Message-Passing (MP) paradigm, and classical spectral preservation guarantees for graph coarsening do not directly lead to theoretical guarantees when performing naive message-passing on the coarsened graph.In this work, we propose a new message-passing operation specific to coarsened graphs, which exhibit theoretical guarantees on the preservation of the propagated signal. Interestingly, and in a sharp departure from previous proposals, this operation on coarsened graphs is oriented, even when the original graph is undirected. We conduct node classification tasks on synthetic and real data and observe improved results compared to performing naive message-passing on the coarsened graph.

paragraphs: Graph coarsening reduces a large graph to a smaller representation, potentially saving substantial training time and memory for graph neural networks. The difficulty is deciding what the smaller graph must preserve. Existing spectral preservation guarantees do not directly guarantee that ordinary message passing on the reduced graph will preserve the signals used by a neural network.

The paper introduces a message-passing operation designed specifically for coarsened graphs. It provides theoretical guarantees about preservation of the propagated signal, addressing the operation that graph neural networks actually perform. A notable feature is that the new operation is oriented even when the original graph is undirected.

Experiments on node classification with synthetic and real data show improvements over naive message passing on coarsened graphs. This supports adapting the propagation rule together with the graph representation. The contribution links compression to the behavior of computation on the compressed object: preserving selected graph properties alone does not automatically establish that the downstream propagation process remains faithful.
summary.tldr: A message-passing rule tailored to coarsened graphs provides signal-preservation guarantees and improves node classification over naive propagation.

title: Graph Coarsening with Message-Passing Guarantees

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) requires the agent to finish a given task while obeying specific constraints. Giving constraints in natural language form has great potential for practical scenarios due to its flexible transfer capability and accessibility. Previous safe RL methods with natural language constraints typically need to design cost functions manually for each constraint, which requires domain expertise and lacks flexibility. In this paper, we harness the dual role of text in this task, using it not only to provide constraint but also as a training signal. We introduce the Trajectory-level Textual Constraints Translator (TTCT) to replace the manually designed cost function. Our empirical results demonstrate that TTCT effectively comprehends textual constraint and trajectory, and the policies trained by TTCT can achieve a lower violation rate than the standard cost function. Extra studies are conducted to demonstrate that the TTCT has zero-shot transfer capability to adapt to constraint-shift environments.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning asks an agent to complete a task while respecting constraints. Expressing those constraints in ordinary language could make them easier to specify and transfer between situations. However, previous language-based approaches typically still require experts to manually turn each constraint into a cost function used during learning.

The paper introduces the Trajectory-level Textual Constraints Translator, or TTCT, as a replacement for that manually designed cost function. Text serves two roles: it describes the constraint and supplies a training signal. The method connects textual requirements with trajectories, the sequences of behavior that the agent produces, so that language can guide policy training.

Empirical results indicate that TTCT interprets constraints and trajectories effectively, and that policies trained with it can have lower violation rates than policies using the standard cost function. Additional studies demonstrate zero-shot transfer to environments where constraints change. These findings support a more flexible route from written requirements to learned behavior, with the reported safety improvement expressed through observed constraint violations.
summary.tldr: TTCT turns textual constraints into training signals for safe reinforcement learning, reducing observed violations and supporting transfer when constraints change.

title: From Text to Trajectory: Exploring Complex Constraint Representation and Decomposition in Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Semantic segmentation and semantic image synthesis are two representative tasks in visual perception and generation. While existing methods consider them as two distinct tasks, we propose a unified framework (SemFlow) and model them as a pair of reverse problems. Specifically, motivated by rectified flow theory, we train an ordinary differential equation (ODE) model to transport between the distributions of real images and semantic masks. As the training object is symmetric, samples belonging to the two distributions, images and semantic masks, can be effortlessly transferred reversibly. For semantic segmentation, our approach solves the contradiction between the randomness of diffusion outputs and the uniqueness of segmentation results. For image synthesis, we propose a finite perturbation approach to enhance the diversity of generated results without changing the semantic categories. Experiments show that our SemFlow achieves competitive results on semantic segmentation and semantic image synthesis tasks. We hope this simple framework will motivate people to rethink the unification of low-level and high-level vision.

paragraphs: SemFlow connects two visual tasks: assigning semantic categories to image pixels and generating an image from a semantic mask. The paper treats them as reverse directions of one problem. This perspective motivates a shared model that transports between the distribution of real images and the distribution of masks, bringing perception and generation into a common framework.

The authors train an ordinary differential equation model motivated by rectified flow. Its symmetric training objective supports movement in both directions between images and masks. For segmentation, this addresses the mismatch between random diffusion outputs and the desired unique segmentation result. The same framework can run in the opposite direction to synthesize images from semantic layouts.

Image synthesis also needs variation: a semantic layout can support diverse appearances. SemFlow introduces a finite perturbation approach to increase this diversity without changing semantic categories. Experiments show competitive performance on both segmentation and semantic image synthesis. The findings support the feasibility of unifying these tasks, while the proposed perturbations accommodate the different output requirements of generation and segmentation.
summary.tldr: SemFlow uses reversible rectified-flow transport between images and semantic masks to perform both segmentation and image synthesis.

title: SemFlow: Binding Semantic Segmentation and Image Synthesis via Rectified Flow

abstract: Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) has emerged as a pivotal approach for jointly learning scene geometry and semantics, enabling downstream applications such as navigation in mobile robotics. The recent generalization to Panoptic Scene Completion (PSC) advances the SSC domain by integrating instance-level information, thereby enhancing object-level sensitivity in scene understanding. While PSC was introduced using LiDAR modality, methods based on camera images remain largely unexplored. Moreover, recent Transformer-based approaches utilize a fixed set of learned queries to reconstruct objects within the scene volume. Although these queries are typically updated with image context during training, they remain static at test time, limiting their ability to dynamically adapt specifically to the observed scene. To overcome these limitations, we propose IPFormer, the first method that leverages context-adaptive instance proposals at train and test time to address vision-based 3D Panoptic Scene Completion. Specifically, IPFormer adaptively initializes these queries as panoptic instance proposals derived from image context and further refines them through attention-based encoding and decoding to reason about semantic instance-voxel relationships. Extensive experimental results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art in-domain performance, exhibits superior zero-shot generalization on out-of-domain data, and achieves a runtime reduction exceeding 14$\times$. These results highlight our introduction of context-adaptive instance proposals as a pioneering effort in addressing vision-based 3D Panoptic Scene Completion.

This extends scene understanding beyond identifying what occupies a location to identifying which object it belongs to. IPFormer studies this task using camera images, a setting the abstract describes as comparatively unexplored.

The method focuses on the queries used to reconstruct objects. Earlier transformer approaches begin with learned queries that remain fixed at test time, limiting their initial adaptation to the particular scene. IPFormer instead derives instance proposals from the image context during both training and testing. Attention-based encoding and decoding then refine these proposals to reason about relationships between object instances and scene voxels.

Starting from scene-dependent proposals gives the reconstruction process information specific to the observed image. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on in-domain data, stronger zero-shot generalization to out-of-domain data, and a runtime reduction exceeding 14 times. These results support context-adaptive initialization as a useful design choice for the evaluated camera-based 3D panoptic completion tasks.
summary.tldr: IPFormer uses image-dependent object proposals to improve camera-based 3D panoptic scene completion, generalization, and runtime.

title: IPFormer: Visual 3D Panoptic Scene Completion with Context-Adaptive Instance Proposals

abstract: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit strong generalization capabilities, enabling them to recognize a wide range of objects across diverse domains without additional training. However, they often retain irrelevant information beyond the requirements of specific target downstream tasks, raising concerns about computational efficiency and potential information leakage. This has motivated growing interest in approximate unlearning, which aims to selectively remove unnecessary knowledge while preserving overall model performance. Existing approaches to approximate unlearning have primarily focused on {\em class unlearning}, where a VLM is retrained to fail to recognize specified object classes while maintaining accuracy for others. However, merely forgetting object classes is often insufficient in practical applications. For instance, an autonomous driving system should accurately recognize {\em real} cars, while avoiding misrecognition of {\em illustrated} cars depicted in roadside advertisements as {\em real} cars, which could be hazardous. In this paper, we introduce {\em Approximate Domain Unlearning (ADU)}, a novel problem setting that requires reducing recognition accuracy for images from specified domains (e.g., {\em illustration}) while preserving accuracy for other domains (e.g., {\em real}). ADU presents new technical challenges: due to the strong domain generalization capability of pre-trained VLMs, domain distributions are highly entangled in the feature space, making naive approaches based on penalizing target domains ineffective. To tackle this limitation, we propose a novel approach that explicitly disentangles domain distributions and adaptively captures instance-specific domain information. Extensive experiments on four multi-domain benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms strong baselines built upon state-of-the-art VLM tuning techniques, paving the way for practical and fine-grained unlearning in VLMs. Code : https://kodaikawamura.github.io/Domain_Unlearning/.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a vision-language model can selectively lose recognition ability for a visual domain while retaining it elsewhere. The distinction is more specific than forgetting an object category. For example, a system might need to recognize real cars while avoiding treating illustrated cars in advertisements as real vehicles.

The authors introduce Approximate Domain Unlearning to formalize this goal. Its central difficulty comes from a strength of pretrained models: their representations connect objects across domains so effectively that the domains become intertwined. Simply penalizing recognition on the domain to be forgotten is therefore ineffective in the setting described. The proposed method explicitly separates domain distributions and adapts to domain information associated with individual examples.

Experiments on four datasets containing multiple domains show significant improvements over strong baselines based on existing vision-language model tuning techniques. These findings support finer control over which domains a model recognizes. The contribution concerns approximate, selective changes in recognition behavior rather than a demonstrated guarantee that every trace of domain knowledge has been erased.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a method for selectively reducing a vision-language model’s recognition of specified domains while preserving recognition elsewhere.

title: Approximate Domain Unlearning for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Diffusion-based generative processes, formulated as differential equation solving, frequently balance computational speed with sample quality. Our theoretical investigation of ODE- and SDE-based solvers reveals complementary weaknesses: ODE solvers accumulate irreducible gradient error along deterministic trajectories, while SDE methods suffer from amplified discretization errors when the step budget is limited. Building upon this insight, we introduce AdaSDE, a novel single-step SDE solver that aims to unify the efficiency of ODEs with the error resilience of SDEs. Specifically, we introduce a single per-step learnable coefficient, estimated via lightweight distillation, which dynamically regulates the error correction strength to accelerate diffusion sampling. Notably, our framework can be integrated with existing solvers to enhance their capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance: at 5 NFE, AdaSDE achieves FID scores of $4.18$ on CIFAR-10, $8.05$ on FFHQ and $6.96$ on LSUN Bedroom. Codes are available https://github.com/WLU-wry02/AdaSDE.
