paragraphs: Diffusion generation involves solving differential equations, and reducing the number of solver steps can compromise sample quality. The paper analyzes two sources of difficulty: deterministic ODE solvers accumulate gradient errors that their trajectories cannot eliminate, while stochastic SDE solvers can amplify errors introduced by taking discrete steps when only a small step budget is available.

AdaSDE addresses this trade-off with a single-step SDE solver that learns one coefficient for each sampling step. Estimated through lightweight distillation, the coefficient adjusts the strength of error correction as generation proceeds. This makes the correction adaptive rather than fixed throughout sampling. The framework can also be combined with existing solvers, extending its usefulness beyond a standalone sampling procedure.

The experiments report state-of-the-art results with five function evaluations: FID scores of 4.18 on CIFAR-10, 8.05 on FFHQ, and 6.96 on LSUN Bedroom. These findings support the paper’s central proposal that adapting stochastic correction can improve the balance between computational cost and generated sample quality.
summary.tldr: AdaSDE learns a per-step coefficient that adapts stochastic error correction to improve diffusion sampling with few function evaluations.

title: Adaptive Stochastic Coefficients for Accelerating Diffusion Sampling

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a biologically plausible and energy-efficient framework for temporal information processing. However, existing studies overlook a fundamental property widely observed in biological neurons—synaptic heterogeneity, which plays a crucial role in temporal processing and cognitive capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce HetSyn, a generalized framework that models synaptic heterogeneity with synapse-specific time constants. This design shifts temporal integration from the membrane potential to the synaptic current, enabling versatile timescale integration and allowing the model to capture diverse synaptic dynamics. We implement HetSyn as HetSynLIF, an extended form of the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model equipped with synapse-specific decay dynamics. By adjusting the parameter configuration, HetSynLIF can be specialized into vanilla LIF neurons, neurons with threshold adaptation, and neuron-level heterogeneous models. We demonstrate that HetSynLIF not only improves the performance of SNNs across a variety of tasks—including pattern generation, delayed match-to-sample, speech recognition, and visual recognition—but also exhibits strong robustness to noise, enhanced working memory performance, efficiency under limited neuron resources, and generalization across timescales. In addition, analysis of the learned synaptic time constants reveals trends consistent with empirical observations in biological synapses. These findings underscore the significance of synaptic heterogeneity in enabling efficient neural computation, offering new insights into brain-inspired temporal modeling. Code available at: https://github.com/dzcgood/HetSyn.

paragraphs: Temporal signals contain information that persists over different durations. HetSyn gives individual synapses in a spiking neural network their own time constants, allowing connections to retain and integrate information at different rates. This draws on the diversity of synaptic behavior observed in biological neurons.

The framework places temporal integration in synaptic currents and implements the idea through HetSynLIF, an extension of the leaky integrate-and-fire neuron. Different parameter configurations recover conventional LIF neurons, threshold-adapting neurons, and models with variation at the neuron level. This makes the proposal a general framework that contains several existing neuron designs as particular configurations.

The authors report improved performance on pattern generation, delayed matching, speech recognition, and visual recognition tasks. They also observe noise robustness, stronger working memory, effectiveness with limited numbers of neurons, and generalization across timescales. Learned time constants show trends consistent with biological observations. These findings support synapse-level temporal diversity as a useful ingredient for processing signals whose relevant information unfolds at multiple speeds.
summary.tldr: HetSyn assigns distinct temporal dynamics to individual synapses, improving reported spiking-network performance, memory, and robustness across tasks.

title: HetSyn: Versatile Timescale Integration in Spiking Neural Networks via Heterogeneous Synapses

abstract: 3D occupancy prediction is crucial for robust autonomous driving systems as it enables comprehensive perception of environmental structures and semantics. Most existing methods employ dense voxel-based scene representations, ignoring the sparsity of driving scenes and resulting in inefficiency. Recent works explore object-centric representations based on sparse Gaussians, but their ellipsoidal shape prior limits the modeling of diverse structures. In real-world driving scenes, objects exhibit rich geometries (e.g., cuboids, cylinders, and irregular shapes), necessitating excessive ellipsoidal Gaussians densely packed for accurate modeling, which leads to inefficient representations. To address this, we propose to use geometrically expressive superquadrics as scene primitives, enabling efficient representation of complex structures with fewer primitives through their inherent shape diversity. We develop a probabilistic superquadric mixture model, which interprets each superquadric as an occupancy probability distribution with a corresponding geometry prior, and calculates semantics through probabilistic mixture. Building on this, we present QuadricFormer, a superquadric-based model for efficient 3D occupancy prediction, and introduce a pruning-and-splitting module to further enhance modeling efficiency by concentrating superquadrics in occupied regions. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes and KITTI-360 datasets demonstrate that QuadricFormer achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining superior efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/zuosc19/QuadricFormer.

paragraphs: Semantic occupancy prediction describes which parts of a 3D scene are occupied and what those regions represent. Dense voxel grids can spend substantial representation effort on sparse driving scenes. Sparse Gaussian representations reduce that burden, but their ellipsoidal shapes can require many components to describe more varied structures accurately.

QuadricFormer represents scenes with superquadrics, geometric primitives with greater shape diversity. The authors build a probabilistic mixture model in which each primitive contributes an occupancy distribution and an associated geometry prior. Semantic information is calculated through the mixture. A pruning-and-splitting module further concentrates the primitives in occupied regions, directing representation capacity toward scene content.

Experiments on nuScenes and KITTI-360 report state-of-the-art prediction performance together with superior efficiency. The approach links geometric expressiveness to compactness: a primitive that better accommodates the structure being modeled can reduce the need for densely packed components. The reported results support superquadrics as an efficient basis for occupancy prediction in the evaluated driving datasets, combining scene geometry and semantics within the same probabilistic representation.
summary.tldr: QuadricFormer uses shape-flexible superquadrics to achieve accurate, efficient 3D semantic occupancy prediction with fewer scene primitives.

title: QuadricFormer: Scene as Superquadrics for 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction

abstract: Robust validation metrics remain essential in contemporary deep learning, not only to detect overfitting and poor generalization, but also to monitor training dynamics. In the supervised classification setting, we investigate whether interactions between training data and model weights can yield such a metric that both tracks generalization during training and attributes performance to individual training samples. We introduce Gradient-Weight Alignment (GWA), quantifying the coherence between per-sample gradients and model weights. We show that effective learning corresponds to coherent alignment, while misalignment indicates deteriorating generalization. GWA is efficiently computable during training and reflects both sample-specific contributions and dataset-wide learning dynamics. Extensive experiments show that GWA accurately predicts optimal early stopping, enables principled model comparisons, and identifies influential training samples, providing a validation-set-free approach for model analysis directly from the training data.

paragraphs: Monitoring generalization usually requires information about whether training progress also improves performance beyond the training examples. This paper investigates whether a useful signal can instead come directly from interactions between individual training samples and the model's weights. Its setting is supervised classification, with an emphasis on monitoring training and understanding sample contributions.

The proposed measure, Gradient-Weight Alignment, quantifies coherence between each sample's gradient and the model weights. The authors associate coherent alignment with effective learning and misalignment with deteriorating generalization. Because the measure is computed per sample, it can describe individual examples as well as broader learning dynamics across the dataset.

Experiments show that GWA predicts optimal early stopping, supports comparisons between models, and identifies influential training samples. The paper also describes it as efficient to compute during training. These findings make GWA a proposed validation-set-free tool for model analysis in the studied classification settings, connecting a training-time measurement to both practical training decisions and the roles played by particular examples.
summary.tldr: Gradient-Weight Alignment uses training-sample gradients and model weights to track generalization and guide model analysis without a validation set.

title: Gradient-Weight Alignment as a Train-Time Proxy for Generalization in Classification Tasks

abstract: How should feedback influence recurrent neural network (RNN) learning? One way to address the known limitations of backpropagation through time is to directly adjust neural activities during the learning process. However, it remains unclear how to effectively use feedback to shape RNN dynamics. Here, we introduce error forcing (EF), where the network activity is guided orthogonally toward the zero-error manifold during learning. This method contrasts with alternatives like teaching forcing, which impose stronger constraints on neural activity and thus induce larger feedback influence on circuit dynamics. Furthermore, EF can be understood from a Bayesian perspective as a form of approximate dynamic inference. Empirically, EF consistently outperforms other learning algorithms across several tasks and its benefits persist when additional biological constraints are taken into account. Overall, EF is a powerful temporal credit assignment mechanism and a promising candidate model for learning in biological systems.

paragraphs: Learning in a recurrent neural network requires assigning responsibility for errors across activity that unfolds over time. This paper explores how feedback can directly guide neural activity during learning, addressing known difficulties with backpropagation through time. Its central question is how to use corrective feedback effectively without imposing unnecessarily strong constraints on the network’s evolving dynamics.

The proposed method, error forcing, guides activity orthogonally toward the zero-error manifold: the set of activity configurations associated with zero error. This geometric rule specifies the direction of correction. Compared with alternatives that more strongly prescribe neural activity, the method exerts less feedback influence on circuit dynamics. The authors also interpret it as approximate dynamic inference from a Bayesian perspective.

Across several tasks, error forcing consistently outperforms the other learning algorithms evaluated. Its benefits remain when additional biological constraints are included. These results support error forcing as a temporal credit-assignment mechanism and a promising candidate model for biological learning. The biological connection is a proposed modeling role, supported by those constrained evaluations.
summary.tldr: Error forcing improves recurrent-network learning by directing neural activity toward zero-error configurations with comparatively restrained feedback.

title: Error Forcing in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: The advancement of AI systems for mental health support is hindered by limited access to therapeutic conversation data, particularly for trauma treatment. We present Thousand Voices of Trauma, a synthetic benchmark dataset of 3,000 therapy conversations based on Prolonged Exposure therapy protocols for Post-traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). The dataset comprises 500 unique cases, each explored through six conversational perspectives that mirror the progression of therapy from initial anxiety to peak distress to emotional processing. We incorporated diverse demographic profiles (ages 18-80, M=49.3, 49.4\% male, 44.4\% female, 6.2\% non-binary), 20 trauma types, and 10 trauma-related behaviors using deterministic and probabilistic generation methods. Analysis reveals realistic distributions of trauma types (witnessing violence 10.6\%, bullying 10.2\%) and symptoms (nightmares 23.4\%, substance abuse 20.8\%). Clinical experts validated the dataset's therapeutic fidelity, highlighting its emotional depth while suggesting refinements for greater authenticity. We also developed an emotional trajectory benchmark with standardized metrics for evaluating model responses. This privacy-preserving dataset addresses critical gaps in trauma-focused mental health data, offering a valuable resource for advancing both patient-facing applications and clinician training tools.

title: Thousand Voices of Trauma: A Large-Scale Synthetic Dataset for Modeling Prolonged Exposure Therapy Conversations

abstract: Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable achievements in recent years, they remain vulnerable to adversarial examples that result in harmful responses. Existing attacks typically focus on optimizing adversarial perturbations for a certain multimodal image-prompt pair or fixed training dataset, which often leads to overfitting. Consequently, these perturbations fail to remain malicious once transferred to attack unseen image-prompt pairs, suffering from significant resource costs to cover the diverse multimodal inputs in complicated real-world scenarios. To alleviate this issue, this paper proposes a novel adversarial attack on MLLMs based on distribution approximation theory, which models the potential image-prompt input distribution and adds the same distribution-fitting adversarial perturbation on multimodal input pairs to achieve effective cross-image/prompt transfer attacks. Specifically, we exploit the Laplace approximation to model the Gaussian distribution of the image and prompt inputs for the MLLM, deriving an estimate of the mean and covariance parameters. By sampling from this approximated distribution with Monte Carlo mechanism, we efficiently optimize and fit a single input‑agnostic perturbation over diverse image‑prompt pairs, yielding strong universality and transferability. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify the strong adversarial capabilities of our proposed attack against prevalent MLLMs spanning a spectrum of images/prompts.

paragraphs: Adversarial perturbations can cause multimodal language models to produce harmful responses. However, a perturbation optimized for a particular image and prompt, or a fixed dataset, may transfer poorly to unfamiliar inputs. This paper studies how to create a shared perturbation that remains effective across different images and prompts.

The approach models a distribution of possible inputs instead of optimizing only against a fixed collection of pairs. It uses a Laplace approximation to obtain a Gaussian representation with estimated mean and covariance parameters. Monte Carlo samples from that approximation then guide optimization of one input-agnostic perturbation across varied image–prompt combinations.

The authors report strong adversarial performance and transferability in experiments involving prevalent multimodal models and a range of images and prompts. The finding is that fitting an approximate input distribution can help reduce the overfitting associated with more narrowly optimized attacks. The reported universality concerns transfer across the evaluated settings; the method’s underlying representation remains an approximation of the potential input distribution.
summary.tldr: Approximating the image–prompt input distribution helps train a shared adversarial perturbation that transfers across varied multimodal inputs.

title: Fit the Distribution: Cross-Image/Prompt Adversarial Attacks on Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Pose-free Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) aims at novel view synthesis (NVS) without relying on accurate poses, exhibiting significant practical value. Image and LiDAR point cloud are two pivotal modalities in autonomous driving scenarios. While demonstrating impressive performance, single-modality pose-free NeRFs often suffer from local optima due to the limited geometric information provided by dense image textures or the sparse, textureless nature of point clouds. Although prior methods have explored the complementary strengths of both modalities, they have only leveraged inherently sparse point clouds for discrete, non-pixel-wise depth supervision, and are limited to NVS of images. As a result, a Multimodal Unified Pose-free framework remains notably absent. In light of this, we propose MUP, a pose-free framework for LiDAR-Camera joint NVS in large-scale scenes. This unified framework enables continuous depth supervision for image reconstruction using LiDAR-Fields rather than discrete point clouds. By leveraging multimodal inputs, pose optimization receives gradients from the rendering loss of point cloud geometry and image texture, thereby alleviating the issue of local optima commonly encountered in single-modality pose-free tasks. Moreover, to further guide pose optimization of NeRF, we propose a multimodal geometric optimizer that leverages geometric relations from point clouds and photometric regularization from adjacent image frames. Besides, to alleviate the domain gap between modalities, we propose a multimodal-specific coarse-to-fine training approach for unified, compact reconstruction. Extensive experiments on KITTI-360 and NuScenes datasets demonstrate MUP's superiority in accomplishing geometry-aware, modality-consistent, and pose-free 3D reconstruction.

paragraphs: MUP reconstructs large scenes and synthesizes new camera and LiDAR views without depending on accurate input poses. Cameras provide rich texture but limited geometric information, while LiDAR point clouds provide sparse geometry without texture. Using either modality alone can leave pose optimization stuck in poor local solutions.

The framework combines the modalities through unified neural fields. A LiDAR field supplies continuous depth supervision for image reconstruction, extending beyond discrete supervision at measured points. Pose updates receive learning signals from both rendered point-cloud geometry and image texture. A multimodal geometric optimizer adds point-cloud geometric relationships and photometric regularization between neighboring image frames to further guide pose estimation.

MUP also uses a modality-specific coarse-to-fine training process to reduce differences between the inputs and obtain a compact reconstruction. Experiments on KITTI-360 and NuScenes show superior geometry-aware and modality-consistent reconstruction in the evaluated pose-free setting. The contribution is joint reconstruction and pose optimization: each sensor's strengths help constrain the other, while the framework supports novel-view synthesis for both modalities.
summary.tldr: MUP jointly reconstructs camera and LiDAR observations, using complementary geometry and texture to improve novel-view synthesis without accurate input poses.

title: Multimodal LiDAR-Camera Novel View Synthesis with Unified Pose-free Neural Fields

abstract: Point clouds captured by scanning sensors are often perturbed by noise, which have a highly negative impact on downstream tasks (e.g. surface reconstruction and shape understanding). Previous works mostly focus on training neural networks with noisy-clean point cloud pairs for learning denoising priors, which requires extensively manual efforts. In this work, we introduce U-CAN, an Unsupervised framework for point cloud denoising with Consistency-Aware Noise2Noise matching. Specifically, we leverage a neural network to infer a multi-step denoising path for each point of a shape or scene with a noise to noise matching schema. We achieve this by a novel loss which enables statistical reasoning on multiple noisy point cloud observations. We further introduce a novel constraint on the denoised geometry consistency for learning consistency-aware denoising patterns. We justify that the proposed constraint is a general term which is not limited to 3D domain and can also contribute to the area of 2D image denoising. Our evaluations under the widely used benchmarks in point cloud denoising, upsampling and image denoising show significant improvement over the state-of-the-art unsupervised methods, where U-CAN also produces comparable results with the supervised methods. In this work, we introduce U-CAN, an Unsupervised framework for point cloud denoising with Consistency-Aware Noise2Noise matching. We achieve this by a novel loss which enables statistical reasoning on multiple noisy point cloud observations. We further introduce a novel constraint on the denoised geometry consistency for learning consistency-aware denoising patterns. We justify that the proposed constraint is a general term which is not limited to 3D domain and can also contribute to the area of 2D image denoising. paragraphs: Noise in scanned point clouds can impair surface reconstruction and shape understanding. Many learned denoisers require paired noisy and clean examples, whose preparation involves substantial manual effort. U-CAN instead learns from multiple noisy observations through a noise-to-noise matching approach, avoiding the requirement for clean training counterparts.

A neural network predicts a multistep denoising path for each point in a shape or scene. A new loss enables statistical reasoning across noisy observations, while an additional constraint encourages consistency in the recovered geometry. These components combine evidence from noisy measurements with a requirement that the denoised output maintain coherent structure.

The authors argue that their consistency constraint is not specific to three-dimensional geometry and can also support image denoising. Evaluations cover point-cloud denoising, upsampling, and two-dimensional image denoising. They report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art unsupervised methods and results comparable to supervised methods. The findings support learning useful denoising behavior from noisy observations when geometry consistency is included in the training objective.
summary.tldr: U-CAN learns denoising from noisy observations using multistep predictions and consistency constraints, with competitive results across point-cloud and image tasks.

title: U-CAN: Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising with Consistency-Aware Noise2Noise Matching

abstract: To enhance controllability in text-to-image generation, ControlNet introduces image-based control signals, while ControlNet++ improves pixel-level cycle consistency between generated images and the input control signal. To avoid the prohibitive cost of back-propagating through the sampling process, ControlNet++ optimizes only low-noise timesteps (e.g., $t < 200$) using a single-step approximation, which not only ignores the contribution of high-noise timesteps but also introduces additional approximation errors. A straightforward alternative for optimizing controllability across all timesteps is Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), a fine-tuning method that increases model preference for more controllable images ($I^{w}$) over less controllable ones ($I^{l}$). However, due to uncertainty in generative models, it is difficult to ensure that win--lose image pairs differ only in controllability while keeping other factors, such as image quality, fixed. To address this, we propose performing preference learning over control conditions rather than generated images. Specifically, we construct winning and losing control signals, $\mathbf{c}^{w}$ and $\mathbf{c}^{l}$, and train the model to prefer $\mathbf{c}^{w}$. This method, which we term \textit{Condition Preference Optimization} (CPO), eliminates confounding factors and yields a low-variance training objective. Our approach theoretically exhibits lower contrastive loss variance than DPO and empirically achieves superior results. Moreover, CPO requires less computation and storage for dataset curation. Extensive experiments show that CPO significantly improves controllability over the state-of-the-art ControlNet++ across multiple control types: over $10\%$ error rate reduction in segmentation, $70$--$80\%$ in human pose, and consistent $2$--$5\%$ reductions in edge and depth maps. The error rate is defined as the difference between the evaluated controllability and the oracle results. Our project is available \textcolor{blue}{\href{https://zonglinl.github.io/CPO_page}{here}}.

Condition Preference Optimization changes what gets compared. It constructs preferred and disfavored control signals and trains the model to prefer the better condition. The paper presents this as removing the confounding factors in image-pair comparisons. It theoretically establishes lower contrastive-loss variance than Direct Preference Optimization and reports lower computation and storage costs for preparing training data.

These findings suggest that choosing cleaner preference comparisons can improve both training efficiency and control fidelity.

title: CPO: Condition Preference Optimization for Controllable Image Generation

abstract: Audio source separation is fundamental for machines to understand complex acoustic environments and underpins numerous audio applications. Current supervised deep learning approaches, while powerful, are limited by the need for extensive, task-specific labeled data and struggle to generalize to the immense variability and open-set nature of real-world acoustic scenes. Inspired by the success of generative foundation models, we investigate whether pre-trained text-guided audio diffusion models can overcome these limitations. We make a surprising discovery: zero-shot source separation can be achieved purely through a pre-trained text-guided audio diffusion model under the right configuration. Our method, named ZeroSep, works by inverting the mixed audio into the diffusion model's latent space and then using text conditioning to guide the denoising process to recover individual sources. Without any task-specific training or fine-tuning, ZeroSep repurposes the generative diffusion model for a discriminative separation task and inherently supports open-set scenarios through its rich textual priors. ZeroSep is compatible with a variety of pre-trained text-guided audio diffusion backbones and delivers strong separation performance on multiple separation benchmarks, surpassing even supervised methods.

paragraphs: Audio source separation aims to recover individual sounds from a mixture. Supervised systems often need extensive labeled data tailored to the task and struggle with the variety of real acoustic scenes. ZeroSep investigates whether a pretrained text-guided audio diffusion model can perform separation without any task-specific training or fine-tuning.

The method first inverts the mixed recording into the diffusion model's latent space. It then uses text conditioning during denoising to guide recovery of individual sources. Under the right configuration, the model's existing generative capabilities support this separation task. Its textual priors also enable open-set scenarios, where the sounds of interest need not be confined to a fixed task-specific set.

The authors show compatibility with multiple pretrained text-guided audio diffusion backbones and strong results across several separation benchmarks, including performance above supervised methods. The zero-training claim concerns adaptation for separation: the approach still relies on a pretrained foundation model. Its main finding is that suitable inversion and text-guided denoising can repurpose that model for source recovery without additional task-specific learning.
summary.tldr: ZeroSep repurposes pretrained text-guided audio diffusion models for source separation through inversion and denoising, without task-specific training.

title: ZeroSep: Separate Anything in Audio with Zero Training

abstract: Multi-modal Knowledge Graph Completion (MMKGC) aims to predict missing entities, relations, or attributes in knowledge graphs by collaboratively modeling the triple structure and multimodal information (e.g., text, images, videos) associated with entities. This approach facilitates the automatic discovery of previously unobserved factual knowledge. However, existing MMKGC methods encounter several critical challenges: (i) the imbalance of inter-entity information across different modalities; (ii) the heterogeneity of intra-entity multimodal information; and (iii) for a given entity, the informational contributions of different modalities are inconsistent across contexts. In this paper, we propose a novel **L**arge model-driven **B**alanced **M**ultimodal **K**nowledge **G**raph **C**ompletion framework, termed LBMKGC. Subsequently, to bridge the semantic gap between heterogeneous modalities, LBMKGC aligns the multimodal embeddings of entities semantically by using the CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training) model. Furthermore, LBMKGC adaptively fuses multimodal embeddings with relational guidance by distinguishing between the perceptual and conceptual attributes of triples. Finally, extensive experiments conducted against 21 state-of-the-art baselines demonstrate that LBMKGC achieves superior performance across diverse datasets and scenarios while maintaining efficiency and generalizability. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/guoynow/LBMKGC.

paragraphs: Multimodal knowledge graph completion predicts missing graph information using both relational structure and content associated with entities. That content can include text, images, or videos. The paper identifies several obstacles: entities have unequal information across modalities, different modalities describe the same entity differently, and their usefulness changes with the relational context.

LBMKGC uses CLIP to bring heterogeneous entity embeddings into better semantic alignment. It then combines those embeddings adaptively with guidance from the relation being considered. Distinguishing perceptual and conceptual attributes of triples helps determine how information should be fused, so the contribution of a modality can depend on the particular prediction.

This design addresses both compatibility between representations and variation in which evidence is useful. The authors compare LBMKGC with 21 state-of-the-art baselines and report superior performance across diverse datasets and scenarios while maintaining efficiency and generalizability. The findings support treating multimodal graph completion as context-dependent evidence combination, with semantic alignment and relational guidance working together to predict missing knowledge.
summary.tldr: LBMKGC combines CLIP-based semantic alignment with relation-guided multimodal fusion to improve knowledge graph completion.

title: LBMKGC: Large Model-Driven Balanced Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion

abstract: Pretrained language models are remarkably effective in aligning with human brain responses elicited by natural language stimuli, positioning them as promising model organisms for studying language processing in the brain. However, existing approaches for both estimating and improving this brain alignment are participant-dependent and highly affected by the amount of data available per participant, hindering both generalization to new participants and population-level analyses. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing a scalable, generalizable brain-tuning method, in which we fine-tune pretrained speech language models to jointly predict fMRI responses from multiple participants. We demonstrate that the resulting brain-tuned models exhibit strong individual brain alignment while generalizing across participants. Specifically, our method leads to 1) a 5-fold decrease in the amount of fMRI data needed to predict brain data from new participants, 2) up to a 50\% increase in the overall brain alignment, and 3) strong generalization to new unseen datasets. Furthermore, this multi-participant brain-tuning additionally improves downstream performance on semantic tasks, suggesting that training using brain data from multiple participants leads to more generalizable semantic representations. Taken together, these findings demonstrate a bidirectional benefit between neuroscience and AI, helping bridge the gap between the two fields. We make our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/bridge-ai-neuro/multi-brain-tuning.

paragraphs: Speech and language models can help study language processing by predicting brain responses to language. Existing methods often depend heavily on the particular participant and the amount of brain data collected from that person. This makes it difficult to transfer a model to someone new or use it to investigate patterns across a population.

The authors fine-tune pretrained speech language models to predict fMRI responses from several participants jointly. This shared training aims to retain alignment with individual brains while learning representations that generalize between people. It moves the learning process beyond fitting a separate participant's responses in isolation.

The resulting models need five times less fMRI data to predict responses from new participants, show up to a 50% increase in overall brain alignment, and generalize strongly to unseen datasets. They also improve on downstream semantic tasks. That last finding suggests that learning from multiple participants' brain responses can improve semantic representations as well as brain prediction. The evidence therefore supports benefits in both directions: better tools for neuroscience and useful training signals for AI.
summary.tldr: Training speech models jointly on multiple participants' brain responses improves brain alignment, data efficiency, and semantic task performance.

title: Brain-tuning Improves Generalizability and Efficiency of Brain Alignment in Speech Models

abstract: Urban warming differs markedly from regional background trends, highlighting the unique behavior of urban climates and the challenges they present. Accurately predicting local urban climate necessitates modeling the interactions between urban surfaces and atmospheric forcing. Although off-the-shelf machine learning (ML) algorithms offer considerable accuracy for climate prediction, they often function as black boxes, learning data mappings rather than capturing physical evolution. As a result, they struggle to capture key land-atmosphere interactions and may produce physically inconsistent predictions. To address these limitations, we propose UCformer, a novel multi-task, physics-guided Transformer architecture designed to emulate nonlinear urban climate processes. UCformer jointly estimates 2-m air temperature $\(T\)$, specific humidity $\(q\)$, and dew point temperature $\(t\)$ in urban areas, while embedding domain and physical priors into its learning structure. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating domain and physical knowledge leads to significant improvements in emulation accuracy and generalizability under future urban climate scenarios. Further analysis reveals that learning shared correlations across cities enables the model to capture transferable urban surface–atmosphere interaction patterns, resulting in improved accuracy in urban climate emulation. Finally, UCformer shows strong potential to fit real-world data: when fine-tuned with limited observational data, it achieves competitive performance in estimating urban heat fluxes compared to a physics-based model.

The system jointly estimates two-meter air temperature, specific humidity, and dew-point temperature. Analysis supports the value of shared cross-city patterns, and fine-tuning with limited observations yields heat-flux estimates competitive with a physics-based model. The contribution combines structured learning with data adaptation: physical priors guide the model, while observations help tailor it to real urban conditions.
summary.tldr: UCformer incorporates physical and domain priors into shared urban-climate prediction.

title: Learning Urban Climate Dynamics via Physics-Guided Urban Surface–Atmosphere Interactions

abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) has achieved remarkable performance, yet its learned model representations and decision rationale remain a black box. This impedes both academic research and practical deployment, since researchers and stakeholders require deeper insights into NCO models. In this paper, we take the first critical step towards interpreting NCO models by investigating their representations through various probing tasks. Moreover, we introduce a novel probing tool named Coefficient Significance Probing (CS-Probing) to enable deeper analysis of NCO representations by examining the coefficients and statistical significance during probing. Extensive experiments and analysis reveal that NCO models encode low-level information essential for solution construction, while capturing high-level knowledge to facilitate better decisions. Using CS-Probing, we find that prevalent NCO models impose varying inductive biases on their learned representations, uncover direct evidence related to model generalization, and identify key embedding dimensions associated with specific knowledge. These insights can be potentially translated into practice, for example, with minor code modifications, we improve the generalization of the analyzed model. Our work represents a first systematic attempt to interpret black-box NCO models, showcasing probing as a promising tool for analyzing their internal mechanisms and revealing insights for the NCO community. The source code is publicly available.

This paper investigates what information those representations contain through a collection of probing tasks. This provides a concrete example of interpretation informing model development. The broader contribution is a systematic approach to inspecting internal representations, with results that make probing a promising tool for understanding neural optimization models and identifying potentially useful changes.
summary.tldr: Coefficient Significance Probing reveals knowledge encoded in neural optimization models and helps inform a demonstrated generalization improvement.

title: Probing Neural Combinatorial Optimization Models

abstract: For continuing tasks, average cost Markov decision processes have well-documented value and can be solved using efficient algorithms. However, it explicitly assumes that the agent is risk-neutral. In this work, we extend risk-neutral algorithms to accommodate the more general class of dynamic risk measures. Specifically, we propose a relative value iteration (RVI) algorithm for planning and design two model-free Q-learning algorithms, namely a generic algorithm based on the multi-level Monte Carlo (MLMC) method, and an off-policy algorithm dedicated to utility-based shortfall risk measures. Both the RVI and MLMC-based Q-learning algorithms are proven to converge to optimality. Numerical experiments validate our analysis, confirm empirically the convergence of the off-policy algorithm, and demonstrate that our approach enables the identification of policies that are finely tuned to the intricate risk-awareness of the agent that they serve.

paragraphs: Average-cost Markov decision processes describe continuing decision problems, but their conventional formulation assumes a risk-neutral agent. This paper extends planning and learning methods to dynamic risk measures. The goal is to find policies that reflect how an agent evaluates risk over time, beyond its preference for lower average cost.

For planning, the authors propose a relative value iteration algorithm. For learning without a model, they develop two Q-learning methods: a general approach using multi-level Monte Carlo and an off-policy approach tailored to utility-based shortfall risk measures. These methods address different settings within the broader effort to incorporate risk preferences into continuing-task decisions.

The relative value iteration method and the Monte Carlo-based Q-learning method are proven to converge to optimality. Numerical experiments support the analysis and provide empirical evidence of convergence for the off-policy method. The experiments also demonstrate policies tuned to the agent’s risk preferences. The distinction in evidence matters: two algorithms receive convergence proofs, while the specialized off-policy algorithm’s convergence is supported by the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper extends average-cost planning and Q-learning to risk-aware decisions, proving optimal convergence for two proposed algorithms.

title: Planning and Learning in Average Risk-aware MDPs

abstract: Training foundation models such as ViTs and LLMs requires tremendous computing cost. Low-rank matrix or tensor factorization offers a parameter-efficient alternative, but often downgrades performance due to the restricted parameter space. In this work, we introduce ${\textbf{Latent Crossing (LaX)}}$ -- a simple yet effective plug-and-play module that enhances the capacity of low-rank models by enabling information flow across low-rank subspaces. We extensively validate the benefits of LaX on pre-training tasks with ViT-Base/Large and LLaMA-like models ranging from 60M to 1B parameters. LaX boosts low-rank model performance to match or exceed the full-rank baselines while using 2-3$\times$ fewer parameters. When equipped with low-rank adapters (i.e., LoRA) for fine-tuning LLaMA-7/13B, LaX consistently improves performance on arithmetic and common sense reasoning tasks with negligible cost.

paragraphs: Low-rank factorization reduces the parameter demands of foundation models by restricting how their weights are represented. That restriction can also reduce performance because the model has a smaller space of possible parameter configurations. Latent Crossing, or LaX, aims to recover useful capacity while retaining the parameter savings of low-rank training.

LaX is a plug-in module that enables information to move across low-rank subspaces. The authors evaluate it during pretraining with ViT-Base and ViT-Large, as well as LLaMA-like language models ranging from 60 million to one billion parameters. In these experiments, the enhanced low-rank models match or exceed full-rank baselines while using two to three times fewer parameters.

The paper also applies LaX to LoRA adapters when fine-tuning LLaMA models with seven and thirteen billion parameters. It consistently improves arithmetic and commonsense reasoning performance with negligible additional cost. The results cover both pretraining and adapter-based fine-tuning, supporting the value of connecting low-rank subspaces across these two uses of parameter-efficient modeling.
summary.tldr: LaX connects low-rank subspaces, helping tested models match or exceed full-rank performance with fewer parameters and improving LoRA fine-tuning.

title: LaX: Boosting Low-Rank Training of Foundation Models via Latent Crossing

abstract: Computing partial differential equation (PDE) operators via nested backpropagation is expensive, yet popular, and severely restricts their utility for scientific machine learning. Recent advances, like the forward Laplacian and randomizing Taylor mode automatic differentiation (AD), propose forward schemes to address this. We introduce an optimization technique for Taylor mode that 'collapses' derivatives by rewriting the computational graph, and demonstrate how to apply it to general linear PDE operators, and randomized Taylor mode. The modifications simply require propagating a sum up the computational graph, which could---or should---be done by a machine learning compiler, without exposing complexity to users. We implement our collapsing procedure and evaluate it on popular PDE operators, confirming it accelerates Taylor mode and outperforms nested backpropagation.

paragraphs: Scientific machine learning often needs derivatives combined into partial differential equation operators. Computing these quantities through nested backpropagation is popular but expensive, which restricts their practical use. Forward differentiation approaches, including Taylor-mode automatic differentiation, offer another route. This paper improves how Taylor mode carries out the required derivative computations.

The proposed optimization rewrites the computational graph to collapse derivatives. Its essential modification is to propagate a sum through the graph. The authors show how this procedure applies to general linear partial differential equation operators and to randomized Taylor mode. The contribution therefore concerns the organization of derivative computation, with applications across these operator settings.

The authors implement the procedure and evaluate it on commonly used differential operators. Their results show faster Taylor-mode computation and better performance than nested backpropagation in those evaluations. They also argue that a machine learning compiler could perform the required graph changes, keeping the added complexity away from users. That compiler integration is presented as a possibility, while the implemented acceleration supplies the empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: Rewriting computational graphs to collapse derivative calculations accelerates Taylor-mode differentiation for partial differential equation operators.

title: Collapsing Taylor Mode Automatic Differentiation

abstract: Recent advancements in low-light video enhancement (LLVE) have increasingly leveraged both RGB and event cameras to improve video quality under challenging conditions. However, existing approaches share two key drawbacks. First, they are tuned for steady low-light scenes, so their performance drops when illumination varies. Second, they assume every sensing modality is always available, while real systems may lose or corrupt one of them. These limitations make the methods brittle in dynamic, real-world settings. In this paper, we propose EVDiffuser, a novel framework for consistent LLVE that integrates RGB and event data through a modality-adaptive diffusion pipeline. By harnessing the powerful priors of video diffusion models, EVDiffuser enables consistent video enhancement and generalization to diverse scenarios under varying illumination, where RGB or events may even be absent. Specifically, we first design a modality-agnostic conditioning mechanism based on a diffusion pipeline by treating the two modalities as optional conditions, which is fine-tuned using augmented and integrated datasets. Furthermore, we introduce a modality-adaptive guidance rescaling that dynamically adjusts the contribution of each modality according to sensor-specific characteristics. Additionally, we establish a benchmark that accounts for varying illumination and diverse real-world scenarios, facilitating future research on consistent event-guided LLVE. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across challenging scenarios (i.e., varying illumination) and sensor-based settings (e.g., event-only, RGB-only), highlighting the generalization of our framework.

paragraphs: Low-light video enhancement can combine RGB images with event-camera data, but the paper identifies two weaknesses in existing approaches. They are often tuned for steady lighting, and they expect both sensors to remain available. Changing illumination or losing a sensing modality can therefore undermine video quality in the situations where enhancement is needed.

This conditioning mechanism allows the same pipeline to operate with both modalities or with either one alone. The model is fine-tuned using augmented and integrated datasets. A guidance rescaling mechanism adjusts how strongly each modality contributes according to its sensor-specific characteristics.

The authors also introduce a benchmark covering varying illumination and diverse real-world scenarios. Their experiments report state-of-the-art performance in challenging lighting conditions and across sensor configurations, including event-only and RGB-only inputs. The contribution combines flexible sensing with video diffusion priors, supporting consistent enhancement in the evaluated settings even when the available input modalities change.
summary.tldr: EVDiffuser adapts video enhancement to changing illumination and optional RGB or event inputs through flexible diffusion conditioning.

title: Event-Guided Consistent Video Enhancement with Modality-Adaptive Diffusion Pipeline

abstract: We study the problem of no-regret learning algorithms for general monotone and smooth games and their last-iterate convergence properties. Specifically, we investigate the problem under bandit feedback and strongly uncoupled dynamics, which allows modular development of the multi-player system that applies to a wide range of real applications. We propose a mirror-descent-based algorithm, which converges in $O(T^{-1/4})$ and is also no-regret. The result is achieved by a dedicated use of two regularizations and the analysis of the fixed point thereof. The convergence rate is further improved to $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the case of strongly monotone games. Motivated by practical tasks where the game evolves over time, the algorithm is extended to time-varying monotone games. We provide the first non-asymptotic result in converging monotone games and give improved results for equilibrium tracking games.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning in multiplayer games when each player receives bandit feedback and follows strongly uncoupled dynamics. The aim is to support modular learning while obtaining both no-regret behavior and convergence of the latest decisions. Last-iterate convergence matters because it concerns the players' current actions, rather than only an average over their learning history.

For smooth monotone games, the authors propose a mirror-descent-based algorithm with a convergence rate of order T to the minus one-quarter, where T is the number of rounds. The algorithm also satisfies a no-regret guarantee. Its analysis relies on two regularizations and their associated fixed point. Under the stronger assumption of strong monotonicity, the convergence rate improves to order T to the minus one-half.

The framework extends to games that change over time. The paper provides a non-asymptotic result for converging monotone games and improved equilibrium-tracking results. These guarantees distinguish stable learning in a fixed game from following changing equilibria, while retaining the limited-feedback and decentralized learning setting.
summary.tldr: A mirror-descent algorithm achieves no regret and last-iterate convergence in monotone games with bandit feedback and strongly uncoupled learning.

title: Uncoupled and Convergent Learning in Monotone Games under Bandit Feedback

abstract: Multimodal models have demonstrated powerful capabilities in complex tasks requiring multimodal alignment, including zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval. However, existing models typically rely on millions of paired multimodal samples, which are prohibitively expensive or infeasible to obtain in many domains. In this work, we explore the feasibility of building multimodal models with limited amount of paired data by aligning pretrained unimodal foundation models. We show that high-quality alignment is possible with as few as tens of thousands of paired samples$\unicode{x2013}$less than 1\% of the data typically used in the field. To achieve this, we introduce STRUCTURE, an effective regularization technique that preserves the neighborhood geometry of the latent space of unimodal encoders. Additionally, we show that aligning last layers is often suboptimal and demonstrate the benefits of aligning the layers with the highest representational similarity across modalities. These two components can be readily incorporated into existing alignment methods, yielding substantial gains across 24 zero-shot image classification and retrieval benchmarks, with average relative improvement of 51.6\% in classification and 91.8\% in retrieval tasks. Our results highlight the effectiveness and broad applicability of our framework for limited-sample multimodal learning and offer a promising path forward for resource-constrained domains.

paragraphs: Multimodal alignment often depends on millions of paired examples, which can be difficult to obtain in specialized domains. This paper instead aligns existing unimodal foundation models using much smaller paired datasets. It shows high-quality alignment with tens of thousands of pairs, less than 1% of the amount typically used in the field.

The proposed STRUCTURE regularizer preserves neighborhood geometry in the encoders' latent spaces during alignment. This carries information about relationships among representations into the alignment process. A second component selects layers with the greatest representational similarity across modalities. The authors find that aligning final layers is often suboptimal, making layer selection another useful part of the method.

Both components can be incorporated into existing alignment approaches. Across 24 zero-shot image-classification and retrieval benchmarks, the paper reports average relative improvements of 51.6% for classification and 91.8% for retrieval. These results support combining structural preservation with compatible layer selection when paired data is scarce. The gains are reported as relative improvements, describing changes against the evaluated alignment methods.
summary.tldr: Preserving latent neighborhood structure and aligning compatible layers enables strong multimodal alignment with tens of thousands of paired examples.

title: With Limited Data for Multimodal Alignment, Let the STRUCTURE Guide You

abstract: Sparse feature selection has been demonstrated to be effective in handling high-dimensional data. While promising, most of the existing works use convex methods, which may be suboptimal in terms of the accuracy of feature selection and parameter estimation. In this paper, we expand a nonconvex paradigm to sparse group feature selection, which is motivated by applications that require identifying the underlying group structure and performing feature selection simultaneously. The main contributions of this article are twofold: (1) computationally, we introduce a nonconvex sparse group feature selection model and present an efficient optimization algorithm, of which the key step is a projection with two coupled constraints; (2) statistically, we show that the proposed model can reconstruct the oracle estimator. Therefore, consistent feature selection and parameter estimation can be achieved. Numerical results on synthetic and real-world data suggest that the proposed nonconvex method compares favorably against its competitors, thus achieving desired goal of delivering high performance.

paragraphs: Some high-dimensional learning problems require selecting useful individual features while also identifying relevant groups of features. The paper addresses these two decisions together through sparse group feature selection. It explores a nonconvex approach because commonly used convex methods may be suboptimal for selecting features accurately and estimating their associated parameters.

The computational contribution is a nonconvex model and an efficient optimization algorithm. A central step projects onto a set defined by two coupled constraints, reflecting the need to handle the selection requirements jointly. The statistical contribution is a result showing that the proposed model can reconstruct an oracle estimator, supporting the possibility of consistent feature selection and parameter estimation.

Numerical experiments use both synthetic and real-world data. Their results suggest favorable performance relative to competing methods. The paper thus combines an algorithmic proposal with a statistical recovery result: it aims to make nonconvex sparse group selection computationally practical while showing how the model can support accurate recovery, beyond the empirical comparisons alone.
summary.tldr: A nonconvex sparse group selection method combines efficient optimization with an oracle-recovery result and favorable numerical comparisons.

title: Efficient Sparse Group Feature Selection via Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: We consider regret minimization in adversarial deterministic Markov Decision Processes (ADMDPs) with bandit feedback. We devise a new algorithm that pushes the state-of-the-art forward in two ways: First, it attains a regret of O(T^2/3) with respect to the best fixed policy in hindsight, whereas the previous best regret bound was O(T^3/4). Second, the algorithm and its analysis are compatible with any feasible ADMDP graph topology, while all previous approaches required additional restrictions on the graph topology.
originalAbstract: We consider regret minimization in adversarial deterministic Markov Decision Processes (ADMDPs) with bandit feedback. We devise a new algorithm that pushes the state-of-the-art forward in two ways: First, it attains a regret of O(T^2/3) with respect to the best fixed policy in hindsight, whereas the previous best regret bound was O(T^3/4). Second, the algorithm and its analysis are compatible with any feasible ADMDP graph topology, while all previous approaches required additional restrictions on the graph topology.

paragraphs: This paper studies decision-making in adversarial deterministic Markov decision processes with bandit feedback. The learner must choose actions while receiving limited feedback about their consequences. Performance is measured through regret relative to the best fixed policy chosen in hindsight, so the comparison asks how much is lost by learning during interaction rather than knowing that policy beforehand.

The proposed algorithm improves the regret bound from the previous O(T^3/4) rate to O(T^2/3), where T represents the interaction horizon. The smaller exponent means the stated cumulative regret guarantee grows more slowly with the horizon. The comparator remains a fixed policy in hindsight; the result does not claim comparison with an unrestricted sequence of changing policies.

A separate contribution concerns the arrangement of states and transitions. Earlier approaches required additional restrictions on the process's graph topology. The new algorithm and analysis accommodate any feasible topology within the adversarial deterministic setting. Thus the paper improves both the regret rate and the range of graph structures covered by the guarantee.
summary.tldr: A new algorithm improves regret to O(T^2/3) for adversarial deterministic MDPs with bandit feedback while accommodating any feasible graph topology.

title: Better Rates for Any Adversarial Deterministic MDP

abstract: Model selection is one of the key issues both in recent research and application of kernel methods. Cross-validation is a commonly employed and widely accepted model selection criterion. However, it requires multiple times of training the algorithm under consideration, which is computationally intensive. In this paper, we present a novel strategy for approximating the cross-validation based on the Bouligand influence function (BIF), which only requires the solution of the algorithm once. The BIF measures the impact of an infinitesimal small amount of contamination of the original distribution. We first establish the link between the concept of BIF and the concept of cross-validation. The BIF is related to the first order term of a Taylor expansion. Then, we calculate the BIF and higher order BIFs, and apply these theoretical results to approximate the cross-validation error in practice. Experimental results demonstrate that our approximate cross-validation criterion is sound and efficient.

paragraphs: Cross-validation helps select a kernel model by evaluating how it performs when portions of the data are withheld. Its computational burden comes from repeatedly training the learning algorithm. This paper proposes approximating the cross-validation criterion using a single solution of the underlying algorithm, reducing the need for repeated fitting.

The approach uses the Bouligand influence function, which describes how a solution responds to an infinitesimal contamination of the original distribution. The authors establish a connection between that local sensitivity and cross-validation. They relate the influence function to a first-order Taylor expansion, then calculate both the basic influence function and higher-order versions to build practical approximations of cross-validation error.

Experiments support the resulting criterion as sound and efficient. The central contribution is to turn information about how a fitted model changes under distributional perturbations into a cheaper model-selection calculation. The result remains an approximation to cross-validation, with the empirical findings supporting its usefulness rather than asserting exact equality with repeated training.
summary.tldr: Bouligand influence functions approximate cross-validation error for kernel methods using only one fitted solution of the learning algorithm.

title: Efficient Approximation of Cross-Validation for Kernel Methods using Bouligand Influence Function

abstract: Denoising auto-encoders (DAEs) have been successfully used to learn new representations for a wide range of machine learning tasks. During training, DAEs make many passes over the training dataset and reconstruct it from partial corruption generated from a pre-specified corrupting distribution. This process learns robust representation, though at the expense of requiring many training epochs, in which the data is explicitly corrupted. In this paper we present the marginalized Denoising Auto-encoder (mDAE), which (approximately) marginalizes out the corruption during training. Effectively, the mDAE takes into account infinitely many corrupted copies of the training data in every epoch, and therefore is able to match or outperform the DAE with much fewer training epochs. We analyze our proposed algorithm and show that it can be understood as a classic auto-encoder with a special form of regularization. In empirical evaluations we show that it attains 1-2 order-of-magnitude speedup in training time over other competing approaches.

paragraphs: Denoising auto-encoders learn representations by reconstructing training examples from corrupted versions. This can encourage robustness, but explicitly generating corruptions over many passes through the data makes training costly. The paper proposes a marginalized denoising auto-encoder that changes how this corruption is handled, while retaining the goal of learning useful representations through denoising.

Instead of repeatedly relying on explicitly corrupted examples, the method approximately averages over the corruption distribution during training. Each epoch thereby accounts, in effect, for infinitely many corrupted copies. This allows the proposed method to match or outperform the ordinary denoising auto-encoder with substantially fewer epochs. The averaging is approximate, so the claim does not depend on computing an exact integral in every case.

The authors also analyze the method as a conventional auto-encoder with a particular form of regularization. This interpretation explains how accounting for corruption changes the learning objective. In empirical evaluations, they report training speedups of one to two orders of magnitude over competing approaches, supporting the practical value of replacing repeated explicit corruption with marginalization.
summary.tldr: Approximate marginalization over corruption lets denoising auto-encoders learn with fewer epochs and yields substantial reported training speedups.

title: Marginalized Denoising Auto-encoders for Nonlinear Representations

abstract: We develop an approach to training generative models based on unrolling a variational auto-encoder into a Markov chain, and shaping the chain’s trajectories using a technique inspired by recent work in Approximate Bayesian computation. We show that the global minimizer of the resulting objective is achieved when the generative model reproduces the target distribution. To allow finer control over the behavior of the models, we add a regularization term inspired by techniques used for regularizing certain types of policy search in reinforcement learning. We present empirical results on the MNIST and TFD datasets which show that our approach offers state-of-the-art performance, both quantitatively and from a qualitative point of view.
originalAbstract: We develop an approach to training generative models based on unrolling a variational auto-encoder into a Markov chain, and shaping the chain’s trajectories using a technique inspired by recent work in Approximate Bayesian computation. We show that the global minimizer of the resulting objective is achieved when the generative model reproduces the target distribution. To allow finer control over the behavior of the models, we add a regularization term inspired by techniques used for regularizing certain types of policy search in reinforcement learning. We present empirical results on the MNIST and TFD datasets which show that our approach offers state-of-the-art performance, both quantitatively and from a qualitative point of view.

paragraphs: A generative model aims to reproduce the distribution of the data it learns from. This paper builds a training approach by unrolling a variational autoencoder into a Markov chain. That construction makes the chain's trajectories part of the learning problem, allowing training to shape how the model progresses through successive states.

The trajectory-shaping technique is inspired by approximate Bayesian computation. The authors show that the resulting objective achieves its global minimum when the generative model reproduces the target distribution. This establishes that matching the desired distribution attains the objective's best value; it does not itself say that every training run reaches that global minimum.

The authors add a regularization term to provide finer control over model behavior, drawing inspiration from regularization used in reinforcement-learning policy search. Experiments on MNIST and TFD show state-of-the-art results in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The work thus combines a distribution-matching objective, control over chain behavior, and empirical evidence for the resulting generative approach.
summary.tldr: A variational autoencoder unfolded into a Markov chain is trained by shaping trajectories toward the target data distribution.

title: Variational Generative Stochastic Networks with Collaborative Shaping

abstract: We study the problem of off-policy value evaluation in reinforcement learning (RL), where one aims to estimate the value of a new policy based on data collected by a different policy. This problem is often a critical step when applying RL to real-world problems. Despite its importance, existing general methods either have uncontrolled bias or suffer high variance. In this work, we extend the doubly robust estimator for bandits to sequential decision-making problems, which gets the best of both worlds: it is guaranteed to be unbiased and can have a much lower variance than the popular importance sampling estimators. We demonstrate the estimator’s accuracy in several benchmark problems, and illustrate its use as a subroutine in safe policy improvement. We also provide theoretical results on the inherent hardness of the problem, and show that our estimator can match the lower bound in certain scenarios.

This problem is often a critical step when applying RL to real-world problems. Despite its importance, existing general methods either have uncontrolled bias or suffer high variance. In this work, we extend the doubly robust estimator for bandits to sequential decision-making problems, which gets the best of both worlds: it is guaranteed to be unbiased and can have a much lower variance than the popular importance sampling estimators. We demonstrate the estimator’s accuracy in several benchmark problems, and illustrate its use as a subroutine in safe policy improvement. We also provide theoretical results on the inherent hardness of the problem, and show that our estimator can match the lower bound in certain scenarios.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation asks how well a new decision policy would perform using data generated by a different policy. This is valuable when evaluating a candidate policy is a prerequisite to adopting it. The paper addresses a central difficulty: existing general approaches can introduce uncontrolled bias or produce estimates with high variance.

The authors extend a doubly robust estimator from bandit problems to sequential decision making. The resulting estimator is guaranteed to be unbiased and can have substantially lower variance than importance sampling estimators. The distinction matters: unbiasedness concerns systematic error, while reduced variance means estimates can fluctuate less across collected datasets. The variance improvement is presented as a possibility, rather than a universal outcome.

Experiments demonstrate accuracy on several benchmark problems and show how the estimator can serve within safe policy improvement. The paper also studies fundamental limits on evaluation accuracy. In certain scenarios, the estimator matches the theoretical lower bound, connecting its practical use with a qualified optimality result about how well the problem can be solved.
summary.tldr: A sequential doubly robust estimator provides unbiased off-policy evaluation with potentially much lower variance than importance sampling.

title: Doubly Robust Off-policy Value Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider the task of evaluating a policy for a Markov decision process (MDP). The standard unbiased technique for evaluating a policy is to deploy the policy and observe its performance. We show that the data collected from deploying a different policy, commonly called the behavior policy, can be used to produce unbiased estimates with lower mean squared error than this standard technique. We derive an analytic expression for the optimal behavior policy — the behavior policy that minimizes the mean squared error of the resulting estimates. Because this expression depends on terms that are unknown in practice, we propose a novel policy evaluation sub-problem, behavior policy search: searching for a behavior policy that reduces mean squared error. We present a behavior policy search algorithm and empirically demonstrate its effectiveness in lowering the mean squared error of policy performance estimates.

The standard unbiased technique for evaluating a policy is to deploy the policy and observe its performance. We show that the data collected from deploying a different policy, commonly called the behavior policy, can be used to produce unbiased estimates with lower mean squared error than this standard technique. We derive an analytic expression for the optimal behavior policy — the behavior policy that minimizes the mean squared error of the resulting estimates. paragraphs: The paper asks how to collect data efficiently when estimating a policy’s performance in a Markov decision process. A standard unbiased approach is to run the policy itself and observe the results. The authors show that running a different behavior policy can also support unbiased estimates, potentially with lower mean squared error.

They derive an analytical expression for the behavior policy that minimizes the mean squared error of the resulting estimates. This identifies the best data-collection policy for that objective in mathematical terms. However, the expression relies on quantities that are unknown in practice, so it cannot simply be used as a ready-made collection strategy.

To address that obstacle, the paper introduces behavior policy search: finding a policy that collects data useful for evaluating the target policy. The proposed search algorithm empirically lowers estimation error. The contribution makes the data-collection policy an explicit part of evaluation design and shows that deploying the target policy is not always the most statistically efficient choice.
summary.tldr: Searching for a separate data-collection policy can reduce policy-evaluation error while preserving unbiased estimates.

title: Data-Efficient Policy Evaluation Through Behavior Policy Search

abstract: This paper studies systematic exploration for reinforcement learning (RL) with rich observations and function approximation. We introduce contextual decision processes (CDPs), that unify most prior RL settings. Our first contribution is a complexity measure, the Bellman rank, that we show enables tractable learning of near-optimal behavior in CDPs and is naturally small for many well-studied RL models. Our second contribution is a new RL algorithm that does systematic exploration to learn near-optimal behavior in CDPs with low Bellman rank. The algorithm requires a number of samples that is polynomial in all relevant parameters but independent of the number of unique contexts. Our approach uses Bellman error minimization with optimistic exploration and provides new insights into efficient exploration for RL with function approximation.

We introduce contextual decision processes (CDPs), that unify most prior RL settings. Our second contribution is a new RL algorithm that does systematic exploration to learn near-optimal behavior in CDPs with low Bellman rank. paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an agent receives rich observations and must use function approximation to guide decisions. The paper introduces contextual decision processes as a framework encompassing most earlier reinforcement-learning settings. Within this framework, it asks what structure makes systematic exploration and learning near-optimal behavior possible with a manageable number of observations.

The central structural measure is Bellman rank. The authors show that low Bellman rank supports tractable learning and that the measure is naturally small in many well-studied models. This shifts attention from the sheer number of distinct contexts to a complexity property that can remain small even when the observation space is large.

The proposed algorithm combines Bellman error minimization with optimistic exploration. For contextual decision processes with low Bellman rank, its sample requirement is polynomial in the relevant parameters and independent of the number of unique contexts. The result supplies a theoretical route to efficient exploration with function approximation. Its guarantee depends on the low-rank structure, rather than applying indiscriminately to every problem with rich observations.
summary.tldr: Low Bellman rank enables systematic reinforcement-learning exploration with sample requirements independent of the number of distinct contexts.

title: Contextual Decision Processes with low Bellman rank are PAC-Learnable

abstract: The Recurrent Neural Networks and their variants have shown promising performances in sequence modeling tasks such as Natural Language Processing. These models, however, turn out to be impractical and difficult to train when exposed to very high-dimensional inputs due to the large input-to-hidden weight matrix. This may have prevented RNNs’ large-scale application in tasks that involve very high input dimensions such as video modeling; current approaches reduce the input dimensions using various feature extractors. To address this challenge, we propose a new, more general and efficient approach by factorizing the input-to-hidden weight matrix using Tensor-Train decomposition which is trained simultaneously with the weights themselves. We test our model on classification tasks using multiple real-world video datasets and achieve competitive performances with state-of-the-art models, even though our model architecture is orders of magnitude less complex. We believe that the proposed approach provides a novel and fundamental building block for modeling high-dimensional sequential data with RNN architectures and opens up many possibilities to transfer the expressive and advanced architectures from other domains such as NLP to modeling high-dimensional sequential data.
