paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks become difficult to train when each input has very many dimensions. The input-to-hidden weight matrix grows large, creating a major obstacle for applications such as video modeling. Existing approaches reduce input dimensionality with feature extractors; this paper instead addresses the size of the mapping within the recurrent model.

The authors factorize the input-to-hidden matrix using Tensor-Train decomposition and learn the factorized representation during training. This provides a more compact way to express the large transformation that connects inputs to hidden states. The method is presented as a general approach for recurrent architectures exposed to high-dimensional sequential data.

On classification tasks across multiple real-world video datasets, the model achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art approaches while its architecture is orders of magnitude less complex. These results support the usefulness of the factorization for video classification. The authors also suggest that it could help bring expressive recurrent architectures from other domains into high-dimensional sequence modeling.
summary.tldr: Tensor-Train factorization greatly reduces recurrent-network complexity while retaining competitive reported performance on video classification.

title: Tensor-Train Recurrent Neural Networks for Video Classification

abstract: Current neural network-based classifiers are susceptible to adversarial examples even in the black-box setting, where the attacker only has query access to the model. In practice, the threat model for real-world systems is often more restrictive than the typical black-box model where the adversary can observe the full output of the network on arbitrarily many chosen inputs. We define three realistic threat models that more accurately characterize many real-world classifiers: the query-limited setting, the partial-information setting, and the label-only setting. We develop new attacks that fool classifiers under these more restrictive threat models, where previous methods would be impractical or ineffective. We demonstrate that our methods are effective against an ImageNet classifier under our proposed threat models. We also demonstrate a targeted black-box attack against a commercial classifier, overcoming the challenges of limited query access, partial information, and other practical issues to break the Google Cloud Vision API.

paragraphs: A black-box attack interacts with a classifier through its outputs rather than accessing the network directly. The paper argues that a common version of this setting gives attackers more access than practical systems often provide: unlimited queries and the complete output for every input. It studies whether attacks remain effective when that access is restricted.

The authors define three settings that separate different restrictions: limited numbers of queries, partial output information, and access only to predicted labels. They develop attacks for these conditions, targeting situations where earlier methods would be impractical or ineffective. The contribution is both a clearer account of attacker access and methods that work within those narrower interfaces.

Experiments demonstrate effectiveness against an ImageNet classifier under the proposed settings. The authors also report a targeted attack against Google Cloud Vision that handles limited queries, partial information, and practical complications. These demonstrations establish vulnerability in the evaluated systems despite restricted access; they do not require assuming that attackers can inspect every internal output.
summary.tldr: The paper develops black-box adversarial attacks that remain effective under query limits, partial outputs, and label-only access.

title: Black-box Adversarial Attacks with Limited Queries and Information

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has achieved many recent successes, but our understanding of its strengths and limitations is hampered by the lack of rich environments in which we can fully characterize optimal behavior, and correspondingly diagnose individual actions against such a characterization. Here we consider a family of combinatorial games, arising from work of Erdos, Selfridge, and Spencer, and we propose their use as environments for evaluating and comparing different approaches to reinforcement learning. These games have a number of appealing features: they are challenging for current learning approaches, but they form (i) a low-dimensional, simply parametrized environment where (ii) there is a linear closed form solution for optimal behavior from any state, and (iii) the difficulty of the game can be tuned by changing environment parameters in an interpretable way. We use these Erdos-Selfridge-Spencer games not only to compare different algorithms, but test for generalization, make comparisons to supervised learning, analyse multiagent play, and even develop a self play algorithm.

paragraphs: Evaluating reinforcement learning is easier when researchers know what an optimal agent should do at every step. Many challenging environments lack that reference, making individual mistakes difficult to diagnose. This paper proposes a family of combinatorial games from work by Erdos, Selfridge, and Spencer as a controlled setting for such evaluation.

The games combine a small, simply parameterized environment with a linear closed-form solution for optimal behavior from any state. Their difficulty can also be changed through interpretable parameters. This combination matters because an environment can remain challenging for learning algorithms while providing a precise standard against which their choices can be assessed.

The authors use the games to compare reinforcement learning algorithms, examine generalization, compare with supervised learning, and analyze multiagent play. They also develop a self-play algorithm. The contribution is a diagnostic environment and a set of investigations into learning behavior; the abstract does not claim that deep reinforcement learning universally solves this game family.
summary.tldr: Erdos-Selfridge-Spencer games offer challenging reinforcement learning environments with known optimal behavior and interpretable difficulty controls.

title: Can Deep Reinforcement Learning Solve Erdos-Selfridge-Spencer Games?

abstract: We introduce the concrete autoencoder, an end-to-end differentiable method for global feature selection, which efficiently identifies a subset of the most informative features and simultaneously learns a neural network to reconstruct the input data from the selected features. Our method is unsupervised, and is based on using a concrete selector layer as the encoder and using a standard neural network as the decoder. During the training phase, the temperature of the concrete selector layer is gradually decreased, which encourages a user-specified number of discrete features to be learned; during test time, the selected features can be used with the decoder network to reconstruct the remaining input features. We evaluate concrete autoencoders on a variety of datasets, where they significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods for feature selection and data reconstruction. In particular, on a large-scale gene expression dataset, the concrete autoencoder selects a small subset of genes whose expression levels can be used to impute the expression levels of the remaining genes; in doing so, it improves on the current widely-used expert-curated L1000 landmark genes, potentially reducing measurement costs by 20%. The concrete autoencoder can be implemented by adding just a few lines of code to a standard autoencoder, and the code for the algorithm and experiments is publicly available.

paragraphs: The concrete autoencoder learns which input features to retain and how to reconstruct the full input from that selection. Its feature selection is global and unsupervised: it identifies an informative subset without relying on target labels. A user specifies how many features should be selected, making the retained measurement budget part of the learning problem.

The encoder is a concrete selector layer, paired with a standard neural network decoder. During training, the selector’s temperature gradually decreases, encouraging it to settle on discrete features while supporting differentiable learning. At test time, the selected measurements feed the decoder, which reconstructs the remaining input features.

The authors report substantial improvements over leading feature selection and reconstruction methods across several datasets. On a large gene expression dataset, the selected genes support imputation of other genes and improve on the expert-curated L1000 landmarks, with a potential 20% reduction in measurement costs. The method also requires only a small modification to a standard autoencoder.
summary.tldr: Concrete autoencoders jointly learn a discrete feature subset and a reconstruction network, with strong empirical results and potential gene measurement savings.

title: Concrete Autoencoders: Differentiable Feature Selection and Reconstruction

abstract: We introduce a novel approach, requiring only mild assumptions, for the characterization of deep neural networks at initialization. Our approach applies both to fully-connected and convolutional networks and easily incorporates batch normalization and skip-connections. Our key insight is to consider the evolution with depth of statistical moments of signal and noise, thereby characterizing the presence or absence of pathologies in the hypothesis space encoded by the choice of hyperparameters. We establish: (i) for feedforward networks, with and without batch normalization, the multiplicativity of layer composition inevitably leads to ill-behaved moments and pathologies; (ii) for residual networks with batch normalization, on the other hand, skip-connections induce power-law rather than exponential behaviour, leading to well-behaved moments and no pathology.

paragraphs: This paper examines deep neural networks at initialization, before training changes their parameters. Its approach follows statistical moments of signal and noise as they pass through successive layers. These quantities help characterize whether the space of functions implied by an architecture and its hyperparameters exhibits the pathologies considered in the analysis.

The framework requires mild assumptions and accommodates both fully connected and convolutional networks, including batch normalization and skip connections. For feedforward networks, the authors establish that repeatedly composing layers produces multiplicative effects that lead to ill-behaved moments. In their analysis, adding batch normalization to a feedforward network does not remove this underlying problem.

The result changes for residual networks with batch normalization. Skip connections replace exponential depth behavior with power-law behavior, yielding well-behaved moments and no pathology of the kind being characterized. The significance is an initialization-level explanation of how architectural choices affect signal and noise propagation. The conclusion concerns this characterization, rather than a general guarantee about every aspect of subsequent training.
summary.tldr: An initialization analysis shows how skip connections with batch normalization prevent the signal-and-noise pathologies identified in feedforward networks.

title: Characterizing Well-Behaved vs. Pathological Deep Neural Networks

abstract: It is known that the Langevin dynamics used in MCMC is the gradient flow of the KL divergence on the Wasserstein space, which helps convergence analysis and inspires recent particle-based variational inference methods (ParVIs). But no more MCMC dynamics is understood in this way. In this work, by developing novel concepts, we propose a theoretical framework that recognizes a general MCMC dynamics as the fiber-gradient Hamiltonian flow on the Wasserstein space of a fiber-Riemannian Poisson manifold. The "conservation + convergence" structure of the flow gives a clear picture on the behavior of general MCMC dynamics. The framework also enables ParVI simulation of MCMC dynamics, which enriches the ParVI family with more efficient dynamics, and also adapts ParVI advantages to MCMCs. We develop two ParVI methods for a particular MCMC dynamics and demonstrate the benefits in experiments.

paragraphs: Langevin dynamics already has a useful interpretation as a gradient flow of KL divergence in Wasserstein space. That perspective supports convergence analysis and has inspired particle-based variational inference. This paper develops a broader geometric framework intended to explain general MCMC dynamics through flows of probability distributions.

The framework represents these dynamics as a fiber-gradient Hamiltonian flow on Wasserstein space over a fiber-Riemannian Poisson manifold. Its central explanatory feature is a decomposition combining conservation and convergence. This structure separates complementary aspects of the dynamics and provides a clearer account of their behavior within a common mathematical description.

The framework also allows MCMC dynamics to be simulated through particle-based variational inference. This creates a route for enriching particle methods with more efficient dynamics while bringing their advantages to MCMC. The authors construct two particle-based methods for a particular MCMC dynamics and demonstrate benefits experimentally. The practical examples support the framework’s ability to generate algorithms, alongside its broader theoretical contribution to understanding sampling dynamics.
summary.tldr: A geometric framework describes general MCMC dynamics through conservation and convergence and enables new particle-based variational simulations.

title: Understanding MCMC Dynamics as Flows on the Wasserstein Space

abstract: In domains such as medicine, it can be acceptable for machine learning models to include sensitive attributes such as gender and ethnicity. In this work, we argue that when there is this kind of treatment disparity, then it should be in the best interest of each group. Drawing on ethical principles such as beneficence ("do the best") and non-maleficence ("do no harm"), we show how to use sensitive attributes to train decoupled classifiers that satisfy preference guarantees. These guarantees ensure the majority of individuals in each group prefer their assigned classifier to (i) a pooled model that ignores group membership (rationality), and (ii) the model assigned to any other group (envy-freeness). We introduce a recursive procedure that adaptively selects group attributes for decoupling, and present formal conditions to ensure preference guarantees in terms of generalization error. We validate the effectiveness of the procedure on real-world datasets, showing that it improves accuracy without violating preference guarantees on test data.

paragraphs: This paper considers settings where using sensitive attributes, such as gender or ethnicity, can be acceptable. It argues that assigning different models to different groups should serve each group's interests. The proposed approach trains separate classifiers while imposing preference guarantees grounded in doing good and avoiding harm.

The guarantees involve two comparisons. Rationality requires a majority of individuals in each group to prefer their assigned classifier to a pooled classifier that ignores group membership. Envy freeness requires that majority to prefer its assigned classifier to the classifier assigned to any other group. These are majority based guarantees within groups; they do not assert that every individual benefits.

A recursive procedure adaptively chooses which group attributes to use when separating classifiers. The authors provide formal conditions for preference guarantees in terms of generalization error. On real datasets, the procedure improves accuracy while maintaining the guarantees on test data. The findings support evaluating group specific modeling through explicit comparisons with both pooled and alternative group models.
summary.tldr: Group specific classifiers improve accuracy in the reported tests while satisfying majority preference guarantees against pooled and other groups' models.

title: Fairness without Harm: Decoupled Classifiers with Preference Guarantees

abstract: Monte-Carlo counterfactual regret minimization (MCCFR) is the state-of-the-art algorithm for solving sequential games that are too large for full tree traversals. It works by using gradient estimates that can be computed via sampling. However, stochastic methods for sequential games have not been investigated extensively beyond MCCFR. In this paper we develop a new framework for developing stochastic regret minimization methods. This framework allows us to use any regret-minimization algorithm, coupled with any gradient estimator. The MCCFR algorithm can be analyzed as a special case of our framework, and this analysis leads to significantly stronger theoretical guarantees on convergence, while simultaneously yielding a simplified proof. Our framework allows us to instantiate several new stochastic methods for solving sequential games. We show extensive experiments on five games, where some variants of our methods outperform MCCFR.
originalAbstract: Monte-Carlo counterfactual regret minimization (MCCFR) is the state-of-the-art algorithm for solving sequential games that are too large for full tree traversals. It works by using gradient estimates that can be computed via sampling. However, stochastic methods for sequential games have not been investigated extensively beyond MCCFR. In this paper we develop a new framework for developing stochastic regret minimization methods. This framework allows us to use any regret-minimization algorithm, coupled with any gradient estimator. The MCCFR algorithm can be analyzed as a special case of our framework, and this analysis leads to significantly stronger theoretical guarantees on convergence, while simultaneously yielding a simplified proof. paragraphs: Solving a sequential game can require considering a tree of possible decisions that is too large to explore fully. Monte-Carlo counterfactual regret minimization, or MCCFR, addresses this problem through sampling: it uses estimates of gradients that can be computed without traversing the entire tree. The paper investigates how to develop stochastic methods beyond this established approach.

Its central contribution is a framework that allows any regret-minimization algorithm to be paired with any gradient estimator. This separates two choices in designing a method: the algorithm used to minimize regret and the estimator supplying its gradient information. MCCFR fits within this framework as a special case, making the framework useful for understanding an existing method as well as constructing new ones.

Analyzing MCCFR through this framework yields significantly stronger theoretical convergence guarantees and a simpler proof. The authors also instantiate several new stochastic methods and evaluate them in experiments across five games. Some variants outperform MCCFR, showing that the framework produces competitive alternatives, while the reported comparison does not establish that every variant is better.
summary.tldr: A general framework for stochastic regret minimization strengthens MCCFR’s convergence guarantees and produces new methods, some of which outperform MCCFR in experiments.

title: Stochastic Regret Minimization in Extensive-Form Games

abstract: Quantization based techniques are the current state-of-the-art for scaling maximum inner product search to massive databases. Traditional approaches to quantization aim to minimize the reconstruction error of the database points. Based on the observation that for a given query, the database points that have the largest inner products are more relevant, we develop a family of anisotropic quantization loss functions. Under natural statistical assumptions, we show that quantization with these loss functions leads to a new variant of vector quantization that more greatly penalizes the parallel component of a datapoint’s residual relative to its orthogonal component. The proposed approach, whose implementation is open-source, achieves state-of-the-art results on the public benchmarks available at ann-benchmarks.com.

Traditional approaches to quantization aim to minimize the reconstruction error of the database points. Based on the observation that for a given query, the database points that have the largest inner products are more relevant, we develop a family of anisotropic quantization loss functions. paragraphs: Maximum inner product search looks for database vectors that score highest against a query. Quantization helps this search scale by replacing database vectors with compact approximations. Conventional quantization aims to reconstruct each vector accurately, but reconstruction accuracy does not directly express which errors matter most for finding highly relevant results.

The paper develops quantization losses that account for the greater relevance of vectors with large inner products. Under statistical assumptions, the resulting method penalizes different directions of approximation error differently. In particular, it penalizes the residual component parallel to the original data vector more strongly than the component perpendicular to it. This changes the compression objective to reflect the search task more closely.

The proposed approach achieves results described as state of the art on the public benchmarks evaluated, and its implementation is open source. The contribution is a task-sensitive way to choose compressed vector representations: the analysis explains why treating all error directions equally can miss distinctions that matter for search.
summary.tldr: Direction-sensitive quantization improves large-scale inner product search by penalizing approximation errors according to their relevance to the search objective.

title: Accelerating Large-Scale Inference with Anisotropic Vector Quantization

abstract: We present a framework for autonomously learning a portable representation that describes a collection of low-level continuous environments. We show that these abstract representations can be learned in a task-independent egocentric space specific to the agent that, when grounded with problem-specific information, are provably sufficient for planning. We demonstrate transfer in two different domains, where an agent learns a portable, task-independent symbolic vocabulary, as well as operators expressed in that vocabulary, and then learns to instantiate those operators on a per-task basis. This reduces the number of samples required to learn a representation of a new task.

We show that these abstract representations can be learned in a task-independent egocentric space specific to the agent that, when grounded with problem-specific information, are provably sufficient for planning. We demonstrate transfer in two different domains, where an agent learns a portable, task-independent symbolic vocabulary, as well as operators expressed in that vocabulary, and then learns to instantiate those operators on a per-task basis. This reduces the number of samples required to learn a representation of a new task.

paragraphs: High-level planning requires a useful abstraction of the detailed environment in which an agent acts. If that abstraction must be learned separately for every task, transferring to a new problem can require substantial additional experience. This paper proposes learning a portable representation that describes a collection of continuous, low-level environments.

The representation is learned in an agent-specific, egocentric space that does not depend on the particular task. It includes a symbolic vocabulary and operators expressed using that vocabulary. For each new task, the agent learns how to instantiate those operators with problem-specific information, separating reusable planning concepts from their particular application.

The authors show that the abstract representations are provably sufficient for planning when grounded with the required problem-specific information. They also demonstrate transfer in two domains, reporting fewer samples needed to learn a representation for a new task. The guarantee therefore concerns grounded representations; portability does not eliminate the task-specific learning needed to connect the shared vocabulary and operators to a particular problem.
summary.tldr: Reusable symbolic representations reduce new-task learning needs and are sufficient for planning when grounded with problem-specific information.

title: Learning Portable Representations for High-Level Planning

abstract: We give the first input-sparsity time algorithms for the rank-$k$ low rank approximation problem in every Schatten norm. Specifically, for a given $n\times n$ matrix $A$, our algorithm computes $Y,Z\in \R^{n\times k}$, which, with high probability, satisfy $\|A-YZ^T\|_p \leq (1+\eps)\|A-A_k\|_p$, where $\|M\|_p = \left (\sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i(M)^p \right )^{1/p}$ is the Schatten $p$-norm of a matrix $M$ with singular values $\sigma_1(M), \ldots, \sigma_n(M)$, and where $A_k$ is the best rank-$k$ approximation to $A$. Our algorithm runs in time $\tilde{O}(\nnz(A) + n^{\alpha_p}\poly(k/\eps))$, where $\alpha_p = 1$ for $p\in [1,2)$ and $\alpha_p = 1 + (\omega-1)(1-2/p)$ for $p>2$ and $\omega \approx 2.374$ is the exponent of matrix multiplication. For the important case of $p = 1$, which corresponds to the more “robust” nuclear norm, we obtain $\tilde{O}(\nnz(A) + n \cdot \poly(k/\epsilon))$ time, which was previously only known for the Frobenius norm $(p = 2)$. Moreover, since $\alpha_p < \omega$ for every $p$, our algorithm has a better dependence on $n$ than that in the singular value decomposition for every $p$. Crucial to our analysis is the use of dimensionality reduction for Ky-Fan $p$-norms.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation replaces a large matrix with a product of two narrower matrices. The goal is to preserve the original matrix while using a restricted rank. This paper develops algorithms for measuring approximation error in every Schatten norm, a family of matrix norms computed from singular values that includes the nuclear and Frobenius norms.

For a given square matrix and target rank, the algorithm returns factors whose error is at most one plus epsilon times the best achievable rank-constrained error, with high probability. Its runtime includes a term proportional to the number of nonzero input entries, plus an additional term depending on matrix size, rank, accuracy, and the selected norm. Dimensionality reduction for Ky-Fan norms is central to the analysis.

The nuclear-norm case receives particular attention: its additional dependence on matrix size is linear, multiplied by a polynomial in rank and inverse accuracy, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. The paper also establishes better matrix-size dependence than singular value decomposition across the stated norms. These results extend fast approximation guarantees beyond the previously available Frobenius-norm case.
summary.tldr: The paper gives input-sparsity-time low-rank approximation algorithms with high-probability near-optimal error guarantees across Schatten norms.

title: Input-Sparsity Low Rank Approximation in Schatten Norm

abstract: We seek to align agent behavior with a user’s objectives in a reinforcement learning setting with unknown dynamics, an unknown reward function, and unknown unsafe states. The user knows the rewards and unsafe states, but querying the user is expensive. We propose an algorithm that safely and efficiently learns a model of the user’s reward function by posing ’what if?’ questions about hypothetical agent behavior. We start with a generative model of initial states and a forward dynamics model trained on off-policy data. Our method uses these models to synthesize hypothetical behaviors, asks the user to label the behaviors with rewards, and trains a neural network to predict the rewards. The key idea is to actively synthesize the hypothetical behaviors from scratch by maximizing tractable proxies for the value of information, without interacting with the environment. We call this method reward query synthesis via trajectory optimization (ReQueST). We evaluate ReQueST with simulated users on a state-based 2D navigation task and the image-based Car Racing video game. The results show that ReQueST significantly outperforms prior methods in learning reward models that transfer to new environments with different initial state distributions. Moreover, ReQueST safely trains the reward model to detect unsafe states, and corrects reward hacking before deploying the agent.

paragraphs: An agent may not know which outcomes a user values or which states are unsafe, while asking the user for guidance is costly. ReQueST learns a reward model by asking about hypothetical behavior. It begins with a generative model of initial states and a forward dynamics model trained on off-policy data.

These models synthesize trajectories that the user labels with rewards, and a neural network learns to predict those rewards. The method actively constructs questions by optimizing tractable proxies for their information value. Because the candidate behaviors are generated through models, producing these queries requires no interaction with the environment.

Evaluations use simulated users in a state-based navigation task and the image-based Car Racing game. ReQueST significantly outperforms prior methods at learning rewards that transfer to environments with different initial-state distributions. The experiments also show safe training of unsafe-state detection and correction of reward hacking before deployment. The findings support using carefully chosen hypothetical behavior to acquire useful feedback without executing those behaviors.
summary.tldr: ReQueST synthesizes informative hypothetical behaviors for user feedback, learning transferable reward models without executing the queried behaviors.

title: Learning Human Objectives by Evaluating Hypothetical Behavior

abstract: Integer programming is a general optimization framework with a wide variety of applications, e.g., in scheduling, production planning, and graph optimization. As Integer Programs (IPs) model many provably hard to solve problems, modern IP solvers rely on heuristics. These heuristics are often human-designed, and tuned over time using experience and data. The goal of this work is to show that the performance of those solvers can be greatly enhanced using reinforcement learning (RL). In particular, we investigate a specific methodology for solving IPs, known as the Cutting Plane Method. This method is employed as a subroutine by all modern IP solvers. We present a deep RL formulation, network architecture, and algorithms for intelligent adaptive selection of cutting planes (aka cuts). Across a wide range of IP tasks, we show that our trained RL agent significantly outperforms human-designed heuristics, and effectively generalizes to larger instances and across IP problem classes. The trained agent is also demonstrated to benefit the popular downstream application of cutting plane methods in Branch-and-Cut algorithm, which is the backbone of state-of-the-art commercial IP solvers.

In particular, we investigate a specific methodology for solving IPs, known as the Cutting Plane Method. This method is employed as a subroutine by all modern IP solvers. Across a wide range of IP tasks, we show that our trained RL agent significantly outperforms human-designed heuristics, and effectively generalizes to larger instances and across IP problem classes. The trained agent is also demonstrated to benefit the popular downstream application of cutting plane methods in Branch-and-Cut algorithm, which is the backbone of state-of-the-art commercial IP solvers.

Practical solvers rely on heuristics to make progress efficiently. This paper asks whether reinforcement learning can improve one important solver decision: selecting cutting planes during the cutting-plane method.

The authors develop a deep reinforcement learning formulation, a network architecture, and algorithms for adaptive cut selection. The learned agent makes choices within an existing optimization procedure. This targets a recurring solver component whose behavior has traditionally depended on heuristics designed and refined by people.

Across a wide range of integer programming tasks, the trained agent significantly outperforms the compared human-designed heuristics. It also generalizes to larger instances and across problem classes in the reported experiments. The authors further demonstrate benefits when the learned selection is used within Branch-and-Cut, a core framework in modern commercial solvers. That integration shows that the learned decision rule can improve a broader solving procedure beyond the isolated cutting-plane setting.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning agent learns adaptive cutting-plane selection, outperforming tested heuristics and improving downstream Branch-and-Cut solving.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Integer Programming: Learning to Cut

abstract: Training agents to autonomously control anthropomorphic robotic hands has the potential to lead to systems capable of performing a multitude of complex manipulation tasks in unstructured and uncertain environments. In this work, we first introduce a suite of challenging simulated manipulation tasks where current reinforcement learning and trajectory optimisation techniques perform poorly. These include environments where two simulated hands have to pass or throw objects between each other, as well as an environment where the agent must learn to spin a long pen between its fingers. We then introduce a simple trajectory optimisation algorithm that performs significantly better than existing methods on these environments. Finally, on the most challenging “PenSpin" task, we combine sub-optimal demonstrations generated through trajectory optimisation with off-policy reinforcement learning, obtaining performance that far exceeds either of these approaches individually. Videos of all of our results are available at: https://dexterous-manipulation.github.io

The paper contributes both a challenging simulated task suite and evidence for combining the two approaches, with the strongest stated combination result tied specifically to pen spinning.
summary.tldr: Combining suboptimal trajectory-optimization demonstrations with off-policy learning substantially improves simulated pen-spinning performance.

title: Solving Challenging Dexterous Manipulation Tasks With Trajectory Optimisation and Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Bias in ranking systems, especially among the top ranks, can worsen social and economic inequalities, polarize opinions, and reinforce stereotypes. On the other hand, a bias correction for minority groups can cause more harm if perceived as favoring group-fair outcomes over meritocracy. Most group-fair ranking algorithms post-process a given ranking and output a group-fair ranking. In this paper, we formulate the problem of underranking in group-fair rankings based on how close the group-fair rank of each item is to its original rank, and prove a lower bound on the trade-off achievable for simultaneous underranking and group fairness in ranking. We give a fair ranking algorithm that takes any given ranking and outputs another ranking with simultaneous underranking and group fairness guarantees comparable to the lower bound we prove. Our experimental results confirm the theoretical trade-off between underranking and group fairness, and also show that our algorithm achieves the best of both when compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Group-fair ranking methods often adjust an existing ranking to improve group representation. Such adjustments can also move individual items downward, creating tension between group-level fairness and preservation of original positions. This paper formalizes that tension through underranking, measured by how an item’s position in the adjusted ranking compares with its original position.

The authors prove a lower bound on the tradeoff achievable when seeking group fairness and underranking guarantees simultaneously. This establishes a mathematical constraint on how well the two objectives can be combined. They then design an algorithm that accepts any given ranking and produces an adjusted ranking with guarantees for both objectives comparable to that lower bound.

Experiments support the predicted tradeoff and show a stronger combination of fairness and underranking performance than the compared state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution makes individual rank displacement an explicit part of fair-ranking design. Its guarantees describe changes relative to the supplied ranking, providing a concrete way to assess the costs of enforcing group fairness alongside the fairness improvement itself.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes the tradeoff between group fairness and downward rank movement, then gives an algorithm with guarantees comparable to its lower bound.

title: On the Problem of Underranking in Group-Fair Ranking

abstract: Real-world machine learning systems are often trained using a mix of data sources with varying cost and quality. Understanding how the size and composition of a training dataset affect model performance is critical for advancing our understanding of generalization, as well as designing more effective data collection policies. We show that there is a simple scaling law that predicts the loss incurred by a model even under varying dataset composition. Our work expands recent observations of scaling laws for log-linear generalization error in the i.i.d setting and uses this to cast model performance prediction as a learning problem. Using the theory of optimal experimental design, we derive a simple rational function approximation to generalization error that can be fitted using a few model training runs. Our approach can achieve highly accurate ($r^2\approx .9$) predictions of model performance under substantial extrapolation in two different standard supervised learning tasks and is accurate ($r^2 \approx .83$) on more challenging machine translation and question answering tasks where many baselines achieve worse-than-random performance.

Predicting model performance therefore requires understanding both how much data is available and how it is divided among sources. This paper develops a scaling-law approach that predicts loss as the size and composition of the training dataset change.

These findings support modeling dataset composition explicitly and provide a basis for making more informed data collection decisions when sources have different costs and qualities.
summary.tldr: A scaling-law model fitted from a few training runs predicts performance as both training-set size and source composition change.

title: Model Performance Scaling with Multiple Data Sources

abstract: Norm emergence is a process where agents in a multi-agent system establish self-enforcing conformity through repeated interactions. When such interactions are confined to a social topology, several self-reinforcing substructures (SRS) may emerge within the population. This prevents a formation of a global norm. We propose incremental social instruments (ISI) to dissolve these SRSs by creating ties between agents. Establishing ties requires some effort and cost. Hence, it is worth to design methods that build a small number of ties yet dissolve the SRSs. By using the notion of information entropy, we propose an indicator called the BA-ratio that measures the current SRSs. We find that by building ties with minimal BA-ratio, our ISI is effective in facilitating the global norm emergence. We explain this through our experiments and theoretical results. Furthermore, we propose the small-degree principle in minimising the BA-ratio that helps us to design efficient ISI algorithms for finding the optimal ties. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world network topologies demonstrate that our adaptive ISI is efficient at dissolving SRS.

paragraphs: Repeated interactions can lead agents to settle on shared norms, but a network’s social structure can split this process into locally reinforcing groups. Each group may sustain its own conformity, preventing a single norm from emerging across the population. The paper studies how adding social ties can dissolve these persistent substructures.

The proposed incremental social instruments create connections between agents. Because each new connection requires effort and cost, the aim is to choose a small number of useful ties. The authors introduce an entropy-based indicator called the BA-ratio to characterize the current self-reinforcing substructures and use it to guide which ties to establish.

Theoretical results and experiments support choosing ties with minimal BA-ratio as a way to facilitate global norm emergence. A small-degree principle helps the authors design efficient algorithms for finding optimal ties under this criterion. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world network topologies show that the adaptive approach efficiently dissolves the substructures, linking a structural measurement to targeted changes in the interaction network.
summary.tldr: Entropy-guided additions of social ties help dissolve locally self-reinforcing groups and facilitate a global norm.

title: From Local to Global Norm Emergence: Dissolving Self-reinforcing Substructures with Incremental Social Instruments

abstract: We introduce the problem of regret minimization in Adversarial Dueling Bandits. As in classic Dueling Bandits, the learner has to repeatedly choose a pair of items and observe only a relative binary ‘win-loss’ feedback for this pair, but here this feedback is generated from an arbitrary preference matrix, possibly chosen adversarially. Our main result is an algorithm whose $T$-round regret compared to the \emph{Borda-winner} from a set of $K$ items is $\tilde{O}(K^{1/3}T^{2/3})$, as well as a matching $\Omega(K^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ lower bound. We also prove a similar high probability regret bound. We further consider a simpler \emph{fixed-gap} adversarial setup, which bridges between two extreme preference feedback models for dueling bandits: stationary preferences and an arbitrary sequence of preferences. For the fixed-gap adversarial setup we give an $\smash{ \tilde{O}((K/\Delta^2)\log{T}) }$ regret algorithm, where $\Delta$ is the gap in Borda scores between the best item and all other items, and show a lower bound of $\Omega(K/\Delta^2)$ indicating that our dependence on the main problem parameters $K$ and $\Delta$ is tight (up to logarithmic factors). Finally, we corroborate the theoretical results with empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decisions where feedback consists only of which of two selected items wins a comparison. For K items and T rounds, the authors give an algorithm with regret scaling as K^(1/3)T^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors. Here, regret grows logarithmically with T, with dependence on K and the inverse squared Borda-score gap. A lower bound establishes tightness in those main parameters up to logarithmic factors. Empirical evaluations support the theoretical results across the settings examined.
summary.tldr: The paper gives near-optimal regret guarantees for learning from pairwise comparisons under adversarial preferences.

title: Adversarial Dueling Bandits

abstract: Parallel tempering (PT) is a class of Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms that constructs a path of distributions annealing between a tractable reference and an intractable target, and then interchanges states along the path to improve mixing in the target. The performance of PT depends on how quickly a sample from the reference distribution makes its way to the target, which in turn depends on the particular path of annealing distributions. However, past work on PT has used only simple paths constructed from convex combinations of the reference and target log-densities. This paper begins by demonstrating that this path performs poorly in the setting where the reference and target are nearly mutually singular. To address this issue, we expand the framework of PT to general families of paths, formulate the choice of path as an optimization problem that admits tractable gradient estimates, and propose a flexible new family of spline interpolation paths for use in practice. Theoretical and empirical results both demonstrate that our proposed methodology breaks previously-established upper performance limits for traditional paths.

paragraphs: Parallel tempering helps sample from a difficult distribution by linking it to an easier reference through intermediate distributions. States are exchanged along this path, and performance depends on how readily a reference sample can reach the target. The choice of intermediate distributions therefore affects how effectively the procedure explores the target.

Traditional paths use convex combinations of the reference and target log-densities. The paper shows that this choice performs poorly when the distributions are nearly mutually singular, meaning their probability mass has very little overlap. It broadens parallel tempering to general path families and formulates path selection as an optimization problem with tractable gradient estimates.

For practical use, the authors introduce flexible paths based on spline interpolation. Both theoretical and empirical results show that the methodology can exceed previously established upper performance limits for traditional paths. The significance is that these limits are tied to the older path construction: optimizing the route between distributions expands the performance available within parallel tempering rather than merely tuning the same conventional route.
summary.tldr: Optimizing flexible paths between reference and target distributions lets parallel tempering exceed performance limits associated with traditional paths.

title: Parallel tempering on optimized paths

abstract: Generation of drug-like molecules with high binding affinity to target proteins remains a difficult and resource-intensive task in drug discovery. Existing approaches primarily employ reinforcement learning, Markov sampling, or deep generative models guided by Gaussian processes, which can be prohibitively slow when generating molecules with high binding affinity calculated by computationally-expensive physics-based methods. We present Latent Inceptionism on Molecules (LIMO), which significantly accelerates molecule generation with an inceptionism-like technique. LIMO employs a variational autoencoder-generated latent space and property prediction by two neural networks in sequence to enable faster gradient-based reverse-optimization of molecular properties. Comprehensive experiments show that LIMO performs competitively on benchmark tasks and markedly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on the novel task of generating drug-like compounds with high binding affinity, reaching nanomolar range against two protein targets. We corroborate these docking-based results with more accurate molecular dynamics-based calculations of absolute binding free energy and show that one of our generated drug-like compounds has a predicted $K_D$ (a measure of binding affinity) of $6 \cdot 10^{-14}$ M against the human estrogen receptor, well beyond the affinities of typical early-stage drug candidates and most FDA-approved drugs to their respective targets. Code is available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/LIMO.

LIMO accelerates this search by optimizing within a learned molecular representation. Its aim is to generate promising structures while making property-directed search faster.

title: LIMO: Latent Inceptionism for Targeted Molecule Generation

abstract: Artificial Neural Networks are functionally equivalent to special-purpose computers. Their inter-neuronal connection weights represent the learnt Neural Program that instructs the networks on how to compute the data. However, without storing Neural Programs, they are restricted to only one, overwriting learnt programs when trained on new data. Here we design Neurocoder, a new class of general-purpose neural networks in which the neural network “codes” itself in a data-responsive way by composing relevant programs from a set of shareable, modular programs stored in external memory. This time, a Neural Program is efficiently treated as data in memory. Integrating Neurocoder into current neural architectures, we demonstrate new capacity to learn modular programs, reuse simple programs to build complex ones, handle pattern shifts and remember old programs as new ones are learnt, and show substantial performance improvement in solving object recognition, playing video games and continual learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper views a neural network’s learned connection weights as a program specifying how it processes data. In an ordinary network, training on new data changes that program and can overwrite previous learning. Neurocoder introduces an architecture that stores modular neural programs in external memory and composes them according to the current data.

The central idea is to treat programs themselves as stored data. Relevant modules can be shared and combined, allowing the network to configure its computation responsively. This makes program reuse an explicit architectural capability, including the possibility of building more complex programs from simpler ones rather than learning every computation as a single undivided set of weights.

Integrated into existing neural architectures, Neurocoder demonstrates modular learning, composition, handling of pattern shifts, and retention of old programs while learning new ones. The authors report substantial performance improvements in object recognition, video games, and continual learning tasks. These findings support stored, reusable programs as a practical mechanism for broadening what a neural architecture can retain and recombine.
summary.tldr: Neurocoder stores and combines reusable neural programs to adapt computation and improve performance across recognition, games, and continual learning.

title: Neurocoder: General-Purpose Computation Using Stored Neural Programs

abstract: Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) methods are the mainstream algorithms for minimax optimization in generative adversarial networks (GANs). Convergence properties of GDA have drawn significant interest in the recent literature. Specifically, for $\min_{x} \max_{y} f(x;y)$ where $f$ is strongly-concave in $y$ and possibly nonconvex in $x$, (Lin et al., 2020) proved the convergence of GDA with a stepsize ratio $\eta_y/\eta_x=\Theta(\kappa^2)$ where $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$ are the stepsizes for $x$ and $y$ and $\kappa$ is the condition number for $y$. While this stepsize ratio suggests a slow training of the min player, practical GAN algorithms typically adopt similar stepsizes for both variables, indicating a wide gap between theoretical and empirical results. In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap by analyzing the local convergence of general nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems. We demonstrate that a stepsize ratio of $\Theta(\kappa)$ is necessary and sufficient for local convergence of GDA to a Stackelberg Equilibrium, where $\kappa$ is the local condition number for $y$. We prove a nearly tight convergence rate with a matching lower bound. We further extend the convergence guarantees to stochastic GDA and extra-gradient methods (EG). Finally, we conduct several numerical experiments to support our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Gradient descent ascent alternates opposing objectives: one variable minimizes a function while another maximizes it. Earlier theory for a strongly concave maximizing variable required a step-size ratio scaling quadratically with its condition number. This makes the minimizing player move relatively slowly, whereas practical GAN methods often use similar step sizes.

The paper examines local convergence for general nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems. It shows that a ratio scaling linearly with the maximizing variable’s local condition number is necessary and sufficient for local convergence to a Stackelberg equilibrium. The local scope is central: the result concerns convergence near the relevant equilibrium, rather than a guarantee from arbitrary starting points.

The authors also prove a nearly tight convergence rate and provide a matching lower bound. They extend convergence guarantees to stochastic gradient descent ascent and extra-gradient methods, then use numerical experiments to support the theory. The analysis narrows the theoretical step-size gap while precisely characterizing the remaining dependence on local conditioning.
summary.tldr: A tight local analysis shows that GDA requires a step-size ratio scaling linearly with local conditioning to converge to a Stackelberg equilibrium.

title: On Convergence of Gradient Descent Ascent: A Tight Local Analysis

abstract: Inspired by recent work of Islamov et al (2021), we propose a family of Federated Newton Learn (\algname{FedNL}) methods, which we believe is a marked step in the direction of making second-order methods applicable to FL. In contrast to the aforementioned work, \algname{FedNL} employs a different Hessian learning technique which i) enhances privacy as it does not rely on the training data to be revealed to the coordinating server, ii) makes it applicable beyond generalized linear models, and iii) provably works with general contractive compression operators for compressing the local Hessians, such as Top-$K$ or Rank-$R$, which are vastly superior in practice. Notably, we do not need to rely on error feedback for our methods to work with contractive compressors. Moreover, we develop \algname{FedNL-PP}, \algname{FedNL-CR} and \algname{FedNL-LS}, which are variants of \algname{FedNL} that support partial participation, and globalization via cubic regularization and line search, respectively, and \algname{FedNL-BC}, which is a variant that can further benefit from bidirectional compression of gradients and models, i.e., smart uplink gradient and smart downlink model compression. We prove local convergence rates that are independent of the condition number, the number of training data points, and compression variance. Our communication efficient Hessian learning technique provably learns the Hessian at the optimum. Finally, we perform a variety of numerical experiments that show that our \algname{FedNL} methods have state-of-the-art communication complexity when compared to key baselines.

paragraphs: Newton-type optimization uses Hessians to describe curvature, but communicating this information creates challenges in federated learning. FedNL addresses them with a family of methods that learn local Hessian information efficiently. Its Hessian-learning procedure does not require revealing training data to the coordinating server and applies beyond generalized linear models.

The method supports general contractive compression operators, including Top-K and Rank-R, without requiring error feedback. Additional variants support partial participation, cubic regularization, line search, and compression in both communication directions. These extensions address distinct practical requirements: not every participant must contribute each time, and information sent to and from the server can be compressed.

The authors prove local convergence rates independent of the condition number, training-data count, and compression variance. They also prove that the Hessian-learning procedure learns the Hessian at the optimum. Numerical experiments report state-of-the-art communication complexity against key baselines. Together, these results advance the use of curvature information in federated optimization, with the convergence-rate claim specifically applying locally.
summary.tldr: FedNL learns compressed Hessians to make Newton-type federated optimization more communication-efficient, with local convergence guarantees and practical participation variants.

title: FedNL: Making Newton-Type Methods Applicable to Federated Learning

abstract: Neural networks’ lack of robustness against attacks raises concerns in security-sensitive settings such as autonomous vehicles. While many countermeasures may look promising, only a few withstand rigorous evaluation. Defenses using random transformations (RT) have shown impressive results, particularly BaRT (Raff et al., 2019) on ImageNet. However, this type of defense has not been rigorously evaluated, leaving its robustness properties poorly understood. Their stochastic properties make evaluation more challenging and render many proposed attacks on deterministic models inapplicable. First, we show that the BPDA attack (Athalye et al., 2018a) used in BaRT’s evaluation is ineffective and likely overestimates its robustness. We then attempt to construct the strongest possible RT defense through the informed selection of transformations and Bayesian optimization for tuning their parameters. Furthermore, we create the strongest possible attack to evaluate our RT defense. Our new attack vastly outperforms the baseline, reducing the accuracy by 83% compared to the 19% reduction by the commonly used EoT attack ($4.3\times$ improvement). Our result indicates that the RT defense on the Imagenette dataset (a ten-class subset of ImageNet) is not robust against adversarial examples. Extending the study further, we use our new attack to adversarially train RT defense (called AdvRT), resulting in a large robustness gain. Code is available at https://github.com/wagnergroup/demystify-random-transform.

abstract: Existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods are typically benchmarked on training sets with balanced class distributions. However, in real-world applications, it is common for the training sets to have long-tailed distributions. In this work, we first demonstrate that existing OOD detection methods commonly suffer from significant performance degradation when the training set is long-tail distributed. Through analysis, we posit that this is because the models struggle to distinguish the minority tail-class in-distribution samples, from the true OOD samples, making the tail classes more prone to be falsely detected as OOD. To solve this problem, we propose Partial and Asymmetric Supervised Contrastive Learning (PASCL), which explicitly encourages the model to distinguish between tail-class in-distribution samples and OOD samples. To further boost in-distribution classification accuracy, we propose Auxiliary Branch Finetuning, which uses two separate branches of BN and classification layers for anomaly detection and in-distribution classification, respectively. The intuition is that in-distribution and OOD anomaly data have different underlying distributions. Our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art method by $1.29%$, $1.45%$, $0.69%$ anomaly detection false positive rate (FPR) and $3.24%$, $4.06%$, $7.89%$ in-distribution classification accuracy on CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT, and ImageNet-LT, respectively. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/amazon-research/long-tailed-ood-detection.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detectors must distinguish unfamiliar inputs from valid examples of known classes. The paper shows that this becomes harder when training classes are highly imbalanced. Its analysis suggests that models confuse rare but legitimate tail-class examples with truly outside inputs, causing those valid examples to be disproportionately rejected as anomalies.

Partial and Asymmetric Supervised Contrastive Learning, or PASCL, explicitly encourages separation between tail-class examples and out-of-distribution samples. The authors also introduce Auxiliary Branch Finetuning to improve ordinary classification. It uses separate batch-normalization and classification branches for anomaly detection and in-distribution classification, motivated by differences between the distributions involved in those two objectives.

Across CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT, and ImageNet-LT, the method improves both anomaly-detection false-positive rate and in-distribution classification accuracy relative to the previous state-of-the-art method evaluated. These results matter together: better anomaly detection is useful only if valid rare categories can still be recognized effectively. The study identifies class imbalance as a practical challenge for detection and provides a training approach aimed directly at the proposed source of confusion.
summary.tldr: PASCL helps distinguish rare legitimate classes from outside inputs, improving detection and classification on long-tailed datasets.

title: Partial and Asymmetric Contrastive Learning for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Long-Tailed Recognition

abstract: Mixture models are universal approximators of smooth densities but are difficult to utilize in complicated datasets due to restrictions on typically available modes and challenges with initialiations. We show that by continuously parameterizing a mixture of factor analyzers using a learned ordinary differential equation, we can improve the fit of mixture models over direct methods. Once trained, the mixture components can be extracted and the neural ODE can be discarded, leaving us with an effective, but low-resource model. We additionally explore the use of a training curriculum from an easy-to-model latent space extracted from a normalizing flow to the more complex input space and show that the smooth curriculum helps to stabilize and improve results with and without the continuous parameterization. Finally, we introduce a hierarchical version of the model to enable more flexible, robust classification and clustering, and show substantial improvements against traditional parameterizations of GMMs.

paragraphs: Mixture models can approximate smooth probability densities, but fitting them to complicated data can be difficult because of initialization and restrictions in typical model forms. This paper changes how a mixture of factor analyzers is parameterized during training. A learned ordinary differential equation continuously parameterizes the mixture, improving its fit compared with direct approaches.

The differential equation serves as a training mechanism rather than a permanent requirement for using the model. After training, the mixture components can be extracted and the neural differential equation discarded. This allows the method to benefit from a richer training construction while leaving behind a low-resource mixture model.

The authors also investigate a smooth training curriculum that moves from an easier latent space, obtained from a normalizing flow, toward the more complex input space. They report that this progression stabilizes and improves results both with and without continuous parameterization. Finally, a hierarchical version supports more flexible, robust classification and clustering, with substantial improvements over traditional Gaussian mixture parameterizations. The paper thus develops complementary changes to parameterization, training progression, and model hierarchy.
summary.tldr: A learned differential equation improves mixture-model fitting during training and can then be discarded to leave a low-resource model.

title: Continuously Parameterized Mixture Models

abstract: Maximizing monotone submodular functions under a matroid constraint is a classic algorithmic problem with multiple applications in data mining and machine learning. We study this classic problem in the fully dynamic setting, where elements can be both inserted and deleted in real-time. Our main result is a randomized algorithm that maintains an efficient data structure with an $\tilde{O}(k^2)$ amortized update time (in the number of additions and deletions) and yields a $4$-approximate solution, where $k$ is the rank of the matroid.
originalAbstract: Maximizing monotone submodular functions under a matroid constraint is a classic algorithmic problem with multiple applications in data mining and machine learning. We study this classic problem in the fully dynamic setting, where elements can be both inserted and deleted in real-time. Our main result is a randomized algorithm that maintains an efficient data structure with an $\tilde{O}(k^2)$ amortized update time (in the number of additions and deletions) and yields a $4$-approximate solution, where $k$ is the rank of the matroid.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maintain a valuable selection of items when the available items keep changing. The objective is monotone and submodular, meaning that adding items does not reduce value and that additional items have diminishing returns. A matroid constraint specifies which selections are feasible.

The setting is fully dynamic: items can be inserted and deleted in real time. Both kinds of change matter because the algorithm must continue maintaining a useful solution as availability evolves. The authors introduce a randomized algorithm with a data structure designed to support these updates efficiently.

Their result combines a factor-four approximation with an amortized update time of approximately k squared, suppressing logarithmic factors, where k is the matroid’s rank. The approximation expresses a controlled gap from the best feasible value, while amortized time describes cost averaged across a sequence of updates. Together, these guarantees address solution quality and maintenance cost in the same framework, extending this classic selection problem to changing data.
summary.tldr: A randomized algorithm maintains a factor-four approximation for submodular selection under matroid constraints as items arrive and disappear.

title: Fully Dynamic Submodular Maximization over Matroids

abstract: Data-free knowledge distillation (KD) helps transfer knowledge from a pre-trained model (known as the teacher model) to a smaller model (known as the student model) without access to the original training data used for training the teacher model. However, the security of the synthetic or out-of-distribution (OOD) data required in data-free KD is largely unknown and under-explored. In this work, we make the first effort to uncover the security risk of data-free KD w.r.t. untrusted pre-trained models. We then propose Anti-Backdoor Data-Free KD (ABD), the first plug-in defensive method for data-free KD methods to mitigate the chance of potential backdoors being transferred. We empirically evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed ABD in diminishing transferred backdoor knowledge while maintaining compatible downstream performances as the vanilla KD. We envision this work as a milestone for alarming and mitigating the potential backdoors in data-free KD. Codes are released at https://github.com/illidanlab/ABD .

paragraphs: Data-free knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a pretrained teacher model to a smaller student without using the teacher's original training data. Instead, the process relies on synthetic or out-of-distribution examples. This paper examines a security concern in that transfer: an untrusted teacher may carry backdoor behavior that can also reach the student.

The authors investigate this risk and introduce Anti-Backdoor Data-Free Knowledge Distillation, abbreviated ABD. It is designed as a defensive component that can be added to data-free distillation methods. Its purpose is to reduce the chance that unwanted backdoor knowledge is transferred alongside useful predictive behavior, making teacher trustworthiness part of the distillation problem.

The empirical evaluation finds that ABD diminishes transferred backdoor knowledge while maintaining downstream performance comparable to ordinary distillation. This supports mitigation in the evaluated setting rather than a guarantee that every backdoor is removed. The paper matters because obtaining a smaller model without the original dataset does not by itself settle the security of the knowledge inherited from its teacher.
summary.tldr: ABD is a plug-in defense that empirically reduces backdoor transfer during data-free distillation while preserving comparable downstream performance.

title: Revisiting Data-Free Knowledge Distillation with Poisoned Teachers

abstract: Contrastive learning (CL) continuously achieves significant breakthroughs across multiple domains. However, the most common InfoNCE-based methods suffer from some dilemmas, such as uniformity-tolerance dilemma (UTD) and gradient reduction, both of which are related to a $\mathcal{P}_{ij}$ term. It has been identified that UTD can lead to unexpected performance degradation. We argue that the fixity of temperature is to blame for UTD. To tackle this challenge, we enrich the CL loss family by presenting a Model-Aware Contrastive Learning (MACL) strategy, whose temperature is adaptive to the magnitude of alignment that reflects the basic confidence of the instance discrimination task, then enables CL loss to adjust the penalty strength for hard negatives adaptively. Regarding another dilemma, the gradient reduction issue, we derive the limits of an involved gradient scaling factor, which allows us to explain from a unified perspective why some recent approaches are effective with fewer negative samples, and summarily present a gradient reweighting to escape this dilemma. Extensive remarkable empirical results in vision, sentence, and graph modality validate our approach’s general improvement for representation learning and downstream tasks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses two difficulties in common InfoNCE-based contrastive learning methods: the uniformity-tolerance dilemma and gradient reduction. The first can cause unexpected performance degradation, while the second concerns weakening gradient contributions. The authors connect both issues to a term in the loss and examine how its behavior affects learning.

Their Model-Aware Contrastive Learning strategy makes the temperature adaptive. Temperature changes with the magnitude of alignment, which the authors use as an indication of confidence in the instance-discrimination task. This lets the loss adjust the strength of penalties applied to hard negative examples as the model changes, addressing the authors' argument that fixed temperature contributes to the first dilemma.

For gradient reduction, the authors derive limits on a gradient-scaling factor and propose gradient reweighting. The analysis also offers a common explanation for why some recent methods work with fewer negative samples. Experiments involving vision, sentences, and graphs report improvements in representation learning and downstream tasks. The approach therefore combines a model-dependent loss adjustment with a separate correction to gradient scaling.
summary.tldr: MACL adapts contrastive-learning temperature to model alignment and reweights gradients to address two difficulties in InfoNCE-based training.

title: Model-Aware Contrastive Learning: Towards Escaping the Dilemmas

abstract: The success of deep learning is greatly attributed to stochastic gradient descent (SGD), yet it remains unclear how SGD finds well-generalized models. We demonstrate that SGD has an implicit regularization effect on the logit-weight Jacobian norm of neural networks. This regularization effect is weighted with the impurity of the probability output, and thus it is active in a certain phase of training. Moreover, based on these findings, we propose a novel optimization method that explicitly regularizes the Jacobian norm, which leads to similar performance as other state-of-the-art sharpness-aware optimization methods.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent often finds neural networks that generalize well, but explaining why remains difficult. This paper identifies an implicit regularization effect on the logit-weight Jacobian norm. That quantity describes the sensitivity of a network's prediction scores to changes in its weights, connecting the training procedure to how strongly those scores respond to parameter changes.

The effect is weighted by the impurity of the network's probability output. Consequently, its influence is tied to the state of the predictions and becomes active during a particular phase of training. This qualification matters: the proposed explanation describes a training-dependent effect, rather than a penalty that acts with the same strength throughout optimization.

Using this finding, the authors design an optimization method that explicitly regularizes the Jacobian norm. They report performance similar to other state-of-the-art sharpness-aware optimization methods. The paper therefore connects an analysis of SGD's implicit behavior to a concrete training objective, showing how a proposed explanation of generalization can motivate an explicit optimizer.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies a prediction-dependent Jacobian regularization effect in SGD and uses it to design an explicit optimization method.

title: Implicit Jacobian regularization weighted with impurity of probability output

abstract: Reinforcement learning is time-consuming for complex tasks due to the need for large amounts of training data. Recent advances in GPU-based simulation, such as Isaac Gym, have sped up data collection thousands of times on a commodity GPU. Most prior works have used on-policy methods like PPO due to their simplicity and easy-to-scale nature. Off-policy methods are more sample-efficient, but challenging to scale, resulting in a longer wall-clock training time. This paper presents a novel Parallel Q-Learning (PQL) scheme that outperforms PPO in terms of wall-clock time and maintains superior sample efficiency. The driving force lies in the parallelization of data collection, policy function learning, and value function learning. Different from prior works on distributed off-policy learning, such as Apex, our scheme is designed specifically for massively parallel GPU-based simulation and optimized to work on a single workstation. In experiments, we demonstrate the capability of scaling up Q-learning methods to tens of thousands of parallel environments and investigate important factors that can affect learning speed, including the number of parallel environments, exploration strategies, batch size, GPU models, etc. The code is available at https://github.com/Improbable-AI/pql.

paragraphs: GPU simulation can collect reinforcement learning experience extremely quickly, but a learning algorithm must keep pace to benefit. On-policy methods such as PPO have been popular because they scale readily. Off-policy methods use samples more efficiently, yet their scaling difficulties can leave them slower in elapsed training time.

Parallel Q-Learning addresses this mismatch by parallelizing data collection, policy learning, and value learning. The scheme is designed specifically for massively parallel GPU simulation on a single workstation. Its organization targets the full learning process, so faster simulation can be accompanied by parallel work on the policy and its value estimates.

The reported experiments show better wall-clock training time than PPO while retaining superior sample efficiency. They demonstrate Q-learning with tens of thousands of parallel environments and investigate how environment count, exploration, batch size, and GPU choice affect learning speed. The findings show that sample-efficient off-policy learning can also be fast in elapsed time when its execution is organized for this simulation setting.
summary.tldr: Parallel Q-Learning coordinates simulation, policy learning, and value learning to outperform PPO in elapsed training time while retaining better sample efficiency.

title: Parallel $Q$-Learning: Scaling Off-policy Reinforcement Learning under Massively Parallel Simulation

abstract: Memory footprint is one of the main limiting factors for large neural network training. In backpropagation, one needs to store the input to each operation in the computational graph. Every modern neural network model has quite a few pointwise nonlinearities in its architecture, and such operations induce additional memory costs that, as we show, can be significantly reduced by quantization of the gradients. We propose a systematic approach to compute optimal quantization of the retained gradients of the pointwise nonlinear functions with only a few bits per each element. We show that such approximation can be achieved by computing an optimal piecewise-constant approximation of the derivative of the activation function, which can be done by dynamic programming. The drop-in replacements are implemented for all popular nonlinearities and can be used in any existing pipeline. We confirm the memory reduction and the same convergence on several open benchmarks.
