paragraphs: Training large neural networks requires retaining information from the forward computation for use during backpropagation. Pointwise activation functions appear throughout modern architectures, and the information stored for these operations contributes to memory consumption. This paper targets that cost by representing the activation-gradient information needed for the backward pass using only a few bits per element.

The authors formulate the task as finding an optimal piecewise-constant approximation to an activation function's derivative. Instead of retaining a high-precision derivative value, the method can represent it using one of a small number of values. Dynamic programming computes the optimal approximation, providing a systematic procedure for choosing the quantization.

The resulting activation operations are implemented as drop-in replacements for popular nonlinearities, allowing them to be incorporated into existing training pipelines. On several open benchmarks, the authors confirm reduced memory use with the same observed convergence. The findings indicate that substantial savings are possible in this particular part of the training memory footprint while preserving the tested models' learning behavior.
summary.tldr: Few-bit Backward reduces training memory by optimally quantizing activation derivatives, with unchanged convergence on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Few-bit Backward: Quantized Gradients of Activation Functions for Memory Footprint Reduction

abstract: We consider guiding denoising diffusion models with general differentiable loss functions in a plug-and-play fashion, enabling controllable generation without additional training. This paradigm, termed Loss-Guided Diffusion (LGD), can easily be integrated into all diffusion models and leverage various efficient samplers. Despite the benefits, the resulting guidance term is, unfortunately, an intractable integral and needs to be approximated. Existing methods compute the guidance term based on a point estimate. However, we show that such approaches have significant errors over the scale of the approximations. To address this issue, we propose a Monte Carlo method that uses multiple samples from a suitable distribution to reduce bias. Our method is effective in various synthetic and real-world settings, including image super-resolution, text or label-conditional image generation, and controllable motion synthesis. Notably, we show how our method can be applied to control a pretrained motion diffusion model to follow certain paths and avoid obstacles that are proven challenging to prior methods.

paragraphs: Loss-Guided Diffusion aims to steer a pretrained diffusion model using a differentiable loss, without additional training. The loss expresses a desired property of the output, allowing generation to be controlled through the sampling process. The framework is designed to integrate with diffusion models and work with various efficient samplers.

The difficulty is computing the guidance signal: its exact form involves an intractable integral. Existing approaches approximate that signal using a single point estimate, and the authors show that this introduces substantial approximation errors. Their alternative uses Monte Carlo sampling, drawing multiple samples from a suitable distribution to reduce the bias of the guidance estimate.

The method is effective in synthetic and real-world settings spanning image super-resolution, text- or label-conditioned image generation, and motion synthesis. In particular, it guides a pretrained motion model to follow specified paths and avoid obstacles that challenged prior methods. These findings connect a better approximation of the guidance term to more effective control across several generation tasks.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo guidance reduces approximation bias when controlling pretrained diffusion models with differentiable losses and no additional training.

title: Loss-Guided Diffusion Models for Plug-and-Play Controllable Generation

abstract: Additive models have been burgeoning in data analysis due to their flexible representation and desirable interpretability. However, most existing approaches are constructed under empirical risk minimization (ERM), and thus perform poorly in situations where average performance is not a suitable criterion for the problems of interest, e.g., data with complex non-Gaussian noise, imbalanced labels or both of them. In this paper, a novel class of sparse additive models is proposed under tilted empirical risk minimization (TERM), which addresses the deficiencies in ERM by imposing tilted impact on individual losses, and is flexibly capable of achieving a variety of learning objectives, e.g., variable selection, robust estimation, imbalanced classification and multiobjective learning. On the theoretical side, a learning theory analysis which is centered around the generalization bound and function approximation error bound (under some specific data distributions) is conducted rigorously. On the practical side, an accelerated optimization algorithm is designed by integrating Prox-SVRG and random Fourier acceleration technique. The empirical assessments verify the competitive performance of our approach on both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Additive models offer flexible predictions while retaining an interpretable structure, but training them to minimize average loss may be unsuitable for some problems. This paper highlights complex non-Gaussian noise and imbalanced labels as motivating cases. It proposes sparse additive models trained through tilted empirical risk minimization.

Tilting changes how individual losses influence the training objective. This gives the model family flexibility to address variable selection, robust estimation, imbalanced classification, and multiple learning objectives. The contribution changes the criterion used to fit the additive model, allowing the influence of examples to reflect goals that ordinary average-loss minimization may handle poorly.

The authors provide a learning-theoretic analysis centered on generalization and function-approximation error bounds, with the latter established under specific data distributions. They also design an accelerated optimization method combining Prox-SVRG with a random Fourier acceleration technique. Experiments on synthetic and real data report competitive performance. The work therefore develops the modeling objective, its theoretical analysis, and an optimization procedure together, with empirical assessments supporting its practical use.
summary.tldr: Tilted sparse additive models adjust the influence of individual losses to support robust, imbalanced, and multiobjective learning.

title: Tilted Sparse Additive Models

abstract: We study variance-dependent regret bounds for Markov decision processes (MDPs). Algorithms with variance-dependent regret guarantees can automatically exploit environments with low variance (e.g., enjoying constant regret on deterministic MDPs). The existing algorithms are either variance-independent or suboptimal. We first propose two new environment norms to characterize the fine-grained variance properties of the environment. For model-based methods, we design a variant of the MVP algorithm (Zhang et al., 2021a). We apply new analysis techniques to demonstrate that this algorithm enjoys variance-dependent bounds with respect to the norms we propose. In particular, this bound is simultaneously minimax optimal for both stochastic and deterministic MDPs, the first result of its kind. We further initiate the study on model-free algorithms with variance-dependent regret bounds by designing a reference-function-based algorithm with a novel capped-doubling reference update schedule. Lastly, we also provide lower bounds to complement our upper bounds.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning guarantee can be more informative when it reflects how variable the environment actually is. Low-variance environments offer opportunities that a variance-independent regret bound cannot capture. This paper develops guarantees that adapt to those opportunities, including the deterministic setting, while retaining strong performance guarantees for stochastic environments.

The authors introduce two environment norms to describe fine-grained variance properties. They then design a model-based variant of the MVP algorithm and analyze regret in terms of those norms. The resulting bound is simultaneously minimax optimal for stochastic and deterministic Markov decision processes, establishing a single guarantee that matches the difficulty of both settings.

Complementary lower bounds help characterize the difficulty of the problems being studied. Together, these contributions make environmental variance central to the analysis and extend that perspective across both model-based and model-free reinforcement-learning approaches.
summary.tldr: New variance measures support a model-based regret bound that is minimax optimal in both stochastic and deterministic environments.

title: Sharp Variance-Dependent Bounds in Reinforcement Learning: Best of Both Worlds in Stochastic and Deterministic Environments

abstract: Noisy gradient descent and its variants are the predominant algorithms for differentially private machine learning. It is a fundamental question to quantify their privacy leakage, yet tight characterizations remain open even in the foundational setting of convex losses. This paper improves over previous analyses by establishing (and refining) the “privacy amplification by iteration” phenomenon in the unifying framework of $f$-differential privacy—which tightly captures all aspects of the privacy loss and immediately implies tighter privacy accounting in other notions of differential privacy, e.g., $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP and Rényi DP. Our key technical insight is the construction of shifted interpolated processes that unravel the popular shifted-divergences argument, enabling generalizations beyond divergence-based relaxations of DP. Notably, this leads to the first exact privacy analysis in the foundational setting of strongly convex optimization. Our techniques extend to many settings: convex/strongly convex, constrained/unconstrained, full/cyclic/stochastic batches, and all combinations thereof. As an immediate corollary, we recover the $f$-DP characterization of the exponential mechanism for strongly convex optimization in Gopi et al. (2022), and moreover extend this result to more general settings.

title: Shifted Interpolation for Differential Privacy

abstract: Harnessing the power of human-annotated data through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is pivotal for advancing Large Language Models (LLMs). In this paper, we delve into the prospect of growing a strong LLM out of a weak one without the need for acquiring additional human-annotated data. We propose a new fine-tuning method called Self-Play fIne-tuNing (SPIN), which starts from a supervised fine-tuned model. At the heart of SPIN lies a self-play mechanism, where the LLM refines its capability by playing against instances of itself. More specifically, the LLM generates its own training data from its previous iterations, refining its policy by discerning these self-generated responses from those obtained from human-annotated data. Our method progressively elevates the LLM from a nascent model to a formidable one, unlocking the full potential of human-annotated demonstration data for SFT. Theoretically, we prove that the global optimum to the training objective function of our method is achieved only when the LLM policy aligns with the target data distribution. Empirically, we evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets including the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard, MT-Bench, and datasets from Big-Bench. Our results show that SPIN can significantly improve the LLM’s performance across a variety of benchmarks and even outperform models trained through direct preference optimization (DPO) supplemented with extra GPT-4 preference data. This sheds light on the promise of self-play, enabling the achievement of human-level performance in LLMs without the need for expert opponents.

paragraphs: Self-Play Fine-Tuning, or SPIN, aims to improve a language model without collecting additional human annotations. It begins with a model that has already undergone supervised fine-tuning and continues to use the existing human demonstration data. The new training signal comes from responses generated by earlier iterations of the model itself.

The model improves by learning to distinguish those self-generated responses from the human demonstrations. Repeating this process makes previous versions of the model part of the training mechanism. The authors prove that the training objective reaches its global optimum only when the model’s policy matches the target data distribution; this characterizes the optimum rather than guaranteeing every training run reaches it.

Evaluations include the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard, MT-Bench, and Big-Bench datasets. SPIN significantly improves performance across several benchmarks and can outperform models trained with direct preference optimization using additional GPT-4 preference data. These results support making better use of existing demonstrations through iterative self-play, with the paper presenting broader human-level performance as a promise of the approach.
summary.tldr: SPIN improves a supervised language model through iterative self-play using existing human demonstrations and responses from earlier model versions.

title: Self-Play Fine-Tuning Converts Weak Language Models to Strong Language Models

abstract: Speculative Sampling (SpS) has been introduced to speed up inference of large language models (LLMs) by generating multiple tokens in a single forward pass under the guidance of a reference model, while preserving the original distribution. We observe that SpS can be derived through maximum coupling on the token distribution. However, we find that this approach is not optimal as it applies maximum coupling incrementally for each new token, rather than seeking a global maximum coupling that yields a faster algorithm, given the tree-space nature of LLM generative distributions. In this paper, we shift our focus from distributions on a token space to those on a tree space. We propose a novel class of Tree Monte Carlo (TMC) methods, demonstrating their unbiasedness and convergence. As a particular instance of TMC, our new algorithm, Accelerated Speculative Sampling (ASpS), outperforms traditional SpS by generating more tokens per step on average, achieving faster inference, while maintaining the original distribution.

paragraphs: Speculative sampling accelerates language-model generation by producing multiple tokens in a forward pass while preserving the model’s original output distribution. This paper examines the probability construction behind that process. It observes that conventional speculative sampling applies maximum coupling, a way of coordinating two distributions, separately at each successive token.

The authors argue that these local decisions do not make full use of the branching structure of possible continuations. They instead study distributions over trees of generated sequences. This leads to Tree Monte Carlo, a broader family of sampling methods for which they establish unbiasedness and convergence, providing theoretical support for the approach.

Accelerated Speculative Sampling is a particular algorithm within that family. The stated result is that it produces more tokens per step on average than conventional speculative sampling and achieves faster inference while retaining the original distribution. The contribution therefore concerns how generation is organized and sampled: considering branches together enables acceleration without changing the distribution the language model is supposed to generate.
summary.tldr: Tree-based speculative sampling generates more tokens per step on average while preserving the language model’s original output distribution.

title: Accelerated Speculative Sampling Based on Tree Monte Carlo

abstract: Mixture of experts (MoE) model is a statistical machine learning design that aggregates multiple expert networks using a softmax gating function in order to form a more intricate and expressive model. Despite being commonly used in several applications owing to their scalability, the mathematical and statistical properties of MoE models are complex and difficult to analyze. As a result, previous theoretical works have primarily focused on probabilistic MoE models by imposing the impractical assumption that the data are generated from a Gaussian MoE model. In this work, we investigate the performance of the least squares estimators (LSE) under a deterministic MoE model where the data are sampled according to a regression model, a setting that has remained largely unexplored. We establish a condition called strong identifiability to characterize the convergence behavior of various types of expert functions. We demonstrate that the rates for estimating strongly identifiable experts, namely the widely used feed forward networks with activation functions $\mathrm{sigmoid}(\cdot)$ and $\tanh(\cdot)$, are substantially faster than those of polynomial experts, which we show to exhibit a surprising slow estimation rate. Our findings have important practical implications for expert selection.

paragraphs: A mixture of experts combines several expert networks using weights supplied by a softmax gate. Although this architecture is widely used, analyzing how reliably its components can be estimated is difficult. This paper studies least-squares estimation for a deterministic mixture-of-experts regression model, moving beyond earlier theory centered on data generated by Gaussian mixture-of-experts models.

The analysis introduces a condition called strong identifiability to characterize estimation convergence for different expert functions. The central comparison concerns feed-forward experts using sigmoid or tanh activations and experts defined by polynomials. The authors show substantially faster estimation rates for the strongly identifiable neural-network experts, while polynomial experts can have surprisingly slow rates.

The result makes expert selection a statistical question as well as an architectural one. Different function choices can change how quickly estimation improves as more data becomes available, even within the same softmax-gated design. The paper's conclusions concern the analyzed regression setting and identifiability condition, providing theoretical guidance about which expert families support more favorable least-squares estimation behavior.
summary.tldr: Strong identifiability explains why least-squares estimation can converge much faster for sigmoid and tanh experts than for polynomial experts.

title: On Least Square Estimation in Softmax Gating Mixture of Experts

abstract: Discrimination and calibration represent two important properties of survival analysis, with the former assessing the model’s ability to accurately rank subjects and the latter evaluating the alignment of predicted outcomes with actual events. With their distinct nature, it is hard for survival models to simultaneously optimize both of them especially as many previous results found improving calibration tends to diminish discrimination performance. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing conformal regression that can improve a model’s calibration without degrading discrimination. We provide theoretical guarantees for the above claim, and rigorously validate the efficiency of our approach across 11 real-world datasets, showcasing its practical applicability and robustness in diverse scenarios.

This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing conformal regression that can improve a model’s calibration without degrading discrimination. paragraphs: Survival models have two distinct responsibilities: ordering subjects accurately and producing predictions that agree with observed events. These properties are called discrimination and calibration. A model can perform well on one without performing well on the other, making their simultaneous improvement an important challenge.

Previous results have often found that improving calibration comes at the expense of discrimination. This paper introduces a post-processing approach based on conformal regression that can improve calibration without degrading discrimination. Applying a correction after prediction offers a way to address the alignment of predicted outcomes with events while preserving the model's ranking performance.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for that claimed combination and evaluate the approach across 11 real-world datasets. The evaluations support its efficiency and applicability across diverse scenarios. The central finding is that the calibration–discrimination tradeoff need not arise for the proposed procedure: better agreement with actual outcomes can coexist with preserved ranking quality, according to the paper's theory and validation.
summary.tldr: A conformal regression post-process can improve survival-model calibration without degrading discrimination.

title: Conformalized Survival Distributions: A Generic Post-Process to Increase Calibration

abstract: We study the problem of best-arm identification with fixed budget in stochastic multi-armed bandits with Bernoulli rewards. For the problem with two arms, also known as the A/B testing problem, we prove that there is no algorithm that (i) performs as well as the algorithm sampling each arm equally (referred to as the uniform sampling algorithm) in all instances, and that (ii) strictly outperforms uniform sampling on at least one instance. In short, there is no algorithm better than the uniform sampling algorithm. To establish this result, we first introduce the natural class of consistent and stable algorithms, and show that any algorithm that performs as well as the uniform sampling algorithm in all instances belongs to this class. The proof then proceeds by deriving a lower bound on the error rate satisfied by any consistent and stable algorithm, and by showing that the uniform sampling algorithm matches this lower bound. Our results provide a solution to the two open problems presented in (Qin, 2022). For the general problem with more than two arms, we provide a first set of results. We characterize the asymptotic error rate of the celebrated Successive Rejects (SR) algorithm (Audibert et al., 2010) and show that, surprisingly, the uniform sampling algorithm outperforms the SR algorithm in some instances.

paragraphs: The paper studies identifying the better of two options with a fixed sampling budget and Bernoulli rewards. Its central result concerns universal improvement: no algorithm can match equal sampling on every problem instance while strictly improving on it for at least one instance. This establishes a precise boundary on attempts to dominate uniform sampling across all such A/B testing problems.

The proof introduces algorithms with consistency and stability properties. The authors show that any algorithm matching uniform sampling everywhere must belong to this class. They then derive an error-rate lower bound for the class and show that uniform sampling attains it. The conclusion does not say that another allocation can never perform better on a particular instance; it rules out doing so without losing somewhere else.

For more than two options, the paper provides initial results rather than the same complete characterization. It determines the asymptotic error rate of Successive Rejects and shows that uniform sampling performs better on some instances. This highlights why adaptive allocation alone does not establish universal superiority.
summary.tldr: For fixed-budget A/B testing with Bernoulli rewards, no algorithm can match uniform sampling on every instance and strictly beat it on another.

title: On Universally Optimal Algorithms for A/B Testing

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) is essential to align them with human values and intentions. This process often utilizes methods like pairwise comparisons and KL divergence against a reference LLM, focusing on the evaluation of full answers generated by the models. However, the generation of these responses occurs in a token level, following a sequential, auto-regressive fashion. In this paper, we introduce Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (TDPO), a novel approach to align LLMs with human preferences by optimizing policy at the token level. Unlike previous methods, which face challenges in divergence efficiency, TDPO integrates forward KL divergence constraints for each token, improving alignment and diversity. Utilizing the Bradley-Terry model for a token-based reward system, our method enhances the regulation of KL divergence, while preserving simplicity without the need for explicit reward modeling. Experimental results across various text tasks demonstrate TDPO’s superior performance in balancing alignment with generation diversity. Notably, fine-tuning with TDPO strikes a better balance than DPO in the controlled sentiment generation and single-turn dialogue datasets, and significantly improves the quality of generated responses compared to both DPO and PPO-based RLHF methods.

This paper introduces Token-level Direct Preference Optimization, or TDPO, to bring the optimization closer to that sequential generation process and improve the balance between preference alignment and output diversity.

TDPO applies forward KL-divergence constraints at each token to regulate differences from a reference model. It uses the Bradley–Terry preference model in a token-based reward formulation while avoiding the need to train an explicit reward model. The approach aims to improve control over divergence throughout generation rather than handling alignment only at the full-response level.

The authors also report significantly better response quality than DPO and PPO-based reinforcement learning from human feedback. These findings support token-level divergence regulation as a useful design choice in the evaluated preference-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: TDPO regulates preference optimization at each token, improving the reported balance between human-preference alignment and generation diversity.

title: Token-level Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: Scaling laws play an instrumental role in the sustainable improvement in model quality. Unfortunately, recommendation models to date do not exhibit such laws similar to those observed in the domain of large language models, due to the inefficiencies of their upscaling mechanisms. This limitation poses significant challenges in adapting these models to increasingly more complex real-world datasets. In this paper, we propose an effective network architecture based purely on stacked factorization machines, and a synergistic upscaling strategy, collectively dubbed Wukong, to establish a scaling law in the domain of recommendation. Wukong’s unique design makes it possible to capture diverse, any-order of interactions simply through taller and wider layers. We conducted extensive evaluations on six public datasets, and our results demonstrate that Wukong consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models quality-wise. Further, we assessed Wukong’s scalability on an internal, large-scale dataset. The results show that Wukong retains its superiority in quality over state-of-the-art models, while holding the scaling law across two orders of magnitude in model complexity, extending beyond 100 GFLOP/example, where prior arts fall short.

paragraphs: Scaling a model is most useful when additional computation produces dependable improvements in quality. The paper argues that recommendation architectures have lacked this behavior because their mechanisms for growing models are inefficient. Wukong combines a new architecture with a matching upscaling strategy to investigate more effective scaling for recommendation.

The architecture consists entirely of stacked factorization machines. Its design allows increasing depth and width to capture diverse interactions of arbitrary order. This matters because enlarging the network also expands the interactions it can represent. The architecture and scaling strategy are therefore designed together, linking model growth to the relationships the recommendation system can learn.

On six public datasets, Wukong consistently exceeds the quality of the state-of-the-art models evaluated. On an internal large-scale dataset, it retains that advantage and exhibits a scaling law across two orders of magnitude in model complexity, extending beyond 100 GFLOP per example. These results provide empirical evidence for useful recommendation-model scaling over the tested range, including a region where the compared approaches fall short.
summary.tldr: Wukong combines stacked factorization machines with coordinated scaling to improve recommendation quality across a broad tested range of model complexity.

title: Wukong: Towards a Scaling Law for Large-Scale Recommendation

abstract: In this paper, we focus on learning a linear time-invariant (LTI) model with low-dimensional latent variables but high-dimensional observations. We provide an algorithm that recovers the high-dimensional features, i.e. column space of the observer, embeds the data into low dimensions and learns the low-dimensional model parameters. Our algorithm enjoys a sample complexity guarantee of order $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n/\epsilon^2)$, where $n$ is the observation dimension. We further establish a fundamental lower bound indicating this complexity bound is optimal up to logarithmic factors and dimension-independent constants. We show that this inevitable linear factor of $n$ is due to the learning error of the observer’s column space in the presence of high-dimensional noises. Extending our results, we consider a meta-learning problem inspired by various real-world applications, where the observer column space can be collectively learned from datasets of multiple LTI systems. An end-to-end algorithm is then proposed, facilitating learning LTI systems from a meta-dataset which breaks the sample complexity lower bound in certain scenarios.

Our algorithm enjoys a sample complexity guarantee of order $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n/\epsilon^2)$, where $n$ is the observation dimension. We further establish a fundamental lower bound indicating this complexity bound is optimal up to logarithmic factors and dimension-independent constants. paragraphs: A system can have simple hidden dynamics while producing observations with many dimensions. This paper studies that situation for linear time-invariant systems. Its algorithm first recovers the observation subspace associated with the hidden variables, embeds the observations into a smaller space, and then learns the low-dimensional dynamical parameters.

The sample requirement scales as n divided by squared error tolerance, up to logarithmic factors, where n is the observation dimension. A matching lower bound establishes optimality up to logarithmic factors and dimension-independent constants. The authors trace the unavoidable linear dependence on observation dimension to errors in learning the observation subspace when high-dimensional noise is present.

The paper then considers multiple related systems whose datasets can collectively reveal that observation subspace. An end-to-end meta-learning algorithm uses this shared information to learn the systems. In certain scenarios, this richer data setting surpasses the single-system sample-complexity lower bound. The distinction matters: sharing evidence across systems changes the learning problem and can reduce the cost of repeatedly discovering the same observation structure.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal sample requirements for learning hidden linear dynamics and shows how shared data across systems can improve them.

title: Learning Low-dimensional Latent Dynamics from High-dimensional Observations: Non-asymptotics and Lower Bounds

abstract: We introduce Score identity Distillation (SiD), an innovative data-free method that distills the generative capabilities of pretrained diffusion models into a single-step generator. SiD not only facilitates an exponentially fast reduction in Fréchet inception distance (FID) during distillation but also approaches or even exceeds the FID performance of the original teacher diffusion models. By reformulating forward diffusion processes as semi-implicit distributions, we leverage three score-related identities to create an innovative loss mechanism. This mechanism achieves rapid FID reduction by training the generator using its own synthesized images, eliminating the need for real data or reverse-diffusion-based generation, all accomplished within significantly shortened generation time. Upon evaluation across four benchmark datasets, the SiD algorithm demonstrates high iteration efficiency during distillation and surpasses competing distillation approaches, whether they are one-step or few-step, data-free, or dependent on training data, in terms of generation quality. This achievement not only redefines the benchmarks for efficiency and effectiveness in diffusion distillation but also in the broader field of diffusion-based generation. The PyTorch implementation is available at https://github.com/mingyuanzhou/SiD.
originalAbstract: We introduce Score identity Distillation (SiD), an innovative data-free method that distills the generative capabilities of pretrained diffusion models into a single-step generator. SiD not only facilitates an exponentially fast reduction in Fréchet inception distance (FID) during distillation but also approaches or even exceeds the FID performance of the original teacher diffusion models. By reformulating forward diffusion processes as semi-implicit distributions, we leverage three score-related identities to create an innovative loss mechanism. This mechanism achieves rapid FID reduction by training the generator using its own synthesized images, eliminating the need for real data or reverse-diffusion-based generation, all accomplished within significantly shortened generation time. Upon evaluation across four benchmark datasets, the SiD algorithm demonstrates high iteration efficiency during distillation and surpasses competing distillation approaches, whether they are one-step or few-step, data-free, or dependent on training data, in terms of generation quality. This achievement not only redefines the benchmarks for efficiency and effectiveness in diffusion distillation but also in the broader field of diffusion-based generation. The PyTorch implementation is available at https://github.com/mingyuanzhou/SiD.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate through a sequence of steps, and distillation aims to transfer that capability into a faster generator. Score identity Distillation, or SiD, trains a single-step generator without using real training data. It also avoids needing images produced through reverse-diffusion generation during the distillation process.

The method reformulates forward diffusion as semi-implicit distributions and derives a training loss from three score-related identities. The generator learns using images it synthesizes itself. The authors report an exponentially fast reduction in Fréchet inception distance, or FID, during distillation, with performance approaching or exceeding that of the original teacher models on this measure.

Across four benchmark datasets, SiD demonstrates high iteration efficiency and better generation quality than the competing distillation approaches examined. Those comparisons include one-step and few-step methods, as well as methods with and without access to training data. The findings connect two benefits: efficient distillation and fast single-step generation, while showing that the reported FID quality need not fall below the teacher’s.
summary.tldr: SiD distills diffusion models into single-step generators using self-generated images and score identities, with rapid FID improvement.

title: Score identity Distillation: Exponentially Fast Distillation of Pretrained Diffusion Models for One-Step Generation

abstract: Recent vision-language pre-trained models (VL-PTMs) have shown remarkable success in open-vocabulary tasks. However, downstream use cases often involve further fine-tuning of VL-PTMs, which may distort their general knowledge and impair their ability to handle distribution shifts. In real-world scenarios, machine learning systems inevitably encounter both covariate shifts (e.g., changes in image styles) and semantic shifts (e.g., test-time unseen classes). This highlights the importance of enhancing out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on covariate shifts and simultaneously detecting semantic-shifted unseen classes. Thus a critical but underexplored question arises: How to improve VL-PTMs’ generalization ability to closed-set OOD data, while effectively detecting open-set unseen classes during fine-tuning? In this paper, we propose a novel objective function of OOD detection that also serves to improve OOD generalization. We show that minimizing the gradient magnitude of energy scores on training data leads to domain-consistent Hessians of classification loss, a strong indicator for OOD generalization revealed by theoretical analysis. Based on this finding, we have developed a unified fine-tuning framework that allows for concurrent optimization of both tasks. Extensive experiments have demonstrated the superiority of our method. The code is available at https://github.com/LinLLLL/CRoFT.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language model can weaken the broad knowledge that helps it handle unfamiliar inputs. CRoFT addresses two kinds of unfamiliarity together: changes in how known classes look, such as a different image style, and the appearance of entirely unseen classes. The desired behavior is to recognize familiar categories despite visual changes while detecting inputs from new categories.

The paper introduces an out-of-distribution detection objective that also supports generalization. Its central result connects reducing the gradient magnitude of energy scores on training data with making the curvature of the classification loss consistent across domains. The theoretical analysis identifies this consistency, expressed through Hessians, as a strong indicator of generalization under distribution shift.

This connection motivates a unified fine-tuning framework that optimizes detection and generalization concurrently. The authors report superior experimental performance for their method. The significance is that the two goals share a training mechanism: an objective designed to help identify unfamiliar classes can also encourage properties associated with recognizing known classes under changed conditions. The theoretical connection supports that design without making generalization an unconditional guarantee.
summary.tldr: CRoFT jointly improves robustness to changed visual conditions and detection of unseen classes through a shared fine-tuning objective.

title: CRoFT: Robust Fine-Tuning with Concurrent Optimization for OOD Generalization and Open-Set OOD Detection

abstract: While there has been plenty of work on generating tests from existing code, there has been limited work on generating tests from issues. A correct test must validate the code patch that resolves the issue. This paper focuses on the scenario where that code patch does not yet exist. Doing so supports two major use-cases. First, it supports TDD (test-driven development), the discipline of "test first, write code later" that has well-documented benefits for human software engineers. Second, it also validates SWE (software engineering) agents, which generate code patches for resolving issues. This paper introduces TDD-Bench-Verified, a benchmark for generating tests from issues, and Otter, an LLM-based solution for this task. Otter augments LLMs with rule-based analysis to check and repair their outputs, and introduces a novel self-reflective action planner. Experiments show Otter outperforming state-of-the-art systems for generating tests from issues, in addition to enhancing systems that generate patches from issues. We hope that Otter helps make developers more productive at resolving issues and leads to more robust, well-tested code.

paragraphs: Otter tackles writing tests from a software issue before a patch exists. The goal is to create a test that can validate a future fix, using the issue as the starting point. These findings make issue-based testing useful both as a standalone development aid and as part of an automated repair workflow. summary.tldr: Otter generates tests from software issues before patches exist, improving evaluated test-generation and patch-generation systems.

title: Otter: Generating Tests from Issues to Validate SWE Patches

abstract: The generalization error (risk) of a supervised statistical learning algorithm quantifies its prediction ability on previously unseen data. Inspired by exponential tilting, Li et al. (2021) proposed the tilted empirical risk (TER) as a non-linear risk metric for machine learning applications such as classification and regression problems. In this work, we examine the generalization error of the tilted empirical risk in the robustness regime under negative tilt. Our first contribution is to provide uniform and information-theoretic bounds on the tilted generalization error, defined as the difference between the population risk and the tilted empirical risk, under negative tilt for unbounded loss function under bounded $(1+\epsilon)$-th moment of loss function for some $\epsilon\in(0,1]$ with a convergence rate of $O(n^{-\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)})$ where $n$ is the number of training samples, revealing a novel application for TER under no distribution shift. Secondly, we study the robustness of the tilted empirical risk with respect to noisy outliers at training time and provide theoretical guarantees under distribution shift for the tilted empirical risk. We empirically corroborate our findings in simple experimental setups where we evaluate our bounds to select the value of tilt in a data-driven manner.

paragraphs: Training losses summarize performance on observed examples, but their relationship to performance on unseen data needs justification. This paper studies tilted empirical risk, a nonlinear loss summary based on exponential tilting. It focuses on negative tilt, the regime associated with robustness, and analyzes the difference between population risk and the tilted training risk.

The authors provide uniform and information-theoretic bounds even when individual losses are unbounded. Their assumption is that the loss has a bounded moment of order 1+ε, with ε between zero and one. Under these conditions, the stated convergence rate is O(n^(−ε/(1+ε))), where n counts training samples. This establishes an application of negative-tilt risk even without distribution shift.

The paper separately studies noisy training outliers and gives robustness guarantees under distribution shift. Simple experiments support the analysis and use the bounds to choose the tilt from data. The work therefore connects a robustness-oriented training criterion to both generalization guarantees and a principled way to set its controlling parameter.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional generalization and robustness guarantees for negative-tilt empirical risk and uses the bounds to guide tilt selection.

title: Generalization and Robustness of the Tilted Empirical Risk

abstract: Interventions in language models (LMs) are applied strategically to steer model behavior during the forward pass. Learnable interventions, also known as representation fine-tuning, aim to apply pointwise control within the concept subspace and have proven effective in altering high-level behaviors. In this work, we extend this approach to the distribution level, enabling the model to learn not only pointwise transformations but also the surrounding regions of the concept subspace. We demonstrate that these methods perform effectively in early layers, with larger standard deviations correlating strongly with improved performance. Across eight commonsense reasoning and seven arithmetic reasoning benchmarks, our distribution-wise interventions consistently outperform pointwise interventions in controllability and robustness. These results illustrate that distribution-wise interventions provide a more comprehensive method for steering model behavior and enabling finer-grained control over language models. The code is at: https://github.com/chili-lab/D-Intervention.

paragraphs: Representation fine-tuning steers a language model by learning interventions in its internal representations during a forward pass. Existing pointwise approaches apply transformations within a concept subspace. This paper extends that idea to distributions, so the learned intervention accounts for surrounding regions of the subspace as well as individual points.

The change broadens what the intervention learns about the representation space. Instead of limiting control to pointwise transformations, it incorporates variation around them. The authors find that these distribution-wise methods work effectively in early model layers. They also observe a strong correlation between larger standard deviations and improved performance; this is reported as an association, rather than a universal causal rule.

Evaluation covers eight commonsense-reasoning and seven arithmetic-reasoning benchmarks. Across these tests, distribution-wise interventions consistently outperform pointwise interventions in controllability and robustness. The findings support using distributions as a richer basis for steering model behavior, with evidence that useful control can occur early in the model and remain effective across the evaluated reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: Distribution-wise representation interventions improve language-model controllability and robustness over pointwise interventions across fifteen reasoning benchmarks.

title: Learning Distribution-wise Control in Representation Space for Language Models

abstract: Current generative models for drug discovery primarily use molecular docking as an oracle to guide the generation of active compounds. However, such models are often not useful in practice because even compounds with high docking scores do not consistently show real-world experimental activity. More accurate methods for activity prediction exist, such as molecular dynamics based binding free energy calculations, but they are too computationally expensive to use in a generative model. To address this challenge, we propose Multi-Fidelity Latent space Active Learning (MF-LAL), a generative modeling framework that integrates a set of oracles with varying cost-accuracy tradeoffs. Using active learning, we train a surrogate model for each oracle and use these surrogates to guide generation of compounds with high predicted activity. Unlike previous approaches that separately learn the surrogate model and generative model, MF-LAL combines the generative and multi-fidelity surrogate models into a single framework, allowing for more accurate activity prediction and higher quality samples. Our experiments on two disease-relevant proteins show that MF-LAL produces compounds with significantly better binding free energy scores than other single and multi-fidelity approaches ( 50% improvement in mean binding free energy score). The code is available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/MF-LAL.

paragraphs: Drug-generation models often use docking scores to steer the search for compounds, yet high docking scores do not consistently translate into experimental activity. More accurate computational assessments, including binding free energy calculations based on molecular dynamics, are expensive. MF-LAL addresses the tension between inexpensive guidance and more informative but costly evaluations.

Its broader contribution is a way to incorporate expensive sources of guidance into generation through jointly learned approximations.
summary.tldr: MF-LAL jointly learns a compound generator and surrogates for multiple evaluation methods, reporting improved binding free energy scores on two protein targets.

title: MF-LAL: Drug Compound Generation Using Multi-Fidelity Latent Space Active Learning

abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) focuses on determining conflict-free paths for multiple agents navigating through a shared space to reach specified goal locations. This problem becomes computationally challenging, particularly when handling large numbers of agents, as frequently encountered in practical applications like coordinating autonomous vehicles. Quantum Computing (QC) is a promising candidate in overcoming such limits. However, current quantum hardware is still in its infancy and thus limited in terms of computing power and error robustness. In this work, we present the first optimal hybrid quantum-classical MAPF algorithms which are based on branch-and-cut-and-prize. QC is integrated by iteratively solving QUBO problems, based on conflict graphs. Experiments on actual quantum hardware and results on benchmark data suggest that our approach dominates previous QUBO formulations and state-of-the-art MAPF solvers.

paragraphs: Multi-agent pathfinding asks how several agents can reach their destinations through a shared space without conflicting with one another. The computational burden grows as more agents must be coordinated. This paper explores a hybrid design that combines classical optimization with quantum computing, while recognizing the limited computing power and error robustness of current quantum hardware.

The authors present optimal hybrid algorithms based on a branch-and-cut-and-prize framework. Quantum computation enters through repeated solution of quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problems, or QUBOs. These subproblems are constructed from conflict graphs, connecting the quantum component to the conflicts that the overall pathfinding algorithm must resolve.

The evaluation includes both actual quantum hardware experiments and benchmark data. The reported results suggest that the approach outperforms earlier QUBO formulations and state-of-the-art pathfinding solvers. The evidence therefore supports this particular integration of quantum subproblems with classical optimization. The algorithmic contribution is an optimal hybrid framework, while the performance advantage is an empirical finding suggested by the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Optimal hybrid quantum-classical pathfinding algorithms solve conflict-graph QUBOs, with experiments suggesting advantages over prior formulations and solvers.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Multi-Agent Pathfinding

abstract: Fairness in human and algorithmic decision-making is crucial in areas such as criminal justice, education, and social welfare. Recently, counterfactual fairness has drawn increasing research interest, suggesting that decision-making for individuals should remain the same when intervening with different values on protected attributes. Nevertheless, the question of "which attributes and individuals should be protected" is rarely discussed in the existing counterfactual fairness literature. For example, when considering leg disability as a protected attribute, the algorithms should not treat individuals with leg disabilities differently in college admissions, but one may naturally consider this factor when selecting runner athletes. In other words, when and how to enforce fairness is expected to depend on the causal relation between the protected attribute and the outcome of interest. Formally, this paper proposes principal counterfactual fairness using the concept of principal stratification from the causal inference literature, focusing on whether an algorithm is counterfactually fair for individuals whose protected attribute has no individual causal effect on the outcome of interest. To examine whether an algorithm satisfies principal counterfactual fairness, we derive the statistical bounds and propose a post-processing approach to achieving principal counterfactual fairness with minimal individual decision changes. Experiments are conducted using synthetic and real-world datasets to verify the effectiveness of our methods.

paragraphs: Counterfactual fairness asks whether a decision would stay the same if an individual's protected attribute were changed. This paper examines a question that such a rule can leave unresolved: which individuals and attributes should receive that protection for a particular outcome? The contribution combines a more targeted fairness definition with tools for evaluating and adjusting an algorithm's decisions.
summary.tldr: Principal counterfactual fairness targets individuals whose protected attribute has no individual causal effect on the outcome of interest.

title: Fairness on Principal Stratum: A New Perspective on Counterfactual Fairness

abstract: We revisit the Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) framework for Online Convex Optimization (OCO) over compact sets, focusing on achieving dynamic regret guarantees. Prior work has highlighted the framework’s limitations in dynamic environments due to its tendency to produce "lazy" iterates. However, building on insights showing FTRL’s ability to produce "agile" iterates, we show that it can indeed recover known dynamic regret bounds through optimistic composition of future costs and careful linearization of past costs, which can lead to pruning some of them. This new analysis of FTRL against dynamic comparators yields a principled way to interpolate between greedy and agile updates and offers several benefits, including refined control over regret terms, optimism without cyclic dependence, and the application of minimal recursive regularization akin to AdaFTRL. More broadly, we show that it is not the "lazy" projection style of FTRL that hinders (optimistic) dynamic regret, but the decoupling of the algorithm’s state (linearized history) from its iterates, allowing the state to grow arbitrarily. Instead, pruning synchronizes these two when necessary.

paragraphs: Online optimization requires making decisions as costs arrive, and dynamic regret evaluates those decisions against a comparator that can change over time. This paper revisits Follow the Regularized Leader, or FTRL, for online convex optimization over compact sets. Earlier concerns attributed poor adaptation to its supposedly lazy updates.

The authors show that FTRL can recover known dynamic regret bounds by combining optimistic treatment of future costs with careful linearization of past costs. This treatment can prune parts of the stored history. Their analysis provides a principled way to move between greedy and agile updates, alongside finer control of regret terms and optimism without cyclic dependence.

The central diagnosis concerns the relationship between stored history and current decisions. If the accumulated linearized history becomes disconnected from the iterates, the internal state can grow arbitrarily. Pruning restores synchronization when needed. The paper thus locates the obstacle in state management rather than the projection style itself, and also supports minimal recursive regularization similar to AdaFTRL.
summary.tldr: Optimistic cost handling and selective history pruning let FTRL recover dynamic regret guarantees by keeping its state aligned with its iterates.

title: On the Dynamic Regret of Following the Regularized Leader: Optimism with History Pruning

abstract: Recent direct preference alignment algorithms (DPA), such as DPO, have shown great promise in aligning large language models to human preferences. While this has motivated the development of many new variants of the original DPO loss, understanding the differences between these recent proposals, as well as developing new DPA loss functions, remains difficult given the lack of a technical and conceptual framework for reasoning about the underlying semantics of these algorithms. In this paper, we attempt to remedy this by formalizing DPA losses in terms of discrete reasoning problems. Specifically, we ask: Given an existing DPA loss, can we systematically derive a symbolic program that characterizes its semantics? We propose a novel formalism for characterizing preference losses for single model and reference model based approaches, and identify symbolic forms for a number of commonly used DPA variants. Further, we show how this formal view of preference learning sheds new light on both the size and structure of the DPA loss landscape, making it possible to not only rigorously characterize the relationships between recent loss proposals but also to systematically explore the landscape and derive new loss functions from first principles. We hope our framework and findings will help provide useful guidance to those working on human AI alignment.

paragraphs: Direct preference alignment methods train language models from preferences, but the growing number of loss functions makes their relationships difficult to understand. This paper develops a conceptual and technical framework for interpreting those losses. Its central question is whether an existing preference objective can be translated into a symbolic program that characterizes its semantics.

The authors formalize preference losses as discrete reasoning problems. Their framework covers approaches involving a single model as well as those using a reference model, and they identify symbolic forms for several common variants. This provides a shared language for describing objectives that otherwise appear as separate mathematical proposals.

The formal view reveals structure in the space of possible preference losses and supports rigorous comparisons among existing methods. It also allows new losses to be derived systematically from first principles. The contribution is therefore a way to reason about and design preference objectives, with the stated aim of guiding alignment research rather than a reported claim that one new objective universally performs best.
summary.tldr: A symbolic logic framework characterizes direct preference losses, clarifies their relationships, and enables systematic derivation of new objectives.

title: Understanding the Logic of Direct Preference Alignment through Logic

abstract: We introduce a highly multimodal transformer to represent many remote sensing modalities - multispectral optical, synthetic aperture radar, elevation, weather, pseudo-labels, and more - across space and time. These inputs are useful for diverse remote sensing tasks, such as crop mapping and flood detection. However, learning shared representations of remote sensing data is challenging, given the diversity of relevant data modalities, and because objects of interest vary massively in scale, from small boats (1-2 pixels and fast) to glaciers (thousands of pixels and slow). We present a novel self-supervised learning algorithm that extracts multi-scale features across a flexible set of input modalities through masked modeling. Our dual global and local contrastive losses differ in their targets (deep representations vs. shallow input projections) and masking strategies (structured vs. not). Our Galileo is a single generalist model that outperforms SoTA specialist models for satellite images and pixel time series across eleven benchmarks and multiple tasks.

paragraphs: Remote sensing combines different kinds of measurements, including optical imagery, radar, elevation, and weather, across space and time. Useful targets also vary greatly in size and speed of change. Galileo addresses the challenge of learning one representation system that can accommodate both this variety of inputs and the different scales relevant to downstream tasks.

The authors introduce a multimodal transformer trained with a self-supervised masked-modeling method. Its training combines global and local contrastive losses. These use different targets—deeper representations and shallower input projections—and different masking strategies, with structured masking distinguished from unstructured masking. The paired objectives are designed to extract features at multiple scales from a flexible selection of modalities.

Galileo is evaluated as a single generalist model across eleven benchmarks and multiple tasks. The authors report that it outperforms state-of-the-art specialist models for satellite images and pixel time series. The stated finding supports combining broad context and local detail within shared remote sensing representations, rather than requiring a separate specialist for each evaluated input setting.
summary.tldr: Galileo learns global and local features across remote sensing modalities, outperforming specialist models across eleven benchmarks.

title: Galileo: Learning Global & Local Features of Many Remote Sensing Modalities

abstract: Self-attention has emerged as a core component of modern neural architectures, yet its theoretical underpinnings remain elusive. In this paper, we study self-attention through the lens of interacting entities, ranging from agents in multi-agent reinforcement learning to alleles in genetic sequences, and show that a single layer linear self-attention can efficiently represent, learn, and generalize functions capturing pairwise interactions, including out-of-distribution scenarios. Our analysis reveals that self-attention acts as a mutual interaction learner under minimal assumptions on the diversity of interaction patterns observed during training, thereby encompassing a wide variety of real-world domains. In addition, we validate our theoretical insights through experiments demonstrating that self-attention learns interaction functions and generalizes across both population distributions and out-of-distribution scenarios. Building on our theories, we introduce HyperFeatureAttention, a novel neural network module designed to learn couplings of different feature-level interactions between entities. Furthermore, we propose HyperAttention, a new module that extends beyond pairwise interactions to capture multi-entity dependencies, such as three-way, four-way, or general $n$-way interactions.

Their analysis requires assumptions about the diversity of interaction patterns in the training data, described as minimal. Experiments support the theoretical account, including generalization across population distributions and to out-of-distribution settings.

The paper also introduces two extensions motivated by this view. HyperFeatureAttention learns couplings between different interactions at the feature level. HyperAttention addresses dependencies involving three, four, or more entities together. These contributions connect attention’s representational abilities to the kinds of relationships a task requires, while the main theoretical findings specifically establish capabilities for pairwise interaction functions under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how linear self-attention can learn pairwise interactions and introduces modules for richer feature and multi-entity dependencies.

title: A Theoretical Study of (Hyper) Self-Attention through the Lens of Interactions: Representation, Training, Generalization

abstract: Existing methods for code generation use code snippets as seed data, restricting the complexity and diversity of the synthesized data. In this paper, we introduce a novel feature tree-based synthesis framework, which revolves around hierarchical code features derived from high-level abstractions of code. The feature tree is constructed from raw data and refined iteratively to increase the quantity and diversity of the extracted features, which captures and recognizes more complex patterns and relationships within the code. By adjusting the depth and breadth of the sampled subtrees, our framework provides precise control over the complexity of the generated code, enabling functionalities that range from function-level operations to multi-file scenarios. We fine-tuned widely-used base models to obtain EpiCoder series, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks at both the function and file levels. In particular, empirical evidence indicates that our approach shows significant potential in the synthesizing of repository-level code data. Our code and data are publicly available.

paragraphs: Synthetic code training data often starts from existing snippets, which can constrain the variety and complexity of the examples produced. EpiCoder introduces a synthesis framework organized around hierarchical code features instead. The goal is to generate examples from a richer description of programming patterns and relationships, giving more direct control over the resulting training material.

The framework constructs a feature tree from raw data and repeatedly refines it to expand the number and diversity of features represented. Sampling subtrees with different depths and breadths controls code complexity. This supports examples ranging from individual function operations to scenarios involving multiple files, connecting the organization of the feature tree to the scope of the generated code.

Their experiments also indicate potential for generating repository-level code data. That repository-scale finding is presented as promising evidence, while the stated benchmark achievements concern function-level and file-level performance.
summary.tldr: EpiCoder synthesizes code from hierarchical feature trees, controlling example complexity and improving function-level and file-level code-generation results.

title: EpiCoder: Encompassing Diversity and Complexity in Code Generation

abstract: There is strong agreement that generative AI should be regulated, but strong disagreement on how to approach regulation. While some argue that AI regulation should mostly rely on extensions of existing laws, others argue that entirely new laws and regulations are needed to ensure that generative AI benefits society. In this position paper, we argue that the debates on generative AI regulation can be informed by evidence on social media regulation. For example, AI companies have faced allegations of political bias which resemble the allegations social media companies have faced. First, we compare and contrast the affordances of generative AI and social media to highlight their similarities and differences. Then, we discuss four specific policy recommendations based on the evolution of social media and their regulation: (1) counter bias and perceptions thereof (e.g., via transparency, oversight boards, researcher access, democratic input), (2) address specific regulatory concerns (e.g., youth wellbeing, election integrity) and invest in trust and safety, (3) promote computational social science research, and (4) take on a more global perspective. Applying lessons learnt from social media regulation to generative AI regulation can save effort and time, and prevent avoidable mistakes.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that debates over generative-AI regulation can benefit from experience with social media. The authors begin by comparing what the two technologies enable and where they differ. Allegations of political bias provide one example of a recurring issue, suggesting that some regulatory questions already have relevant evidence and institutional experience.

The paper develops four recommendations from that comparison. It calls for addressing bias and perceptions of bias through measures such as transparency, oversight, researcher access, and democratic participation. It also recommends focusing on concrete concerns, including youth wellbeing and election integrity, while investing in trust and safety. The remaining recommendations emphasize computational social science research and a more global perspective.

The proposed value of this approach is to save effort and avoid preventable mistakes by learning from earlier regulatory developments. Because the argument explicitly considers differences as well as similarities, it supports informed adaptation of lessons rather than assuming the technologies are identical. The contribution is a policy agenda grounded in that comparison.
summary.tldr: The paper draws four generative-AI policy recommendations from social media regulation, emphasizing bias, concrete harms, research, and global perspectives.

title: Position: Generative AI Regulation Can Learn from Social Media Regulation

abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are effective solutions for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models; however, their memory requirements scales with the size of the model, $\mathcal{O}(dr)$, where $d$ is the model’s hidden dimension and $r$ is the rank. Our proposal, FrameFT, models the parameter update $\Delta W$ with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers, enabling highly efficient updates. Only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored/optimized, strongly reducing the memory footprint and parameter count. The sparse structure of the coefficient matrix in FrameFT and the sparsity in the Fusion Frames, give sizable compute benefits. Our technical analysis shows that FrameFT allows obtaining formal convergence results. We evaluate our method across a suite of supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, primarily focusing on language tasks, but also report applicability to vision models. Our empirical evaluations show that FrameFT achieves performance on par with or exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, but needs far fewer trainable parameters and less memory.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models by training a smaller set of parameters. Even methods such as LoRA have adaptation memory requirements that grow with hidden dimension and rank. FrameFT addresses this remaining cost by representing weight updates through sparse coefficients in a mathematical construction called a Fusion Frame basis.

The basis can be generated algorithmically and shared across layers, while only its sparse coefficients are stored and optimized. This separates the structure used to express an update from the small set of values learned for a task. Sparsity in both the coefficients and the frames also provides computational benefits beyond reducing the trainable parameter count.

The paper supplies formal convergence results and evaluates supervised fine-tuning, primarily on language tasks, with applicability also reported for vision models. FrameFT matches or exceeds leading parameter-efficient methods while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and less memory. Its central contribution is a different representation of adaptation, designed to make the update itself cheaper to learn and retain.
summary.tldr: FrameFT expresses weight updates with sparse coefficients in shared, algorithmically generated bases to reduce fine-tuning memory and computation.

title: Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames

abstract: Pruning is a common approach to reduce the memory footprint and inference cost of large vision and language models. As these architectures continue to scale, one-shot pruning methods - i.e. approaches that prune the network without any retraining - have become increasingly attractive. Many popular one-shot pruning methods (e.g., WoodFisher, CAP, SparseGPT, and ALPS) typically optimize a quadratic objective under sparsity constraints. However, in practice, this objective is affected by multiple sources of uncertainty, including noise in the calibration data and variability introduced by algorithmic updates. To address these issues, we introduce RobOP, a robust optimization framework that explicitly accounts for such uncertainties. RobOP is modular and flexible, and can be applied with any existing pruning method through simple modifications motivated by our theoretical framework. We demonstrate that by taking into account uncertainty, RobOP offers improvements over prior pruning approaches. Our framework applies tractably across a range of stylized uncertainty sets, enabling robust one-shot pruning at scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/mazumder-lab/RobOP.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a model’s memory requirements and inference cost by removing parts of the network. One-shot pruning is especially attractive for large models because it avoids retraining. This paper examines a weakness in the quadratic optimization objectives used by many such methods: the quantities being optimized are affected by uncertainty.

The authors introduce RobOP, a robust optimization framework that explicitly accounts for uncertainty from sources such as noisy calibration data and variability in algorithmic updates. Its modular design allows existing pruning methods to incorporate the framework through modifications guided by the authors’ theory. This makes uncertainty handling an addition to established pruning approaches.

The reported results show improvements over prior pruning approaches when uncertainty is taken into account. The framework remains computationally tractable for a range of stylized uncertainty sets, supporting one-shot pruning at scale. The contribution is a way to make pruning decisions account for variation in their optimization inputs while retaining the practical appeal of pruning without retraining.
summary.tldr: RobOP improves one-shot model pruning by incorporating uncertainty in calibration data and algorithmic updates into the optimization.

title: A Robust Optimization Guided Pruning Framework for Vision and Large Language Models

abstract: The two-sample testing problem, a fundamental task in statistics and machine learning, seeks to determine whether two sets of samples, drawn from underlying distributions $p$ and $q$, are in fact identically distributed (i.e. whether $p=q$). A popular and intuitive approach is the classifier two-sample test (C2ST), where a classifier is trained to distinguish between samples from $p$ and $q$. Yet despite simplicity of the C2ST, its reliability hinges on access to a near-Bayes-optimal classifier, a requirement that is rarely met and difficult to verify. This raises a major open question: can a weak classifier still be useful for two-sample testing? We show that the answer is a definitive yes. Building on the work of Hu & Lei (2024), we analyze two conformal variants of the C2ST that convert the scores from any trained classifier—even if weak, biased, or overfit—into exact, finite-sample p-values. We establish two key theoretical properties of the conformal C2ST: (i) finite-sample Type-I error control, and (ii) non-trivial power that degrades gently in tandem with the error of the trained classifier. The upshot is that even poorly performing classifiers can yield powerful and reliable two-sample tests. This general framework finds a powerful application in Bayesian inference, particularly for validating Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) models, where the task of comparing a learned posterior approximation $q(\theta \mid y)$ to the true posterior $p(\theta \mid y)$ can be framed as a two-sample test. Empirically, the Conformal C2ST outperforms classical discriminative tests across a wide range of benchmarks for this task. Our results establish the conformal C2ST as a practical, theoretically grounded diagnostic tool.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. One intuitive approach trains a classifier to tell the collections apart. However, the reliability of conventional classifier-based tests hinges on a classifier being close to optimal, a demanding property that is difficult to verify.

This paper analyzes two conformal versions of that approach. They turn scores from any trained classifier, including weak, biased, or overfit classifiers, into exact finite-sample p-values. The authors establish control of false positives and nontrivial power, meaning an ability to detect genuine distributional differences. Power degrades gently as classifier error increases, separating reliable error control from the need for exceptionally accurate classification.

The framework is applied to checking neural posterior estimation models, which approximate Bayesian posterior distributions. Comparing an approximation with the true posterior becomes a two-sample testing problem. Across the reported benchmarks for this application, the conformal tests outperform classical discriminative tests. The findings make imperfect classifiers useful as statistical diagnostic tools while preserving an explicit account of their detection strength.
summary.tldr: Conformal calibration turns even weak classifier scores into valid two-sample tests whose detection power degrades gently with classifier error.

title: Conformal C2ST: Turning weak classifiers into strong two-sample tests

abstract: Recent class-incremental learning (CIL) methods built on large pre-trained vision models have shown that strong performance can be retained even under strict data access constraints. This raises a fundamental question: which properties of pre-trained representations make such recovery possible in the class-incremental setting? In this work, we show that class-level feature statistics play a central role in enabling effective CIL under strong pre-training. When the visual backbone is frozen, maintaining simple class-wise statistical estimators of features can recover a substantial fraction of the performance achieved by static joint training across diverse benchmarks. We make this observation explicit through deliberately minimal reference points built on frozen CLIP representations. In particular, we demonstrate that competitive performance can be achieved without continual parameter updates, by performing class-incremental inference based solely on class-level statistical estimators instantiated from frozen features. Our findings suggest that class-level statistics constitute an important and previously underemphasized component of recent PTM-based CIL approaches, offering a complementary perspective for understanding their strong empirical performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/HdTgon/baseCIL.
