paragraphs: Class-incremental learning adds new categories over time under restrictions on access to data. Strong pretrained vision models have made this setting increasingly effective, raising a question about what drives that performance. This paper examines how much can be explained by simple class-level statistics of an already learned representation.

The authors construct deliberately minimal reference methods using frozen CLIP features. Rather than continually updating the visual backbone, they maintain statistical estimators for each class and use those estimators for incremental inference. Across diverse benchmarks, this recovers a substantial fraction of the performance of static joint training, where classes are learned together.

The results show that competitive performance can arise without continual parameter updates in the studied setting. They identify class-level feature statistics as an important, previously underemphasized contributor to the success of approaches built on strong pretrained models. This offers a complementary interpretation of recent progress: some adaptation can be carried by accumulated statistical summaries when the frozen representation already supplies useful features.
summary.tldr: Simple class-level statistics of frozen pretrained features recover substantial class-incremental performance without continual parameter updates.

title: On the Power of Statistics in Class-Incremental Learning with Pretrained Models

abstract: Recent work has demonstrated the potential of contrastive steering for jailbreaking Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing methods rely on limited and inherently biased contrastive prompts and require laborious manual tuning of steering strength, limiting their robustness and effectiveness. In this paper, we leverage the idea of model extraction to guide the learned steering vectors to approximate the ideal one and propose tuning the steering strength adaptively based on contrastive activations’ statistics. Experiments demonstrate that our method notably improves the effectiveness and robustness of probe-based steering, without any extra contrastive prompts or laborious manual tuning. Being an attack paper, this paper focuses on revealing the breakdown of fortified LLMs, raising the average harmfulness score from 6% to 70%. Our code is available at https://github.com/fhdnskfbeuv/adaptiveSteering.

paragraphs: This paper investigates an attack that steers a language model’s internal activations to undermine its safeguards. Earlier contrastive steering methods derive steering directions from contrasting prompts, but the authors identify two weaknesses: those prompts provide limited, biased evidence, and choosing how strongly to apply the direction requires substantial manual adjustment.

The proposed approach addresses both the direction and its strength. It draws on model extraction to guide learned steering vectors toward an ideal direction. Separately, it uses statistical properties of contrastive activations to adjust steering strength automatically. The intended benefit is a more effective and robust attack without collecting additional contrastive prompts or repeatedly tuning the intervention by hand.

In the reported experiments, the method improves probe-based steering and raises the average harmfulness score from 6% to 70%. That quantity is a harmfulness score, rather than a stated attack success rate. The findings expose a vulnerability in the evaluated safeguarded models: their protective behavior can break down under adaptive interventions in internal representations.
summary.tldr: Adaptive internal steering strengthens jailbreak attacks by improving steering directions and automatically adjusting their strength.

title: Adaptive Probe-based Steering for Robust LLM Jailbreaking

abstract: Nowcasting forms the first line of defense against rapidly evolving weather hazards, where even minutes of delay can lead to severe societal impacts. However, existing systems predominantly extrapolate 2D radar reflectivity, which struggles under rapid intensification regimes. We introduce StormInsight, a multi-scale modeling framework that enables coherent reconstruction of the three-dimensional evolution of convective systems while explicitly conditioning on the ambient environment. StormInsight integrates multi-source observations—including radar, satellite, and station—with reanalysis fields through two components: (i) Storm Evolution Encoder that explicitly disentangles convective system state form vertical thermodynamic coupling and large-scale environmental forcing; (ii) Convective System Decoder that predicts future echos by adaptively aggregating cross-layer interactions conditioned on evolving environmental conditions. To support comprehensive evaluation, we build a new benchmark StormBench that integrates observational and reanalysis data across regions. On this benchmark, StormInsight consistently achieves the best performance, reducing MAE by 12.4% and improving the mCSI by 34.0%.

paragraphs: StormInsight models the three-dimensional evolution of convective weather systems for nowcasting. Many existing systems extrapolate two-dimensional radar reflectivity, which struggles when storms intensify rapidly. The paper instead explicitly conditions storm evolution on the surrounding environment and interactions across vertical layers.

The framework combines radar, satellite, and station observations with reanalysis fields. Its Storm Evolution Encoder separates the convective system’s state from vertical thermodynamic coupling and large-scale environmental forcing. The Convective System Decoder then predicts future radar echoes by adaptively combining interactions across layers under changing environmental conditions. This organization gives both the storm’s internal structure and its broader environment explicit roles in prediction.

The authors also introduce StormBench, a benchmark combining observational and reanalysis data across regions. On this benchmark, StormInsight consistently achieves the best reported performance, reducing mean absolute error by 12.4% and improving mCSI by 34.0%. The results support incorporating environmental conditioning and vertical coupling into the evaluated forecasting task, especially given the motivating difficulty of rapid intensification.
summary.tldr: StormInsight predicts three-dimensional storm evolution using environmental conditions and vertical interactions, improving results on the new StormBench benchmark.

title: StormInsight: Hierarchical Environmental Forcing and Vertical Coupling for Convective Systems Evolution

abstract: We characterize the pre-softmax attention matrix $\mathbf{QK^\top}$ in transformers as an associative memory matrix encoding pairwise associations between input features. By decomposing this matrix into its symmetric and skew-symmetric parts, we interpret the symmetric component as governing the structure of the energy landscape, and the skew-symmetric component as driving circulation on that landscape. Leveraging the energy formulation induced by the symmetric component, we derive Hopfield-style stability measures that quantify the stability of retrieved features. We observe meaningful correlations between Hopfield-style stability measures and the fidelity–diversity trade-offs in generation. Finally, we propose a controllable knob to modulate this trade-off by modifying the circulation of the underlying dynamics. Code is available at our Project Page (https://hyeon-cho.github.io/Balancing/).

paragraphs: This paper studies the balance between fidelity and diversity in diffusion generation through the internal structure of transformer attention. It treats the attention matrix before softmax as an associative memory: a representation of pairwise relationships between input features. This connects attention to questions about which features are retrieved and how stable that retrieval is.

The authors separate this matrix into symmetric and skew-symmetric components. In their interpretation, the symmetric part defines an energy landscape, while the skew-symmetric part drives circulation across that landscape. The symmetric component also supplies an energy formulation from which they derive Hopfield-style measures of feature stability.

The authors observe meaningful correlations between these stability measures and the fidelity–diversity trade-off. They then propose adjusting circulation as a control for that trade-off. The contribution combines an interpretation of attention with a way to influence generation. The reported correlations support the connection between stability and generation behavior, without establishing that stability alone determines either fidelity or diversity.
summary.tldr: Decomposing attention into energy and circulation components yields stability measures and a control for diffusion models’ fidelity–diversity trade-off.

title: Balancing Fidelity and Diversity in Diffusion Models via Symmetric Attention Decomposition: Hopfield Perspective

abstract: Tokenization is a hardcoded compression step which remains in the training pipeline of Large Language Models (LLMs), despite a general trend towards architectures becoming increasingly end-to-end. Prior work has shown promising results at scale in bringing this compression step inside the LLMs’ architecture with heuristics to draw token boundaries, and also attempts to learn these token boundaries with straight-through estimates, which treat the problem of drawing discrete token boundaries as a continuous one. We show that these token boundaries can instead be learned using score function estimates, which have tighter theoretical guarantees due to directly optimizing the problem of drawing discrete token boundaries to minimize loss. We observe that techniques from reinforcement learning, such as time discounting, are necessary to reduce the variance of this score function sufficiently to make it practicable. We demonstrate that the resultant method outperforms prior proposed straight-through estimates, both qualitatively and quantitatively at the $100$ million parameter scale.
originalAbstract: Tokenization is a hardcoded compression step which remains in the training pipeline of Large Language Models (LLMs), despite a general trend towards architectures becoming increasingly end-to-end. Prior work has shown promising results at scale in bringing this compression step inside the LLMs’ architecture with heuristics to draw token boundaries, and also attempts to learn these token boundaries with straight-through estimates, which treat the problem of drawing discrete token boundaries as a continuous one. We show that these token boundaries can instead be learned using score function estimates, which have tighter theoretical guarantees due to directly optimizing the problem of drawing discrete token boundaries to minimize loss. We observe that techniques from reinforcement learning, such as time discounting, are necessary to reduce the variance of this score function sufficiently to make it practicable. We demonstrate that the resultant method outperforms prior proposed straight-through estimates, both qualitatively and quantitatively at the $100$ million parameter scale.

paragraphs: Tokenization compresses input into the units a language model processes, yet its boundaries often remain hardcoded outside end-to-end learning. Earlier approaches have brought boundary selection into the model using heuristics or straight-through estimates that treat discrete choices as continuous during optimization. This paper investigates learning those boundaries directly as discrete decisions.

The authors use score-function estimates to optimize boundary selection for lower loss. They report tighter theoretical guarantees than straight-through estimates because the objective directly addresses the discrete boundary problem. Making this practical requires controlling estimator variance. Techniques from reinforcement learning, including time discounting, are found necessary to reduce that variance sufficiently in the proposed method.

At the 100-million-parameter scale, the resulting approach outperforms previously proposed straight-through estimates in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. The finding establishes a practical route to learned token boundaries at the tested scale, connecting a theoretically better-matched optimization method with the variance reduction needed to use it. The contribution concerns making tokenization itself trainable as part of the model’s learning process.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement-learning variance reduction makes direct optimization of discrete token boundaries practical, outperforming straight-through estimates at the 100-million-parameter scale.

title: You Can Learn Tokenization End-to-End with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Building on recent formalizations of root cause analysis for rare events (“outliers”) in structural equation models, we propose a formal definition of a causal pathway and discuss its testable implications. We identify conditions under which these implications depend only on a causal abstraction defined by the pathway of rare events, rather than on the full causal graph of the underlying system. Accordingly, we introduce an abstraction of causal structure to pathways of rare events that bridges simple verbal causal explanations and detailed causal modeling.

paragraphs: Explaining a rare event often involves describing a causal pathway: a sequence of relevant events that connects an initiating cause to an unusual outcome. This paper gives that idea a formal definition, building on work that analyzes the root causes of outliers using structural equation models. It also examines what observable implications such a pathway should have.

The central question is how much causal detail is needed to assess an explanation. The authors identify conditions under which the pathway's testable implications depend only on an abstraction built from the rare events along that pathway. Under those conditions, evaluating the implications does not require the full causal graph of the underlying system.

This provides a bridge between a short verbal account of what caused an event and a detailed mathematical model of the entire system. The pathway retains enough causal structure to have testable consequences while omitting other system details when the stated conditions permit. Its value lies in making compact rare-event explanations precise enough to be examined and potentially falsified.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes rare-event causal pathways and identifies conditions under which their testable implications require only a pathway-level abstraction.

title: Formalizing and Falsifying Causal Pathways of Rare Events

abstract: Biological learning proceeds from easy to difficult tasks, gradually reinforcing perception and robustness. Inspired by this principle, we address Context-Entangled Content Segmentation (CECS)—a challenging setting where objects share intrinsic visual patterns with their surroundings, as in camouflaged object detection. Conventional segmentation networks predominantly rely on architectural enhancements but often ignore the learning dynamics that govern robustness under entangled data distributions. We introduce CurriSeg, a dual-phase learning framework that unifies curriculum and anti-curriculum principles to improve representation reliability. In the Curriculum Selection phase, CurriSeg dynamically selects training data based on the temporal statistics of sample losses, distinguishing hard-but-informative samples from noisy or ambiguous ones, thus enabling stable capability enhancement. In the Anti-Curriculum Promotion phase, we design Spectral-Blindness Fine-Tuning, which suppresses high-frequency components to enforce dependence on low-frequency structural and contextual cues. Combined with Sharpness-Aware Minimization, this promotes convergence to flatter minima and strengthens generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CurriSeg achieves consistent improvements across diverse CECS benchmarks without adding parameters or increasing total training time, offering a principled view of how progression and challenge interplay to foster robust and context-aware segmentation. Code will be released.

paragraphs: Segmenting an object becomes difficult when it shares visual patterns with its surroundings, as happens with camouflage. CurriSeg addresses this setting by changing how the model learns. The paper emphasizes training dynamics as a source of robustness, complementing a research focus that has often centered on architectural changes.

The first phase selects training examples using statistics of their losses over time. This helps distinguish difficult but informative examples from noisy or ambiguous ones. The second phase deliberately suppresses high-frequency image components, encouraging the model to rely on broader structural and contextual information. This challenging fine-tuning stage follows the earlier phase of controlled capability development.

CurriSeg combines that second phase with Sharpness-Aware Minimization to encourage flatter optimization minima and better generalization. Experiments show consistent improvements across diverse context-entangled segmentation benchmarks without adding parameters or increasing total training time. The results support coordinating example selection and later perceptual challenges to improve robustness when local appearance offers weak evidence about object boundaries.
summary.tldr: CurriSeg improves difficult object segmentation through adaptive example selection followed by training that emphasizes broader structure and context.

title: Refining Context-Entangled Content Segmentation via Curriculum Selection and Anti-Curriculum Promotion

abstract: Network data are ubiquitous across the social sciences, biology, and information systems. Generating realistic synthetic network data has broad applications from network simulation to scientific discovery. However, many existing black-box approaches for network generation tend to overfit observed data while overlooking characteristic network structure, and incur substantial computational overhead at scale. These practical challenges call for synthetic network generation methods that are both efficient and capable of capturing structural properties of networks. In this paper, we introduce Synthetic Network Generation via Latent Embedding Reconstruction (SyNGLER), a general and efficient framework for synthetic network generation that builds on latent space network models. Given an observed network, SyNGLER first learns low-dimensional latent node embeddings via a latent space network model and then reconstructs the latent space by building a distribution-free generator over these embeddings. For generation, SyNGLER first samples (or resamples) node embeddings from the generator in the latent space and then produces synthetic networks using the latent space network model. Through the latent space framework, SyNGLER preserves unique characteristics in networks such as sparsity and node degree heterogeneity, while allowing for efficient training with lower computational cost than many existing deep architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees by developing consistency results on the distance between the true and synthetic edge distributions. Empirical studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of SyNGLER, which efficiently produces networks that better preserve key network characteristics such as network moments and degree distributions compared with existing approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/FeifanJiang/syngler.

paragraphs: SyNGLER generates synthetic networks while aiming to preserve structural properties of an observed network. The motivation is that some black-box generators overfit the available data, miss characteristic network structure, and become computationally expensive at scale. The proposed framework organizes generation around a low-dimensional representation of the network’s nodes.

To produce a new network, it samples or resamples node embeddings and uses the latent space model to generate connections. This separates learning a useful representation from producing new configurations of nodes and edges.

The framework preserves properties such as sparsity and variation in node degrees while requiring less training computation than many existing deep architectures. The paper develops consistency results concerning the distance between true and synthetic edge distributions. Empirical studies also show better preservation of network moments and degree distributions than existing approaches, supporting both the efficiency and structural usefulness of the design.
summary.tldr: SyNGLER generates networks through sampled latent node embeddings, preserving key structural properties with relatively low computational cost.

title: Efficient Synthetic Network Generation via Latent Embedding Reconstruction

abstract: We propose a novel algorithm for incremental Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization. The algorithm processes each input byte in worst-case $\mathcal{O}(\log^2 t)$ time, leading to an overall complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n \log^2 t)$, where $n$ is the input length and $t$ is the maximum token length. The algorithm incrementally maintains BPE tokenization results for every prefix of the input text, implementing the standard BPE merge procedure defined by a fixed set of merge rules. This enables efficient partial tokenization in streaming settings. Functioning as a drop-in replacement for standard BPE, our approach achieves a speedup of up to ${\sim}3\times$ over Hugging Face’s tokenizers, and demonstrates significant latency reductions over OpenAI’s tiktoken on pathological inputs. We further introduce an eager output algorithm that enables streaming output, emitting tokens as soon as token boundaries are determined during incremental tokenization. Overall, our results demonstrate that BPE tokenization can be performed incrementally with strong worst-case guarantees, while providing practical latency benefits in modern large language model pipelines. The source code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/mtc-inc-bpe.

The authors also introduce eager output, which emits a token once its boundary has been determined. Maintaining a prefix tokenization and deciding when tokens can be emitted are therefore both addressed.

Practical results include speedups of up to approximately three times over Hugging Face's tokenizers and significant latency reductions relative to tiktoken on pathological inputs. The findings combine worst-case computational guarantees with measured implementation benefits. The reported comparisons have distinct scopes: the tiktoken latency result specifically concerns difficult inputs, while the threefold figure is a maximum observed speedup.
summary.tldr: The algorithm incrementally maintains standard BPE tokenization with worst-case time guarantees and emits streaming tokens as their boundaries become determined.

title: Incremental BPE Tokenization

abstract: Scene graphs provide structured abstractions for scene understanding, yet they often overfit to spurious correlations, severely hindering out-of-distribution generalization. To address this limitation, we propose CURVE, a causality-inspired framework that integrates variational uncertainty modeling with uncertainty-guided structural regularization to suppress high-variance, environment-specific relations. Specifically, we apply prototype-conditioned debiasing to disentangle invariant interaction dynamics from environment-dependent variations, promoting a sparse and domain-stable topology. Empirically, we evaluate CURVE in zero-shot transfer and low-data sim-to-real adaptation, verifying its ability to learn domain-stable sparse topologies and provide reliable uncertainty estimates to support risk prediction under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Scene graphs describe a scene through entities and their relationships, but those relationships can reflect accidental patterns specific to a training environment. Such patterns become unreliable when the environment changes. CURVE addresses this by seeking a sparse relationship structure that remains stable across domains, using uncertainty to help determine which relations deserve less emphasis.

The framework combines variational uncertainty modeling with structural regularization guided by that uncertainty. Relations with high variation tied to particular environments are suppressed. A prototype-conditioned debiasing component further separates stable interaction dynamics from environment-dependent variation. The approach is inspired by causal reasoning and uses that perspective to organize representation learning around interactions that transfer more reliably.

The authors evaluate CURVE through zero-shot transfer and adaptation from simulation to reality with little data. They report domain-stable sparse graph structures and reliable uncertainty estimates that support risk prediction under distribution shifts. The findings connect two useful outcomes: more transferable scene representations and uncertainty information that helps assess risk when observations differ from the training environment.
summary.tldr: CURVE uses uncertainty-guided regularization to learn sparse scene relationships that transfer more reliably across environments.

title: CURVE: Learning Causality-Inspired Invariant Representations for Robust Scene Understanding via Uncertainty-Guided Regularization

abstract: Embodied systems experience the world as ’a symphony of flows’: a combination of many continuous streams of sensory input coupled to self-motion, interwoven with the dynamics of external objects. These sensory streams and the underlying dynamics of the world obey smooth, time-parameterized symmetries which existing world models ignore. Without a memory that respects this structure, partial observability presents a major obstacle to existing methods: each observation reveals only a fraction of the world, while unobserved regions continue to evolve. In this work, we introduce Flow Equivariant World Modeling, a framework that leverages time-parameterized symmetries within a latent memory for stable and accurate dynamics prediction over long horizons. The latent memory shifts and transforms equivariantly with self-motion and inferred external object motion, keeping information about out-of-view regions aligned as time progresses. We demonstrate the advantage of this framework over state-of-the-art diffusion, memory-augmented, and recurrent world model architectures on 2D and 3D partially observed video world modeling benchmarks. More broadly, our results suggest that predictive representations become more powerful when they are organized in line with the temporal and dynamical structure of the world they model. Project page: https://flowequivariantworldmodels.github.io/

paragraphs: A system moving through an environment sees only part of the world at any moment. Objects outside its current view can continue moving, while its own motion changes how remembered locations relate to the next observation. This paper addresses the resulting prediction problem by giving a world model memory that explicitly follows these evolving relationships.

Flow Equivariant World Modeling organizes latent memory around smooth transformations over time. The memory shifts consistently with the system's own movement and with inferred motion of external objects. In practical terms, stored information is transformed as the scene evolves, so knowledge about regions outside the current view remains aligned with the changing world.

The authors demonstrate advantages over diffusion-based, memory-augmented, and recurrent world models on partially observed 2D and 3D video benchmarks. The results support more stable and accurate predictions over long horizons. More broadly, they suggest that a predictive representation benefits from organizing memory according to the temporal structure of its environment, rather than treating remembered observations as temporally fixed information.
summary.tldr: Flow Equivariant World Models transform memory with self-motion and inferred object motion to improve prediction in partially observed environments.

title: Flow Equivariant World Models: Structured Memory for Dynamic Environments

abstract: Efficient long-context understanding is increasingly vital for large language model (LLM) applications such as multi-turn dialogue and program analysis. However, the core self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, creating a fundamental computational bottleneck. Existing sparse attention methods alleviate this issue but face trade-offs: training-based methods are costly and cannot be directly applied as acceleration plugins for other models, while inference-time methods often compromise efficiency or cross-modal generality. To address these limitations, we present UniSparse, a unified mechanism that introduces the notion of composite tokens—compact representations that aggregate multi-granularity contextual information. Building on this abstraction, UniSparse dynamically constructs sparse attention through multi-granularity compression and block-level selection, enabling efficient and hardware-friendly execution on GPU. Across multiple modalities and tasks ranging from synthetic benchmarks to real-world applications, UniSparse consistently surpasses state-of-the-art sparse attention methods (e.g., MInference, XAttention, FlexPrefill) in both accuracy and efficiency, achieving $\ge$ 99% of full-attention accuracy and up to 2.61$\times$ faster attention computation than FlashAttention.

Sparse attention reduces the connections that must be evaluated, but the abstract identifies practical trade-offs in existing methods: some require costly training, while others lose efficiency or work less generally across modalities. UniSparse aims to address these concerns within one mechanism.

Its central abstraction is the composite token, a compact representation that combines contextual information at several levels of detail. UniSparse uses these representations to compress context and select blocks for attention dynamically. Combining information across granularities guides sparse computation, while block-level selection makes the resulting workload suitable for efficient GPU execution.

summary.tldr: UniSparse uses compressed context at multiple granularities to select efficient attention blocks while retaining nearly all full-attention accuracy in the reported evaluations.

title: A Unified Sparse Attention via Multi-Granularity Compression

abstract: Recent unified models integrate multimodal understanding and generation within a single framework. However, an “understanding-generation gap” persists, where models can capture user intent but often fail to translate this semantic knowledge into precise pixel-level manipulation. This gap results in two bottlenecks in anything-to-image task (X2I): the attention entanglement bottleneck, where blind planning struggles with complex prompts, and the visual refinement bottleneck, where unstructured feedback fails to correct imperfections efficiently. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that empowers unified models to autonomously switch between generation strategies based on instruction complexity and model capability. To achieve this, we construct a hierarchical data pipeline that constructs execution paths across three adaptive modes: direct generation for simple cases, self-reflection for quality refinement, and multi-step planning for decomposing complex scenarios. Building on this pipeline, we contribute a high-quality dataset with over 50,000 samples and implement a two-stage training strategy comprising SFT and RL. Specifically, we design step-wise reasoning rewards to ensure logical consistency and intra-group complexity penalty to prevent redundant computational overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing baselines on X2I, achieving superior generation fidelity among simple-to-complex instructions.

paragraphs: A unified multimodal model can understand an instruction yet struggle to turn that understanding into an accurate image. This paper separates that gap into difficulties with planning complex requests and correcting visual imperfections through unstructured feedback. Its proposed framework teaches models to choose a generation strategy according to instruction complexity and their own capability.

The training pipeline provides three types of execution paths. Simple requests can use direct generation, outputs needing improvement can use self-reflection, and complex requests can use multiple planning steps. A hierarchical data pipeline supplies more than 50,000 examples, followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The reinforcement learning design rewards reasoning at individual steps for logical consistency and applies a complexity penalty within groups to discourage redundant computation. Together, these mechanisms aim to make extra reasoning useful without making it the default for every request. Experiments report better image-generation fidelity than existing baselines across simple and complex instructions. The contribution is an adaptive approach to generation and refinement within a unified model.
summary.tldr: An adaptive training framework teaches unified multimodal models when to generate directly, reflect, or plan across multiple steps.

title: Breaking Dual Bottlenecks: Evolving Unified Multimodal Models into Self-Adaptive Interleaved Visual Reasoners

abstract: Understanding the geometry of learned distributions is fundamental to improving and interpreting diffusion models, yet systematic tools for exploring their landscape remain limited. Standard latent-space interpolations fail to respect the structure of the learned distribution, often traversing low-density regions. We introduce a framework based on the string method that computes continuous paths between samples by evolving curves under the learned score function. Operating on pretrained models without retraining, our approach interpolates between three regimes: pure generative transport, which yields continuous sample paths; gradient-dominated dynamics, which recover minimum energy paths (MEPs); and finite-temperature string dynamics, which compute principal curves—self-consistent paths that balance energy and entropy. We demonstrate that the choice of regime matters in practice. For image diffusion models, MEPs contain high-likelihood but unrealistic “cartoon” images, confirming prior observations that likelihood maxima appear unrealistic; principal curves instead yield realistic morphing sequences despite lower likelihood. For protein structure prediction, our method computes transition pathways between metastable conformers directly from models trained on static structures, yielding paths with physically plausible intermediates. Together, these results establish the string method as a principled tool for probing the modal structure of diffusion models—identifying modes, characterizing barriers, and mapping connectivity in complex learned distributions.

paragraphs: Interpolating between generated samples can reveal how a model organizes its learned distribution, but ordinary latent-space interpolation may pass through low-density regions. This paper adapts the string method to evolve entire curves under a diffusion model’s learned score function. The method works with pretrained models and requires no retraining.

Different settings of the framework produce different kinds of paths. Generative transport yields continuous sample trajectories; gradient-dominated dynamics recover minimum-energy paths; and finite-temperature dynamics produce principal curves that balance energy and entropy. These findings support the string method as a tool for examining how learned modes connect and what barriers separate them. They also show why choosing a path solely for high likelihood can give a different picture from choosing one that reflects realistic variation.
summary.tldr: The string method maps paths through pretrained diffusion models, revealing how realistic transitions can differ from high-likelihood paths.

title: Probing the Geometry of Diffusion Models with the String Method

abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is a cornerstone of flow-matching models, significantly enhancing visual quality and prompt adherence. However, high guidance scales inherently violate the optimal transport dynamics, leading to visual artifacts and mode collapse. In this paper, we investigate the mechanisms of this failure through the lens of velocity moment decomposition. Our analysis reveals that the distributional shift induced by CFG decouples into two geometric components: a Linear Barycentric Drift that shifts the global distribution center, and a Quadratic Energetic Instability that injects surplus kinetic energy, disrupting the transport cost and triggering variance explosion. To mitigate these issues, we introduce MIST (Moment-aligned Invariant Stability Transform), a training-free method designed to confine the sampling trajectory to the learned data manifold. MIST comprises two hierarchical stages: (1) Invariant Alignment (IA), a global statistical rectifier that restores structural integrity by removing the linear drift and realigning the energy profile; and (2) Stability Thresholding (ST), a local dynamical regulator that enforces Lipschitz-like smoothness via temporal decay and spatial suppression. MIST enables robust, high-fidelity generation across a wide range of guidance scales while consistently improving performance at moderate scales. Extensive experiments on diverse text-to-image and text-to-video benchmarks demonstrate that MIST outperforms standard CFG and state-of-the-art corrections, establishing a new benchmark for robust guidance in flow-based generative models.

Extensive experiments on diverse text-to-image and text-to-video benchmarks demonstrate that MIST outperforms standard CFG and state-of-the-art corrections, establishing a new benchmark for robust guidance in flow-based generative models.

paragraphs: Classifier-free guidance helps flow-matching models follow prompts and improve visual quality, but strong guidance can produce artifacts and collapsed diversity. This paper analyzes that failure through the moments of the model’s velocity field. It identifies two effects: a shift in the distribution’s center and excess kinetic energy that disrupts transport and can drive variance explosion.

MIST is a training-free correction with two stages. Invariant Alignment removes the global drift and readjusts the energy profile. Stability Thresholding then regulates local dynamics through temporal decay and spatial suppression, enforcing a Lipschitz-like smoothness condition. The two stages address different scales of the same problem: global statistical displacement and unstable local behavior along the sampling trajectory.

The method is designed to keep generation close to the learned data manifold across a wide range of guidance strengths. Experiments on text-to-image and text-to-video benchmarks report improvements over standard guidance and leading correction methods, including consistent gains at moderate guidance scales. These findings connect a geometric explanation of guidance failures to a correction applied during sampling, without requiring model retraining.
summary.tldr: MIST stabilizes guided flow generation without retraining by correcting global velocity statistics and regulating local sampling dynamics.

title: MIST: Moment-Aligned Invariant Stability Transform for Robust Flow Matching

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) has emerged as a fundamental tool in modern machine learning, yet its computational cost remains a significant bottleneck for large-scale applications. While harnessing the massive parallelism of modern GPU hardware is critical for efficiency, the de facto standard Sinkhorn algorithm, despite its ease of parallelization, often suffers from slow convergence in challenging problems. More recently, the sparse-plus-low-rank quasi-Newton method offers a balance between convergence rate and per-iteration complexity; however, its efficiency on GPUs is severely hindered by the serial nature of sparse matrix symbolic analysis and irregular memory access patterns. To bridge this gap, we present cuRegOT, a high-performance GPU solver tailored for entropic-regularized OT. We introduce a suite of algorithmic and architectural optimizations, including an amortized symbolic analysis strategy to mitigate CPU bottlenecks, an asynchronous Sinkhorn iterates generation mechanism, and a fused kernel for bandwidth-efficient gradient evaluation. These strategies are backed by rigorous theoretical guarantees ensuring algorithmic convergence. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that cuRegOT achieves significant speedups over state-of-the-art GPU-based solvers across a variety of benchmark tasks.

The widely used Sinkhorn algorithm maps well onto parallel hardware yet can converge slowly on difficult cases. A sparse-plus-low-rank quasi-Newton approach offers a promising balance between convergence speed and work per iteration, but its computational structure creates GPU bottlenecks.

cuRegOT addresses those bottlenecks for entropic-regularized optimal transport. The contribution therefore concerns both the optimization method and its execution: faster convergence becomes practically useful when the surrounding computation is organized to suit the hardware.
summary.tldr: cuRegOT combines optimization and GPU execution improvements to accelerate entropic optimal transport while retaining convergence guarantees.

title: cuRegOT: A GPU-Accelerated Solver for Entropic-Regularized Optimal Transport

abstract: Medical audio data is difficult to collect due to privacy regulations and high annotation costs arising from domain expertise. Thus, existing benchmarks tend to underrepresent complex medical audio scenarios. To address this challenge, we present MedMosaic, a medical audio question–answering dataset designed to benchmark language and audio reasoning models under realistic clinical constraints. MedMosaic features a diverse range of medical audio types, including condition-related physiological sounds, carefully constructed synthetic voices to mimic speech with artifacts as well as real short and long length clinical conversations to model varying context lengths. The dataset also features a total of 46,701 question-answer pairs, spanning categories such as multiple-choice, sequential multi-turn, and open-ended question–answers, enabling systematic evaluation of multi-hop reasoning and answer generation capabilities. Benchmarking 13 audio and multimodal reasoning models reveals that reasoning remains challenging for all evaluated systems, with substantial performance variation across question types. In particular, even state-of-the-art model like Gemini-2.5-pro can only achieve 68.1% accuracy approximately. These findings underscore persistent limitations in medical reasoning and highlight the need for more robust, domain-specific multimodal reasoning models. A sample of benchmark data is available here:https://shorturl.at/Lyp33

paragraphs: Medical audio is difficult to collect and annotate because of privacy requirements and the expertise needed to interpret it. MedMosaic addresses the resulting gaps in evaluation with a question-answering dataset covering several kinds of medical sound. Its purpose is to test audio and language reasoning under realistic clinical constraints.

The dataset combines condition-related physiological sounds, synthetic voices designed to mimic speech artifacts, and real clinical conversations of different lengths. Its 46,701 question–answer pairs include multiple-choice questions, sequential multi-turn exchanges, and open-ended answers. This variety allows evaluation of both answer generation and reasoning that connects information across multiple steps or longer contexts.

Performance varies substantially with question type, and Gemini-2.5-pro reaches approximately 68.1% accuracy. These findings identify persistent weaknesses in the evaluated models’ medical reasoning. They also show why a benchmark spanning different sounds, context lengths, and response formats can reveal capabilities that a narrower evaluation would not cover.
summary.tldr: MedMosaic provides 46,701 medical audio question–answer pairs and reveals substantial reasoning challenges across 13 evaluated models.

title: MedMosaic: A Challenging Large Scale Benchmark of Diverse Medical Audio

abstract: Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization is widely used in reinforcement learning, but it becomes infinite under support mismatch and can degenerate in low-noise regimes. Using a unified information-geometric framework, we introduce KL analogs by replacing the Fisher–Rao geometry in the dynamical formulation of the KL with transport-based geometries, and derive closed-form expressions for common distribution families. Between elliptic distributions, these divergences remain finite for degenerating equal covariances and yield a geometric interpretation of regularization heuristics used in Kalman ensemble methods. We demonstrate the utility of these divergences in KL-regularized optimal control. In the fully tractable setting of linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise, the classical KL reduces to a quadratic control penalty that becomes singular as process noise vanishes. Our variants remove this singularity and yield well-posed problems. On a double integrator and a cart-pole example, the resulting controls preserve nontrivial feedback and achieve better closed-loop performance.

paragraphs: KL divergence is commonly used to regularize control and reinforcement learning, but it can become infinite when distributions have mismatched support and degenerate as noise decreases. This paper constructs related divergences using transport-based geometries in place of the Fisher–Rao geometry in a dynamical formulation of KL divergence.

The authors derive closed-form expressions for common distribution families. For elliptic distributions with equal covariances that degenerate, the new divergences remain finite. They also provide a geometric interpretation of regularization heuristics in Kalman ensemble methods. These properties motivate using the alternatives in control problems where ordinary KL regularization becomes problematic as randomness vanishes.

The control analysis considers linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise, a fully tractable setting. Ordinary KL becomes a quadratic control penalty that turns singular in the zero-noise limit; the proposed variants remove that singularity and make the problems well-posed. Experiments on a double integrator and cart-pole show nontrivial feedback and better closed-loop performance, illustrating the practical consequences of the changed regularization geometry.
summary.tldr: Transport-based KL analogs remove a vanishing-noise singularity in the analyzed control setting and improve closed-loop performance in two examples.

title: Well-Posed KL-Regularized Control via Wasserstein and Kalman–Wasserstein KL Divergences

abstract: Multi-modal object Re-Identification (ReID) aims to retrieve the same object across different modalities by exploiting their complementary visual information. Recent advances leverage Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to generate descriptive textual annotations as auxiliary supervision. However, existing approaches usually adopt these generated texts directly, overlooking the varying correspondence degrees between visual and textual modalities. Such neglect may lead the model to treat strong- and weak-correspondence image–text pairs equally, limiting its ability to learn discriminative associations and hindering effective optimization. To overcome this limitation, we propose a Correspondence Cognitive Learning (CCL) framework that explicitly models the correspondence degree and facilitates a progressive learning process from easy to hard pairs. CCL is composed of two synergistic modules. The Correspondence-Guided Semantic Refinement (CGSR) module dynamically refines visual representations using text semantics according to the correspondence difficulty estimated from the previous epoch, thereby enhancing feature alignment under imperfect associations. The Cognitive-Driven Dynamic Optimization (CDDO) module presents a self-paced weighting mechanism that adaptively adjusts the optimization focus by emphasizing easy pairs at the early stage and gradually integrating harder ones as training evolves. Together, these modules enhance feature-level alignment and optimization adaptivity, yielding robust and discriminative multi-modal representations. Extensive experiments on three multi-modal object ReID benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of our method.

paragraphs: Multi-modal object re-identification aims to find the same object across different kinds of visual input. Generated text descriptions can help supervise this learning, but some descriptions match their images more closely than others. Treating all image–text pairs equally can therefore weaken the associations the model learns and make optimization less effective.

Correspondence Cognitive Learning explicitly estimates how well each pair corresponds and uses that estimate in two ways. Its semantic refinement module adjusts visual representations using text, guided by the pair's difficulty estimated in the preceding training epoch. Its dynamic optimization module changes the weight assigned to pairs over training, initially emphasizing easier matches and progressively incorporating harder ones.

The two modules coordinate what information shapes the representations and when difficult examples receive attention. Experiments on three multi-modal object re-identification benchmarks report superior performance. The findings support treating generated descriptions as supervision of varying correspondence quality, with progressive learning helping the model build more discriminative representations despite imperfect image–text associations.
summary.tldr: CCL improves multi-modal object re-identification by adapting feature refinement and training weights to image–text correspondence difficulty.

title: Correspondence Cognitive Learning for Multi-Modal Object Re-Identification

abstract: We study offline black-box optimization (BBO), aiming to discover improved designs from an offline dataset of designs and labels, a problem common in robotics, DNA, and materials science with limited labeled samples. While recent work applies autoregressive LLMs to BBO by formatting tasks as natural-language prompts, their left-to-right design generation struggles to capture the strong bidirectional dependencies inherent in design problems. To address this, we propose adapting diffusion LLMs to offline BBO to leverage their bidirectional modeling capabilities. However, a domain gap exists between the natural text pre-training of diffusion LLMs and the heterogeneous signals in BBO (prompts, designs, and labels). To bridge this gap, we construct a unified prompt—response corpus and introduce delimiter tokens to explicitly mark field boundaries for domain adaptation. We further propose a two-stage post-training framework to align the diffusion LLM generation with high-label designs. The first stage performs supervised fine-tuning on the unified dataset via masked-response prediction, and the second stage adopts reinforcement learning with rewards defined by label improvements. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on Design-Bench under small-data settings. Code for our work is available here: https://github.com/zpointS/DiBO.

paragraphs: Offline black-box optimization seeks better designs using an existing dataset of designs and their labels, often with few labeled examples. The paper argues that left-to-right language generation struggles with design problems whose parts depend strongly on one another in both directions. It adapts diffusion language models to take advantage of their bidirectional modeling.

A central challenge is the mismatch between natural-language pretraining and the mixture of prompts, designs, and labels used in optimization. The authors build a unified prompt-response corpus and add delimiter tokens to mark field boundaries. This gives the model an explicit structure for distinguishing the different kinds of information during adaptation.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on Design-Bench under small-data conditions. The findings support combining bidirectional generation with domain-specific formatting and reward-based refinement to search for improved designs from limited offline examples.
summary.tldr: Diffusion language models adapted with structured data and two-stage training achieve state-of-the-art small-data optimization results on Design-Bench.

title: Training Diffusion Language Models for Black-Box Optimization

abstract: Emergent misalignment can arise when a language model is fine-tuned on a narrowly scoped supervised objective: the model learns the target behavior, yet also develops undesirable out-of-domain behaviors. We investigate a mechanistic approach to preventing emergent misalignment by identifying a small set of internal features that reliably control the misaligned behavior and then discouraging the model from strengthening these features during fine-tuning. Across six fine-tuning domains, blocking (i.e., constraining) a fixed set of features achieves up to 95% relative reduction in emergent misalignment with no degradation in model quality or target-task performance. We strengthen validity with disjoint selection/evaluation splits, multiple independent judges, multiple random seeds for key settings, quality metrics, and extensive ablations demonstrating that the reduction in misalignment is specific to the identified mechanism. We also characterize a limiting regime in which misalignment re-emerges under prolonged fine-tuning, present evidence consistent with rerouting through alternative features or layers, and evaluate modifications that partially restore the misalignment-blocking effect. Overall, our results show that targeted training-time constraints on internal mechanisms can mitigate emergent misalignment without degrading target-task performance.

BLOCK-EM investigates whether this emergent misalignment can be reduced by intervening on the internal features that control it. The authors test the finding using separate feature-selection and evaluation splits, multiple independent judges, and multiple random seeds in key settings. Their ablations support the interpretation that the effect depends on the identified mechanism.

The paper also identifies a limit: prolonged fine-tuning can bring misalignment back. Evidence is consistent with the behavior shifting through other features or layers, and evaluated modifications partially recover the blocking effect. The findings therefore support targeted internal constraints as a training-time mitigation, while showing that the initially identified feature set may not remain sufficient throughout extended training.
summary.tldr: Constraining selected internal features substantially reduces emergent misalignment in tested settings, although extended fine-tuning can weaken the protection.

title: BLOCK-EM: Preventing Emergent Misalignment via Latent Blocking

abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to acquire new knowledge from a non-stationary data stream while retaining performance on previously learned tasks. Memory-based replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing and revisiting past samples, but their effectiveness is fundamentally constrained by limited memory capacity, as each stored example represents only a single data instance. In this work, we propose data reassembly for CL, a new paradigm that significantly increases memory efficiency by reassembling composite replay samples from existing training data. Instead of storing raw training examples, we partition the current task training data into elementary patches and dynamically reassemble them into coherent replay instances through an energy-based optimization framework. The proposed objective jointly enforces semantic compatibility with target labels and global consistency among assembled patches. To make this optimization tractable, we derive an efficient variational inference algorithm that constructs a compact yet diverse set of reassembled samples for replay. Extensive theoretical analysis and experiments across multiple CL benchmarks demonstrate that data reassembly consistently outperforms existing memory-based approaches, achieving stronger retention of past knowledge while maintaining competitive computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new knowledge while retaining what it learned earlier. Replaying stored examples helps prevent forgetting, but a limited memory buffer restricts how much past experience can be revisited. This paper proposes increasing the usefulness of that memory by constructing replay examples from reusable pieces of training data.

The method partitions current-task data into elementary patches instead of storing complete raw examples. An energy-based optimization process assembles patches into replay instances, evaluating both whether they fit the intended label and whether the pieces form a globally coherent sample. These two requirements matter together: label-compatible fragments alone need not make a consistent whole. An efficient variational inference algorithm makes the assembly process tractable and produces a compact, diverse replay set.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and experiments across multiple continual learning benchmarks. They report consistently better retention than existing memory-based methods while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. The central result is that replay memory can represent more useful variation when stored material can be recombined into coherent training instances.
summary.tldr: Energy-based data reassembly builds coherent replay examples from reusable patches, improving memory efficiency and knowledge retention in continual learning.

title: Beyond Buffer Limits: Energy-Based Data Reassembly for Continual Learning

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) excels at new tasks from minimal examples, yet we still lack a mechanistic explanation of how few-shot prompts shape a model’s function vector (FV)–a causal activation direction that drives task behavior on the ICL query. Across tasks and models, an $n$-shot FV is well-approximated by a linear combination of example-level sub-FVs, suggesting additive and composable contributions from individual demonstrations. Beyond additivity, we show that models contextualize individual examples’ representations based on prior examples to adaptively reweight which demonstrations dominate the FV: attention shifts toward examples that are more informative and less ambiguous under the context. Finally, a causal decomposition separates Query–Key routing from Value updates, finding that contextualization’s most consistent contributions to FV quality arise from Query–Key alignment–particularly in ambiguous settings–while Value-mediated effects are more heterogeneous. Together, these results unify additive superposition with context-dependent attention reweighting into a mechanistic, testable account of how few-shot prompts implement tasks.

paragraphs: Few-shot prompts can teach a language model a task through demonstrations, but the internal mechanism remains difficult to explain. This paper studies function vectors: activation directions that causally influence how the model performs the task on a query. The authors ask how individual examples contribute to the vector formed by a complete prompt.

Across the examined tasks and models, the full function vector is well approximated by a linear combination of contributions from individual demonstrations. Those contributions are also contextual: earlier examples change how later examples are represented. Attention consequently shifts toward demonstrations that are more informative and less ambiguous in the surrounding context. Approximate additivity therefore coexists with adaptive weighting.

A causal decomposition separates Query–Key routing, which governs attention alignment, from Value updates. The most consistent benefits of contextualization come from Query–Key alignment, particularly when examples are ambiguous; Value-related effects vary more. Together, these findings give a testable account of how demonstrations combine and why their context changes which examples most strongly shape task behavior.
summary.tldr: Few-shot demonstrations contribute approximately additive function vectors whose influence is adaptively reweighted through context-dependent attention.

title: How Few-Shot Examples Add Up: A Causal Decomposition of Function Vectors in In-Context Learning

abstract: Estimating treatment effects from observational text is increasingly practical with Large Language Models (LLMs). However, applying causal representation learning directly to high-dimensional LLM embeddings faces a fundamental barrier: empirical Wasserstein matching suffers from the curse of dimensionality, rendering standard generalization guarantees effectively vacuous. We propose SPIKED-CFR, a framework bridging this gap by assuming a Spiked Structure, where treatment selection bias is assumed to manifest primarily as a low-dimensional treated–control discrepancy in the semantic representation. We develop Wasserstein Projection Pursuit, a minimax objective that adversarially learns an orthogonal projection on the Stiefel manifold to identify and balance only this subspace while preserving prognostic information. Under a spiked structure, we show the projected discrepancy can be estimated at a rate governed by the intrinsic dimension $k \ll D$, and we derive a tighter PEHE generalization bound that depends on $k$ rather than the ambient embedding dimension. Experiments on four semi-synthetic benchmarks and four real-world clinical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness over strong baselines.

paragraphs: Language-model embeddings make observational text usable for treatment-effect estimation, but their high dimensionality complicates causal representation learning. In particular, empirical Wasserstein matching becomes statistically difficult enough that standard generalization guarantees can be effectively uninformative. SPIKED-CFR addresses this problem through an explicit assumption about where treatment selection bias appears.

Its spiked-structure assumption says that the discrepancy between treated and control representations lies primarily in a low-dimensional subspace. Wasserstein Projection Pursuit adversarially learns an orthogonal projection to identify and balance that discrepancy while preserving information useful for predicting outcomes. This focuses matching on the assumed bias-bearing directions within the larger semantic representation.

Under the stated structure, the authors show that discrepancy estimation depends on intrinsic dimension k rather than the full embedding dimension D. They also derive a tighter PEHE generalization bound, concerning error in heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation. Experiments on four semi-synthetic and four real-world clinical benchmarks report improved accuracy and robustness over strong baselines. The theoretical benefit therefore depends on the spiked assumption, with empirical results supporting the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: SPIKED-CFR improves causal learning from text embeddings by balancing a low-dimensional bias subspace under an explicit spiked-structure assumption.

title: Spiked-CFR: Causal Representation Learning from LLMs via Wasserstein Projection Pursuit

abstract: Experimental design has emerged as a powerful approach for improving the sample efficiency of A/B testing, yet existing designs rely critically on correctly specified models. We study robust sequential experimental design under model misspecification and develop a unified framework that covers both contextual bandit and dynamic settings. Theoretically, we prove that our design bounds the worst-case mean squared error of the estimated treatment effect. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach using synthetic and real-world datasets from a leading technology company.

paragraphs: Experimental design can make A/B tests more sample-efficient by guiding how an experiment collects evidence. That benefit can depend on the model used to design the experiment being correct. This paper studies sequential design when the model is misspecified, focusing on the reliability of the estimated treatment effect.

The authors develop a unified framework covering contextual bandit and dynamic settings. Bringing these settings together allows the analysis to address sequential experiments across both forms of interaction. The central theoretical result bounds the worst-case mean squared error of the treatment-effect estimate. This measures estimation error directly and makes robustness to model misspecification part of the design objective.

The proposed approach is evaluated using synthetic data and real-world datasets from a leading technology company, with the authors reporting evidence of effectiveness. The combination of a worst-case error bound and empirical evaluation supports experimental design that accounts for imperfect models. Its stated contribution is a robust framework for sequential treatment-effect estimation, connecting sample-efficient experimentation with protection against the modeled uncertainty.
summary.tldr: The paper develops sequential A/B-test designs with worst-case treatment-effect error bounds under model misspecification.

title: Robust Sequential Experimental Design for A/B Testing

abstract: Long-context LLM inference faces a fundamental conflict: head-adaptive compression algorithms (e.g., Top-$p$ nucleus sampling) offer superior accuracy by dynamically fluctuating memory budgets, yet modern inference engines (e.g., vLLM) demand rigid, static memory patterns to leverage CUDA Graphs and PagedAttention. We resolve this “Static-Dynamic” mismatch with HARD-KV, a unified framework that that bridges dynamic selection with rigid system constraints. HARD-KV introduces a Cascade Cache hierarchy, managing the token lifecycle across dense, sparse, and condensed tiers. Crucially, we propose a Logits Calibration mechanism that normalizes diverse importance metrics into a unified probability space, enabling consistent Top-$p$ budgeting across heterogeneous heads. To bridge the efficiency gap, we offer a system-level solution, which rewrites fragmented, dynamic indices into contiguous physical layouts compatible with high-performance inference engine. Extensive experiments on math-reasoning benchmarks (AIME, U-Math) verify that HARD-KV achieves up to 2$\times$ throughput improvement over static baselines while maintaining high-fidelity generation in 10k+ token scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/SuDIS-ZJU/HARDInfer.

paragraphs: HARD-KV addresses a mismatch between adaptive cache compression and efficient inference systems. Different attention heads can benefit from retaining different amounts of information, with those amounts changing dynamically. However, inference engines use rigid memory patterns to exploit mechanisms such as CUDA Graphs and PagedAttention. A good selection rule therefore needs a compatible physical memory organization.

The framework introduces a Cascade Cache with dense, sparse, and condensed tiers to manage cached tokens through their lifecycle. Its Logits Calibration mechanism maps different importance measures into a common probability space. This makes Top-p budgeting consistent across heads whose raw importance scores may otherwise be difficult to compare.

A system-level component then converts fragmented dynamic indices into contiguous physical layouts suitable for high-performance inference. This connects flexible token selection to the engine’s memory requirements. Experiments on AIME and U-Math report throughput improvements of up to twofold over static baselines while maintaining high-fidelity generation in scenarios exceeding 10,000 tokens. The findings emphasize that cache compression benefits depend on coordinating selection quality with the execution system.
summary.tldr: HARD-KV makes adaptive attention-cache compression compatible with rigid inference memory layouts, reporting up to twice the throughput of static baselines.

title: HARD-KV: Head-Adaptive Regularization for Decoding-time KV Compression

abstract: World models have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) by enabling policy learning in imagination, thereby reducing the need for direct interaction with the real environment. However, most existing world model methods are trained independently for each task or perform multi-task learning using offline datasets, failing to fully exploit the latent relationships among tasks in online interactive scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose TaskLoom, a knowledge-sharing world model architecture for online RL. TaskLoom adopts a grouped two-stage training paradigm: first, the tasks are divided into several groups based on the similarity of world model gradients, and fine-grained knowledge is shared among tasks within each group; second, coarse-grained knowledge is exchanged across groups, enabling hierarchical knowledge transfer and reuse. Experimental results show that TaskLoom outperforms baseline methods on widely used benchmarks such as Proprio Control, Visual Control and Meta-World, validating the effectiveness of the proposed knowledge-sharing mechanism for both low-dimensional state and high-dimensional visual inputs.

paragraphs: World models let reinforcement-learning agents learn policies through imagined experience, reducing their need for direct environmental interaction. Training a separate world model for each task can leave useful connections between tasks unexplored. TaskLoom introduces a knowledge-sharing architecture for the online setting, where agents continue interacting with their environments during learning.

Its two-stage process first groups tasks according to the similarity of their world-model gradients. Tasks within a group share fine-grained knowledge. A second stage exchanges coarser knowledge across groups. This hierarchical organization provides different levels of sharing according to the relationships captured by the grouping process.

The distinction matters because the architecture can reuse closely related information within groups while also transferring broader information between them. Experiments on Proprio Control, Visual Control, and Meta-World show improvements over baseline methods. The results cover both low-dimensional state inputs and high-dimensional visual observations. They support the proposed sharing mechanism across these input settings and show that relationships among tasks can be useful during online world-model learning.
summary.tldr: TaskLoom improves online world-model learning by sharing detailed knowledge within related task groups and broader knowledge across groups.

title: TaskLoom: Weaving Knowledge Across Tasks in World Models

abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is a standard way to adapt multimodal large language models, yet extremely low-rank settings—especially rank-1 LoRA—are often unstable. We show that this instability is not solely due to limited capacity: in the rank-1 regime, optimization is highly sensitive to the update direction. Concretely, pretrained vision and text features form mismatched anisotropic regions, yielding a dominant "gap" direction that acts like a translation component and disproportionately steers early gradients under rank-1 constraints. Analyzing pretrained representations, we identify a modality-gap axis that dominates early gradient flow, while a random rank-1 initialization is unlikely to align with it, leading to weak gradients and training collapse. We propose Gap-Init, a geometry-aware initialization that aligns the rank-1 LoRA direction with an estimated modality-gap vector from a small calibration set, while keeping the initial LoRA update zero. Across multiple vision-language tasks and backbones, Gap-Init consistently stabilizes rank-1 training and can match or outperform strong rank-8 baselines. Our results suggest that at the extreme low-rank limit, initial alignment can matter as much as rank itself.

paragraphs: Rank-1 LoRA offers an extremely constrained way to adapt a multimodal model, but training can be unstable. This paper shows that limited capacity is not the only explanation. With just one adaptation direction, the relationship between initialization and the geometry of pretrained vision and text features becomes especially influential.

The authors identify a dominant modality-gap axis arising from mismatched, anisotropic feature regions. This direction acts like a translation component and strongly influences early gradients. Random rank-1 initialization is unlikely to align with it, contributing to weak gradients and training collapse. Gap-Init estimates the gap vector from a small calibration set and aligns the LoRA direction with it while keeping the initial update zero.

It shows that, in the evaluated extreme low-rank settings, choosing an appropriate initial direction can matter as much as increasing rank.
summary.tldr: Gap-Init aligns rank-1 LoRA with a measured vision–text gap direction, stabilizing training and sometimes matching or exceeding rank-8 baselines.

title: When Is Rank-1 Enough? Geometry-Guided Initialization for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

abstract: Point cloud completion and generation are important across many 3D tasks, where both fidelity and sampling efficiency matter. Prevailing high-fidelity approaches rely on long sampling schedules, which incur substantial inference latency. Few-step alternatives typically use rectification or distillation, leading to multi-stage training pipelines and potential quality trade-offs. We present 3D MeanFlow (3DMF), a distillation-free model that performs one-step average-velocity transport for point cloud completion and generation. We optimize an instantaneous-average consistency objective and impose a shape-level constraint to stabilize training. Additionally, we introduce PointPlug, integrating completion into 3D object detectors and evaluating its impact. PointPlug uses adaptive selection that balances benefit and latency. Across standard benchmarks, 3DMF achieves one-step sampling with an order-of-magnitude speedup while maintaining competitive fidelity. On nuScenes and KITTI, inserting PointPlug improves all evaluated detectors under comparable settings.

We present 3D MeanFlow (3DMF), a distillation-free model that performs one-step average-velocity transport for point cloud completion and generation. paragraphs: Completing a partial point cloud and generating a new one both require producing convincing three-dimensional shapes. High-quality methods often do this through many sampling steps, which increases inference time. Existing approaches that reduce the number of steps commonly depend on rectification or distillation, adding training stages and potentially trading away quality.

3D MeanFlow learns to produce the result with one step of average-velocity transport, without distillation. Its training objective makes instantaneous and average velocities consistent, while a constraint on the overall shape helps stabilize learning. Together, these components support learning a direct transformation rather than relying on a long sampling sequence.

The paper also introduces PointPlug, which inserts point-cloud completion into object detectors and adaptively selects when to use it by balancing benefit against latency. Benchmark results report an order-of-magnitude sampling speedup with competitive fidelity. On nuScenes and KITTI, PointPlug improves every evaluated detector under comparable settings, connecting faster shape completion to gains in a downstream detection task.
summary.tldr: 3D MeanFlow completes and generates point clouds in one sampling step, delivering faster sampling with competitive fidelity and improving evaluated object detectors.

title: 3D MeanFlow: One-Step Point Cloud Completion and Generation via Average-Velocity Transport

abstract: Quantization followed by parameter-efficient fine-tuning has emerged as a promising paradigm for downstream adaptation under tight GPU memory constraints. However, this sequential pipeline fails to leverage the intricate interaction between quantization bit-width and LoRA rank. Specifically, a carefully optimized quantization allocation with low quantization error does not always translate to strong fine-tuning performance, and different bit-width and rank configurations can lead to significantly varying outcomes under the same memory budget. To address this limitation, we propose AutoQRA, a joint optimization framework that simultaneously optimizes the bit-width and LoRA rank configuration for each layer during the mixed quantized fine-tuning process. To tackle the challenges posed by the large discrete search space and the high evaluation cost associated with frequent fine-tuning iterations, AutoQRA decomposes the optimization process into two stages. First, it first conducts a global multi-fidelity evolutionary search, where the initial population is warm-started by injecting layer-wise importance priors. This stage employs specific operators and a performance model to efficiently screen candidate configurations. Second, trust-region Bayesian optimization is applied to locally refine promising regions of the search space and identify optimal configurations under the given memory budget. This approach enables active compensation for quantization noise in specific layers during training. Experiments show that AutoQRA achieves performance close to full-precision fine-tuning with a memory footprint comparable to uniform 4-bit methods.
