paragraphs: Compressing a language model and then adapting it with low-rank adapters creates two linked choices: how precisely each layer stores its weights and how much adapter capacity that layer receives. The paper shows why choosing them separately is inadequate. Low quantization error does not always predict strong fine-tuning, and configurations using the same memory can produce substantially different outcomes.

AutoQRA searches jointly over each layer’s quantization bit-width and adapter rank. Its first stage explores configurations broadly using an evolutionary search with different evaluation fidelities. Layer-importance information helps initialize the search, while specialized operators and a performance model screen candidates. A second stage uses trust-region Bayesian optimization to refine promising parts of the configuration space.

This joint allocation lets training compensate for quantization noise in particular layers while respecting a memory budget. Experiments report performance close to full-precision fine-tuning with memory usage comparable to uniform four-bit methods. The result supports treating compression and adaptation capacity as a coordinated allocation problem, rather than assuming that the best initial compression will also produce the best adapted model.
summary.tldr: AutoQRA jointly selects layer precision and adapter rank to approach full-precision fine-tuning performance within a four-bit-like memory footprint.

title: AutoQRA: Joint Optimization of Mixed-Precision Quantization and Low-rank Adapters for Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning

abstract: Artificial agentic systems increasingly operate as behavioral systems by interacting with dynamic environments, pursuing goals, and adapting over time. Yet, current evaluation methods largely focus on performance outcomes, not the underlying behavioral processes that produce them. This paper argues that AI agents must be evaluated like other behavioral systems: through systematic observation, perturbation, and interpretation of their actions. We draw on lessons from the behavioral sciences to motivate this position, and propose a research agenda focused on developing rigorous behavioral tests. These include methods for recovering decision strategies from action sequences, constructing environments that isolate behavioral differences, and probing emergent dynamics in multi-agent systems. Taken together, these directions offer a roadmap for developing a science of AI behavior.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that evaluating an AI agent requires studying how it acts over time. Agents interact with changing environments, pursue objectives, and adapt, making them behavioral systems in the authors’ account. Current evaluations often emphasize final performance, which leaves the processes producing that performance insufficiently examined.

Drawing on behavioral science, the authors propose systematic observation, deliberate changes to an agent’s circumstances, and interpretation of its actions. Their agenda includes methods for inferring decision strategies from sequences of actions. It also includes designing environments that make behavioral differences easier to distinguish, so evaluation can investigate how an agent reaches an outcome as well as whether it succeeds.

A further direction concerns behavior that emerges when multiple agents interact. Here, the object of study extends from individual action choices to the dynamics of the interacting system. Together, these proposals outline a science of AI behavior with dedicated testing methods. The paper’s contribution is this evaluation agenda: treating actions and their organization as evidence about an agent, alongside measures of task performance.
summary.tldr: AI agents should be evaluated through behavioral experiments that examine decision strategies and interactions as well as outcomes.

title: Position: Behavioral Systems Require Behavioral Tests

abstract: Researchers rarely observe the mechanistic drivers of scientific processes directly. Instead, they observe proxies, which are measurable quantities correlated with one or more of these latent drivers. This position paper argues that mechanistic learning from high-dimensional proxies is generically underdetermined. Many incompatible mechanisms induce essentially the same observational relationships on the support of the data, so predictive success and coherent explanations are insufficient evidence of mechanism discovery. Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) models can therefore generate scientific hypotheses that sound plausible while the underlying mechanism remains unidentified. The problem is particularly acute with large language models (LLMs), which tend to collapse entire equivalence classes of explanations into a single fluent narrative. The paper proposes concrete standards for “mechanistic AI,” norms that are necessary if AI-centered workflows are to support science rather than merely simulate it.

paragraphs: Scientific data often measure proxies for the processes researchers want to understand. A proxy may correlate with several hidden drivers without directly revealing any of them. This paper argues that learning mechanisms from high-dimensional proxies is generally underdetermined: different and incompatible mechanisms can produce essentially the same relationships within the observed data.

That ambiguity changes what successful prediction can establish. A model may predict well and provide a coherent explanation while leaving the underlying mechanism unidentified. The authors argue that AI-generated scientific hypotheses can therefore sound convincing without resolving which process produced the observations. They highlight language models as a particular concern because a fluent account can compress multiple compatible explanations into one narrative.

The paper proposes standards for work described as mechanistic AI. Its central demand is that claims about discovering mechanisms confront the problem of identification, rather than treating predictive performance or explanatory coherence as sufficient evidence. The significance is a clearer boundary between generating plausible scientific hypotheses and establishing which underlying structure the available observations actually support.
summary.tldr: Accurate predictions and persuasive explanations do not establish a mechanism when incompatible mechanisms fit the same observations.

abstract: Distributed reinforcement learning (DRL) has been studied as an approach to learn control policies thorough interactions between distributed agents and environments. The main emphasis of DRL has been put on the way to learn sub-optimal policies with the least or limited sharing of agents' perceptions. In this study, we introduce a new concept, privacy-preservation, into DRL. In our setting, agents' perceptions, such as states, rewards, and actions, are not only distributed but also are desired to be kept private. This can occur when agents' perceptions include private or confidential information. Conventional DRL algorithms could be applied to such problems, but do not theoretically guarantee privacy preservation. We design solutions that achieve optimal policies in standard reinforcement leering settings without requiring the agents to share their private information by means of well-known cryptographic primitive, secure function evaluation.

paragraphs: Distributed reinforcement learning involves agents learning control policies through interactions with environments. Earlier work emphasized obtaining useful policies while limiting how much agents share about their experiences. This paper adds a stronger requirement: states, rewards, and actions may contain confidential information that agents want to keep private.

Limiting communication alone does not provide a theoretical privacy guarantee. The authors therefore formulate privacy preservation as an explicit part of the distributed learning problem. This shifts attention to whether the necessary joint learning computations can be performed without requiring agents to disclose their private information to one another.

Their solutions use secure function evaluation, a cryptographic primitive for computing with private inputs. In standard reinforcement learning settings, the proposed constructions achieve optimal policies without requiring the agents to share those private inputs. The contribution connects the learning objective with a cryptographic mechanism, showing how policy optimization and the stated privacy requirement can be addressed together in the considered settings.
summary.tldr: Secure function evaluation allows distributed agents to learn optimal policies in standard settings without sharing their private states, rewards, or actions.

title: Privacy-preserving reinforcement learning

abstract: We propose a nonparametric extension to the factor analysis problem using a beta process prior. This beta process factor analysis (BP-FA) model allows for a dataset to be decomposed into a linear combination of a sparse set of factors, providing information on the underlying structure of the observations. As with the Dirichlet process, the beta process is a fully Bayesian conjugate prior, which allows for analytical posterior calculation and straightforward inference. We derive a variational Bayes inference algorithm and demonstrate the model on the MNIST handwritten digits and HGDP-CEPH cell line panel datasets.

This beta process factor analysis (BP-FA) model allows for a dataset to be decomposed into a linear combination of a sparse set of factors, providing information on the underlying structure of the observations. As with the Dirichlet process, the beta process is a fully Bayesian conjugate prior, which allows for analytical posterior calculation and straightforward inference. We derive a variational Bayes inference algorithm and demonstrate the model on the MNIST handwritten digits and HGDP-CEPH cell line panel datasets.

paragraphs: Factor analysis explains observations through combinations of underlying factors. This paper proposes a Bayesian nonparametric extension using a beta process prior, called beta process factor analysis. The model decomposes data into linear combinations of a sparse set of factors, providing a representation of structure underlying the observed measurements.

Sparsity is central to that representation: the decomposition emphasizes a limited set of contributing factors. The beta process supplies the Bayesian prior underlying the extension. The authors highlight its conjugacy, which supports analytical posterior calculations and straightforward inference. This connects the modeling choice to the practical problem of learning the hidden factor structure from data.

The paper derives a variational Bayes inference algorithm and demonstrates the model on MNIST handwritten digits and the HGDP-CEPH cell line panel. These applications show the proposed factor representation being used with two different datasets. The contribution combines a sparse nonparametric model with an explicit inference procedure, making the proposed decomposition something that can be fitted to observations.
summary.tldr: Beta process factor analysis provides a Bayesian nonparametric model for sparse linear factor decompositions, with variational inference and dataset demonstrations.

title: Nonparametric factor analysis with beta process priors

abstract: We consider finite horizon Markov decision processes under performance measures that involve both the mean and the variance of the cumulative reward. We show that either randomized or history-based policies can improve performance. We prove that the complexity of computing a policy that maximizes the mean reward under a variance constraint is NP-hard for some cases, and strongly NP-hard for others. We finally offer pseudo-polynomial exact and approximation algorithms.
originalAbstract: We consider finite horizon Markov decision processes under performance measures that involve both the mean and the variance of the cumulative reward. We show that either randomized or history-based policies can improve performance. We prove that the complexity of computing a policy that maximizes the mean reward under a variance constraint is NP-hard for some cases, and strongly NP-hard for others. We finally offer pseudo-polynomial exact and approximation algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies finite-horizon Markov decision processes where performance depends on both the average cumulative reward and its variance. Considering variance changes the objective: two policies with similar expected rewards may differ in how variable their outcomes are. One problem examined is maximizing expected reward while imposing a constraint on that variability.

The authors show that randomizing decisions or using the history of the process can improve performance. These are possibility results: they establish that such policy choices can matter, without claiming that every problem requires them. The findings make the policy class part of the optimization issue, because restricting how decisions are made can exclude better mean-variance tradeoffs.

The paper also establishes computational difficulty. Finding a policy that maximizes the mean under a variance constraint is NP-hard in some cases and strongly NP-hard in others. Alongside these hardness results, the authors offer pseudo-polynomial exact algorithms and approximation algorithms. The contribution therefore combines an account of useful policy flexibility with complexity results and algorithmic approaches.
summary.tldr: Mean-variance objectives can benefit from randomized or history-based policies, but optimizing them is computationally hard in the cases analyzed.

title: Mean-Variance Optimization in Markov Decision Processes
Cognitive Economy in a Fluid Task Environment
